MODULES.title: From Requirements to Constraints
MODULES.tag: Six numbers turn a vague AI ask into something you can actually design against
MODULES.why: The architecture was decided in the kickoff meeting, before anyone drew a box — you just weren't shown the decision. A sentence like "add AI search to the portal" carries no constraints, so every person in the room silently fills the blanks with their own, and two quarters later you discover you all built different products. Six numbers, written down and sourced, eliminate most of the design space in an afternoon and give you something to defend a diagram with.
MODULES.mental: Requirements arrive as an index card with six blanks: quality bar, latency budget, cost ceiling, volume, blast radius, freshness. Until every blank carries a number and a source, you are not architecting — you are guessing with vocabulary. Every later module in this course spends this card. Fill it, or don't draw anything.
concepts: Thresholds, not booleans

Requirements for probabilistic systems are thresholds on distributions. "It should be accurate" is unarchitectable. "At least 92% on a 300-case golden set, abstaining on 8% or less" eliminates three architectures before you draw a box, because it names a measurement, a set, a bar, and an escape valve.
The six fields

Quality bar plus the measurement that defines it; p95 latency plus interaction mode; cost per task and per month; volume as steady plus peak multiplier; blast radius; freshness tolerance. Six is the minimum set that determines a shape — with five, the shape is still ambiguous, and you'll find out which one was missing during load testing.
Source, not just number

Every number carries who said it and what would falsify it. A latency budget invented by the architect is a preference; one derived from an abandonment curve is a constraint. Unsourced numbers get renegotiated the first time they become inconvenient, which is always the week before launch.
The three-question elicitation

Who is harmed by a wrong answer; what does the user do in the next ten seconds; what does the status quo cost per task today. Three questions a PM can answer without an engineer translating, and they fill five of the six fields.
Blast radius

The worst single wrong output, written as one concrete sentence about one specific user. This field, not the ask, picks the architecture: it decides whether you owe the system a verification seam, an abstention path, or a human in the loop — and each of those is a rung you have to climb and pay for.
The impossible triangle

Quality, latency and cost: name the one you are formally refusing to optimise, and get it signed. The requirement you decline to meet is itself a requirements artifact. Declining in writing costs an awkward meeting; declining silently costs an incident review.
Falsification pass

For each number, write what evidence would show it is wrong and who owns that evidence. Numbers that survive a falsification pass survive design review. Numbers that don't were opinions wearing a decimal point, and they will move under pressure.
mistakes: Accepting "it should be accurate" and quietly translating it into your own private threshold
Writing the latency budget as an average, then meeting it while the p95 is four times worse
Costing per model call when the unit that has to close is the task, which may be seven calls
Filling the card alone, so the first stakeholder review re-opens every number from scratch
Treating blast radius as a compliance checkbox instead of the field that selects the shape
flags: "Just make it accurate" — no measurement, no set, no threshold, no abstention allowance
"It has to feel real-time" — no number, and nobody has checked what users actually tolerate
"It should handle anything a customer asks" — unbounded scope against a bounded budget
"We'll work out the cost after launch" — the unit economics were never modelled at all
"Legal signed off on the demo" — blast radius assessed against a scripted happy path
ask: What measurement, on what set, at what threshold, decides that this works?
What does the user do in the ten seconds after the system is confidently wrong?
What does the status quo cost per task today, in money or in minutes?
Which of quality, latency and cost are we formally refusing to optimise, and who signed that?
How stale can an answer be before it stops being annoying and starts being harmful?

MODULES.title: Cost, Latency & Reliability Budgets
MODULES.tag: Every box in your diagram debits three accounts, and you only get to overdraw once
MODULES.why: Nobody argues with a diagram. Everybody argues with a number. Budgets are how an architecture stops being a matter of taste: once each stage has a millisecond, cent and reliability allocation, "let's add a verification step" becomes a subtraction anyone in the room can check, and it either fits or it doesn't. Teams that skip this step don't avoid the arithmetic — they just do it after launch, in an incident channel, with a customer watching.
MODULES.mental: Every request carries three envelopes: milliseconds, cents, and nines. Every stage you add debits all three, and none of them refill. Architecture is deciding who gets to spend — and the discipline is that you allocate down from the SLO, never sum up from whatever you happened to build.
concepts: Top-down allocation

Start at the number you promised, subtract the fixed floors, and what remains is the entire allowance for cleverness. Summing bottom-up from what you already built produces a number, but it is a description of your system, not a budget — and a description can never fail.
Fixed floors

Network round trips, index lookups, and output-token generation time are not negotiable by design cleverness. Subtract them first. On an interactive surface they frequently eat half the budget, and knowing that before you design stops you allocating money you never had.
Reliability composes multiplicatively

Five stages at 99.5% is 97.5% end to end, not 99.5%. Every box you add is a tax on the product of the chain, which is why box count is a reliability decision and not just an elegance one. The arithmetic is unforgiving and it never gets mentioned in a design review.
You may not sum p95s

Stages do not have their bad day simultaneously. Summing p95s systematically over-states the real p95 — often by 15-25% — so it isn't just wrong, it silently deletes architecture options you could have afforded. Compose with a root-sum-square of the spreads, or simulate.
Availability and correctness are two budgets

Did it answer, and was it right. Classic systems only need the first. Conflating them is precisely why quality regressions have no error budget, no alert, and no owner — the dashboard is green while the product is wrong.
Cost per task, not per call

A task may be seven calls, plus retries, plus the ones that failed and were paid for anyway. Per-call cost is an accounting number. Per-task cost is the number the unit economics close or fail against, and it is the only one worth putting on a slide.
Budget the p95 cost, not the mean

Retries and variable output length give cost a fat tail. A mean of $0.057 with a p95 of $0.097 means one task in twenty costs 70% more than you modelled — at scale, that tail is the difference between a margin and a surprise.
mistakes: Summing p95 latencies to get an end-to-end p95, then designing against a number that's 20% pessimistic
Quoting per-stage availability in a review when only the composed product is real
Modelling cost on the happy path, excluding retries, failures, and the abandoned partial tasks you still paid for
Having an availability error budget and no correctness error budget, so quality regressions page nobody
Building bottom-up, then reverse-engineering an SLO that your existing latency happens to satisfy
flags: "Our p95 is the sum of the stage p95s" — the composition is wrong in a knowable direction
"Each service is three nines" — nobody has multiplied them together in front of the room
"It costs about two cents a call" — the task is six calls and nobody has said so
"Quality dipped last month" — said calmly, because no error budget was ever burned
"We'll add a verification pass" — proposed with no subtraction from any envelope
ask: What are the fixed floors on this surface, and what's actually left to allocate?
What's the composed availability — the product, not the best stage in the chain?
What does a task cost at p95, including retries and the failures we pay for anyway?
Which stage do we cut first if the budget halves, and has anyone written that down?
What burns the correctness error budget, and who gets paged when it's gone?

MODULES.title: System Shapes: Picking the Architecture
MODULES.tag: Six reference shapes, and the spec-card fact that picks between them
MODULES.why: There are not a hundred AI architectures. There are about six, and the interesting question was never which one is best — it's which one your spec card lets you get away with. Most production disappointment traces back to a team that climbed two rungs higher than they needed for a reason nobody wrote down, and now can't tell whether the reason still holds.
MODULES.mental: Six rungs on a shape ladder, each roughly an order of magnitude more expensive to operate than the last: single call → prompt chain → retrieval read path → single-agent tool loop → orchestrator-worker → offline batch pipeline. You climb only when a specific number on the spec card forces you to, and you write down which number it was. That sentence is the whole module.
concepts: The lowest feasible rung

Your job is not the most capable architecture, it's the least capable one that clears the card. Capability you don't need still costs you: operate burden, failure surface, observability spend, and the review time of everyone who inherits it.
Forcing constraint

The specific spec-card number that made the rung below infeasible, recorded next to the decision. Without it, the choice can never be re-litigated — and constraints change constantly, so an architecture with no recorded forcing constraint is one nobody is allowed to simplify.
Operate cost, not build cost

The ladder is ordered by what a shape costs to own, not what it costs to write. A batch pipeline is the cheapest rung per task and the most expensive to run — backfills, reprocessing, freshness monitoring, and a schedule that pages someone.
Failure modes introduced

Each rung adds new ways to be wrong, not just more of the old ones. Climbing is a trade of one failure profile for another, and the profile you're taking on should appear in the decision record beside the capability you're buying.
Degradation behaviour

What the shape does when it cannot do its job. This is a selection criterion, not an afterthought: a shape whose degraded mode is "nothing" is a different product on its worst day than one that falls back to keyword results or yesterday's run.
Composite with contracts

Most real systems are three shapes, not one — commonly a batch pipeline feeding a read path with an escape hatch behind it. Draw them as separate shapes with an explicit contract on each seam, because the seams are where you'll be debugging.
The escape hatch is a budget line

The expensive rung you keep for the hard 3% is priced by how often it fires. If that share drifts from 3% to 25%, blended cost per task nearly doubles — so the hatch needs a rate cap and a dashboard, not just a condition.
mistakes: Climbing a rung for capability nobody on the card asked for, then owning it for three years
Choosing a shape from a conference talk rather than from the binding number on your own card
Recording the decision but not the forcing constraint, so nobody can ever safely simplify it
Drawing a composite system as one blob, hiding the seams that will produce most incidents
Ignoring operate cost because build cost was comparable — the headcount arrives later, quietly
flags: "We went with agents because it's more flexible" — flexibility is not a spec-card field
"Nobody remembers why it's built this way" — the forcing constraint was never written down
"It's one system" — said about something with three distinct shapes and no named contracts
"We'll simplify it later" — no rung below has ever been re-tested against the current card
"The fallback path handles that" — nobody has measured what share of traffic the fallback takes
ask: Which number on the spec card made the rung below this one infeasible?
Is that number still true, and when did anyone last check?
What does this shape do on its worst day — what exactly does it degrade to?
How many people does it take to operate this, steady state, including the on-call?
What share of traffic takes the expensive path, and what's the cap when that drifts?

MODULES.title: Failure-Mode Architecture
MODULES.tag: AI systems fail with a 200 OK, so you enumerate the failures the status code hides
MODULES.why: Classic systems have the decency to fail loudly. A timeout throws, a null dereferences, a bad migration takes the pod down and pages you. AI systems' worst failures return successfully: a 200, a well-formed body, a confident paragraph, and a wrong answer that no runtime on earth will raise for you. Which means every failure class either has a detector you deliberately designed, or a structure that makes it impossible, or it is simply happening to your customers right now and you do not know. This module is the pre-build pass that decides which is which. You come out of it with a scored table, a design-change backlog, and the ability to answer the review question nobody in your org currently answers: how would we find out?
MODULES.mental:
Hold one picture for this whole module: the silent 200.

Every response your system emits leaves through the same door, wearing the same status code. The correct answer and the catastrophically wrong one are dressed identically. Your load balancer sees a 200. Your error rate is 0.02%. Your dashboards are green. And somewhere in the last hour, the system posted the wrong amount to a ledger, cited a contract clause that was superseded in March, and told a customer something that will cost you the account.

None of that raised. None of it ever will. The transport succeeded, and transport success is the only thing the runtime knows how to measure.

So the architecture has to supply what the runtime cannot: for every way this thing can be wrong, either a detector you designed on purpose, or a structure that makes the failure unreachable. There is no third option, and "we will monitor it" is not a detector — it is a promise to build one, and it only counts once you can name what the check compares against. The silent 200 is the reason failure-mode work moves from operations to architecture.
concepts: Detectability is the first column you fill, not the last

Most teams score severity and likelihood, argue about them, then bolt detection on at the end as an afterthought. Invert it. Detectability decides which of the three dispositions is even legal for a row, so it has to be established before anyone proposes a fix. A row you cannot observe cannot be mitigated — only redesigned or accepted — and knowing that up front saves the meeting.
The RPN you can actually defend

Severity x likelihood x detection-difficulty, each 1-10, all three scored higher-is-worse. Detection 1 means a deterministic check catches it before the response ships; detection 10 means only an angry customer can tell you. The absolute number is meaningless; the ranking is the product. Its real job is forcing three separate judgements into the open instead of letting one loud voice collapse them into a vibe.
Three dispositions, and only three

A rail is an inline gate that runs before the response ships and can block it. A sampler is an async scorer that tells you a rate, days later, on a fraction of traffic. An amputation is a design change that removes the surface the failure needs to exist. Detectability picks: detection 1-3 earns a rail, 4-7 earns a sampler, above 7 earns neither.
The undetectable-and-severe quadrant

High severity plus detection above 7 is the only quadrant with a forced move. You do not get to mitigate it, because a mitigation you cannot verify is a story you tell in review. The legal moves are a constrained output set, a restricted action, a schema the answer must satisfy, a deterministic lookup replacing a generated answer, or a human gate. All five shrink the surface; none of them are monitoring.
Linear modes you budget, compounding modes you cap

A per-row classification error is linear: eight rows, eight independent chances, and the arithmetic behaves. Drift, partial writes and context pollution are compounding: step three inherits step two's contamination, so its error rate is larger than step two's was. At a 4% base with 35% growth per step, eight steps is 72% chance of a bad step against a linear 28%. Compounding modes get a step ceiling, not a better prompt.
Severity is spec-card arithmetic, not a feeling

Severity comes straight off the blast-radius line of your spec card, converted to a number: how many customers, how much money, is it reversible, does it cross a tenant boundary, does it end up in a regulator's inbox. Two engineers who both start from the spec card converge on severity within a point. Two engineers who start from intuition argue for forty minutes and land wherever the senior one was.
The table is a dated artifact with an owner

An FMEA that lives in someone's head is a conversation. One with a date, an owner, a row count, and a linked design-change backlog is an architectural commitment you can be held to, and re-run against on the next provider bump or feature expansion. Rescore it when the action surface widens, when volume crosses an order of magnitude, or when a new failure mode shows up in the wild.
mistakes: Scoring severity and likelihood carefully and leaving detection at a hand-wave, which is exactly the column that decides what you are allowed to do about the row
Answering an undetectable high-severity row with "we will add an alert", which commits you to a detector nobody has designed and quietly closes the row
Ranking purely by severity, so a 10-severity once-a-year row eats the quarter while a 6-severity daily invisible one ships to production untouched
Treating the FMEA as a launch checklist rather than a living register, so the action surface widens three times and the table is never rescored
Assuming failure rates compose linearly across a multi-step flow, which understates every mode where a step inherits the previous step's output
flags: "Error rate is 0.02%" offered as evidence of quality, when the only thing measured is whether the transport succeeded
A risk register where every row's mitigation is a dashboard, an alert, or a metric, and none is a change to what the system can produce
Nobody can answer "how would we find out?" for the top-severity failure mode without saying the word "customer"
The word "monitoring" appearing in a design doc before any detector has been specified in terms of what it compares against
A multi-step flow whose per-step accuracy is quoted and whose end-to-end accuracy has never been computed
ask: For our worst failure mode, what is the detector, what does it compare the output against, and how many minutes until it fires?
Which rows on this table can only be discovered by a customer telling us, and what design change is queued for each?
Which of our failure modes compound per step, and what caps the step count?
When was this table last rescored, and what changed in the system since then?
If this exact failure happened at 09:00 today, what is the first artifact that would show it, and who is looking at that artifact?

MODULES.title: Blast Radius & Autonomy Tiers
MODULES.tag: Every action the system can take is an action an attacker can trigger
MODULES.why: There is a question that decides more about your system's safety than any control you will ever add, and most design docs never ask it: if one model turn were fully compromised — every instruction in it written by someone hostile — what is the worst thing that turn could do? Not "how do we stop that from happening." Assume it happened. Read the answer out loud. If it makes the room go quiet, you have a design problem, and no amount of prompt hardening is going to fix it, because you cannot patch your way out of a capability you granted. This module inventories the action surface, assigns each path an autonomy tier, and then does the arithmetic that turns tiers from a governance nicety into an engineering lever — one that is frequently worth more than a model upgrade you cannot buy.
MODULES.mental:
The image for this module is the bulkheads.

A ship does not survive a hull breach because the hull is strong. It survives because the hull is divided. Water comes in, floods one compartment, and stops — not because anyone talked it out of spreading, but because a steel wall is there and water does not negotiate with steel. The compartment boundary is a structural fact, decided in a shipyard years before the iceberg.

Your system survives a bad generation the same way. Not because the generation was good, and not because a rail talked it down, but because the set of actions reachable from that generation was bounded by structure — a token that does not carry the scope, an allowlist resolved from data the attacker never touched, an operation that requires a second human. Structure, not persuasion.

The design question follows directly. You do not ask how strong the hull is. You ask where the walls are, and you keep moving them inward until the answer to "what floods" is boring. A prompt is a request. A bulkhead is a fact.
concepts: Capability is privilege, and privilege is a design decision

The moment a tool is in the model's reach, it is in the reach of anything that can influence the model's context — which includes every document, email, ticket and web page that flows in. So the security question is not defensive, it is inventory: what is the complete set of actions a turn can take, who authorised each one, and what is the union of their effects. That set is what you design against, and it only shrinks by removing things from it.
The four autonomy tiers

Suggest, draft-with-approval, act-with-undo, act-irreversibly. These are not a maturity ladder to climb — they are a placement decision per action path, made from what a wrong answer costs. Most systems have several tiers running at once, and the mistake is granting one tier to a whole feature rather than to each individual write path. The tier is a property of the action, not the product.
Required correctness is a function of reversibility

This is the module's central arithmetic. Fix your tolerance for bad actions per month and your volume, and each tier implies a per-generation accuracy requirement. At 20,000 actions a month and a tolerance of four, acting irreversibly demands 99.98%, act-with-undo demands 99.90%, approval-gated demands 99.60%, and suggest-only demands 93.3%. A tier demotion is a model improvement you cannot purchase, and it ships this week.
Containment primitives you actually place

Four that earn their keep: capability tokens scoped narrower than the invoking user, so a compromised turn cannot do what the human could; idempotency keys plus compensating actions, so a retry is safe and a mistake is undoable; dual control on irreversible operations, so one bad turn is not sufficient; and allowlisted egress, so bytes can only leave to destinations chosen before the untrusted content arrived. Each is a wall, not an argument.
Isolation has to survive the cache, the trace and the log

Tenant boundaries are usually enforced at the query and forgotten everywhere else. A semantic cache keyed on question text will happily serve tenant A's answer to tenant B, and that answer will look completely correct — which is exactly why it is a reportable event and not a bug report. Carry the tenant identifier into every cache key, trace attribute and log line, then test the boundary from both sides.
The trifecta test, in one line

Private data reachable, untrusted content reachable, egress capability present — all three inside the same turn is an escalation path, regardless of how good the rails are. Say it as a single question in review: can this turn read something valuable, read something an attacker wrote, and send bytes somewhere? If yes, break one leg or write down that you are accepting it.
The worst-case sentence

For every action path, one sentence written in plain language: what happens if this fires wrongly, at the worst moment, on the largest account. "There is no unsend" is a sentence that changes budgets. "Recoverable in a click" is a sentence that unblocks a launch. The inventory is only useful when every row has one, and the exercise of writing them is where half the tier demotions get discovered.
mistakes: Designing against prompt injection as the threat, rather than designing so a fully compromised turn is boring, which is the only version of the goal you can actually achieve
Granting an autonomy tier to a feature instead of to each write path, so one low-stakes justification carries a high-stakes action along with it
Handing the agent a service token with the invoking user's full scope, when the turn needs three operations and the user can perform three hundred
Enforcing tenant isolation in the query layer only, leaving the cache, trace store and logs as a boundary that was never actually drawn
Retrying a non-idempotent action after a timeout, converting an ambiguous failure into a confirmed duplicate side effect
flags: Nobody in the room can list every action the system can take without opening the code, which means the action surface has never been designed, only accumulated
"The model would never do that" offered as a control, with no experiment behind it and no consequence if it turns out to be false
An agent whose tools include both a reader of customer-supplied text and anything that sends, posts or pays, with no boundary named between them
Undo described as "we can restore from backup", which is a recovery procedure and not a reversibility class
Autonomy described as a roadmap milestone ("fully autonomous by Q3") rather than as a per-action decision derived from what wrong costs
ask: If a single turn were entirely attacker-authored, what is the worst thing it could do, in one sentence?
Which token does this action execute with, and is its scope narrower than the human who triggered it?
Which of our actions are genuinely irreversible, and what would it take to demote each one a tier?
Where does untrusted text enter the context, and what is the shortest path from there to something that sends bytes outward?
How is the tenant identifier carried through the cache key, the trace and the log, and who has tested that boundary from the other side?

MODULES.title: Capacity, Saturation & the Degradation Ladder
MODULES.tag: What your system does at 10x is a design decision, not an emergent property
MODULES.why: Every system has a behaviour at ten times its normal load. Yours has one right now. The only question is whether anybody chose it, or whether it is going to be revealed to you at 09:14 on a Monday by a queue nobody sized and a provider quota nobody negotiated. Capacity for AI systems is not a CPU problem — it is a quota-and-concurrency problem, and the arithmetic is unusually tractable: tokens per task, tasks per second, a peak multiplier, a service time, and Little's Law. Do it in an afternoon and you get a number to negotiate with, a worker pool that is right rather than lucky, and the artifact this module actually exists to produce: a written ladder of degraded states, each one signed off by the person who owns the customer relationship, before anyone needs it.
MODULES.mental:
The image is the brownout ladder.

Power grids do not go from on to off. When supply cannot meet demand, the operator walks down a pre-agreed sequence: voltage reduction first, then interruptible industrial customers, then rotating blocks — each rung defined years in advance, each with a named authority who signed it, each with a known and accepted consequence. Nobody invents a rung at 3am. The decisions were made in daylight, by people who understood what each one costs, and the night shift's job is to execute the ladder, not to design it.

Your system needs exactly that, and almost certainly does not have it. What it has instead is a queue somebody added to absorb bursts, a timeout that fires at an arbitrary number, and an implicit final rung — fall over — that nobody wrote down and nobody authorised.

So write the ladder. Five rungs, each with a trigger, what turns off, what the customer sees, what the quality delta is, and who pre-authorised it. Every rung you have not written is a rung someone will improvise at 3am, and improvised rungs are how an outage becomes an incident.
concepts: Capacity is the smaller of your fleet and your quota

Your worker pool sets one ceiling and the provider's tokens-per-minute and requests-per-minute grants set another, and the binding constraint is whichever is lower. Teams size the fleet carefully and discover the quota during the incident. Compute both numbers, in the same units, on the same page — tasks per minute — and put the min() in the design doc, because that is your real capacity and nothing else is.
Required throughput comes straight off the spec card

Volume times tokens per task gives you tokens per minute, and the only subtlety is that output tokens usually count for more against a throughput meter than input tokens do. Carry an output weight as a parameter, apply the peak multiplier from the spec card, add headroom, and you have the number you take to a quota negotiation — which has a lead time, and therefore belongs on the schedule, not in the launch week.
Little's Law sizes the pool before you guess at it

L = lambda x W. Arrival rate times time in system gives the number of tasks in flight, and that is the floor on concurrency — not a target, a floor. At 3.7 tasks a second and 9 seconds each, 33 things are in flight at all times. Any pool smaller than 34 cannot keep up at all, and a pool of exactly 34 is running at 98% utilisation, which is a different kind of disaster.
The queueing cliff

Wait time is not linear in utilisation, it is asymptotic. Same load, same service time, only the worker count changing: 42 workers gives 79% utilisation and a 0.11 second wait; 36 workers gives 93% and 1.86 seconds; 34 gives 98% and 11.7 seconds. Six workers moved and the wait went up a hundredfold. Above roughly 80%, utilisation stops being an efficiency metric and becomes a latency risk.
A queue without admission control makes p95 worse for everyone

This is the counter-intuitive one. A queue added to absorb bursts does not create capacity; it converts rejection into waiting, and it distributes that waiting across every user including the ones who would otherwise have been served instantly. If arrivals exceed service rate, backlog grows without bound and every request inherits the whole accumulated delay. A queue is only a lever when it has a depth cap and an admission rule that refuses honestly at the boundary.
Four levers, four different customer costs

Shed refuses some requests entirely so the rest stay fast. Queue makes everyone wait so nobody is refused. Degrade serves everyone at lower quality. Borrow moves traffic to a second provider or a smaller model, paying in cost or in quality. They are not interchangeable and they are not ranked — they trade different currencies, and choosing between them at 3am with a director on the call is how an outage becomes an incident.
The rung is only real when it has all five fields

Trigger, what gets disabled, what the customer sees, the quality delta, and the named pre-authorizer. Four fields is a suggestion. The fifth is the one that makes it executable at 3am, because the on-call engineer is not authorised to decide that support answers get worse tonight — but they are authorised to execute a rung that the VP of Support signed in March.
mistakes: Sizing the worker fleet from latency requirements and discovering the provider quota is the binding constraint during the first real peak
Adding a queue to absorb bursts with no depth cap and no admission rule, which converts a fast failure for a few into a slow failure for everyone
Targeting high utilisation as an efficiency win, when above roughly 80% the queueing curve turns the last few points of utilisation into most of your p95
Writing a degradation plan with a trigger and an action but no named pre-authorizer, so the on-call engineer at 3am has a runbook they are not empowered to execute
Treating failover as a pure capacity lever when the failover target has never been evaluated on your task, which turns a capacity incident into an undetected quality incident
flags: Nobody can state the system's tokens-per-minute ceiling from memory, which means it has never been compared against the peak the spec card already predicted
"We added a queue" offered as the answer to a load problem, with no depth cap, no admission rule, and no statement of what happens when the queue is full
A degradation plan that goes straight from fully working to an error page, with no rungs in between and no quality delta stated for any of them
Failover configured to a provider or model that has never been run against the golden set, so the save silently degrades quality instead of preserving it
Peak multipliers described qualitatively ("Mondays are busy") when the spec card already carries a number that could have been multiplied through weeks ago
ask: What is our tokens-per-minute ceiling today, and what multiple of our observed peak is it?
At what utilisation does our worker pool run at peak, and what is the wait time two points above that?
If the queue fills, what happens - and is that behaviour written down or is it whatever the runtime does by default?
Which rung of the degradation ladder are we authorised to pull without waking anyone, and who signed it?
Has the failover target been run against the golden set, and what was the quality delta?

MODULES.title: Seams, Substitution & the Real Cost of Buying
MODULES.tag: You aren't choosing a vendor, you're choosing how expensive it will be to stop
MODULES.why: Every vendor decision cuts a seam into your system, and the seam decides what leaving costs, not the contract and not the price sheet. Teams argue unit price and feature grids for six weeks, sign, and then discover the number that mattered was engineer-weeks to unwind. This module makes that number computable before you commit, so "we're locked in" becomes a figure you chose rather than one you found out.
MODULES.mental: Every vendor decision cuts a seam into your system, the surface where their thing meets yours. Where you put that seam, and how much of your behaviour crosses it, is your exit cost. There is no other number. Not the contract, not the discount, not the feature grid, the seam. So stop asking which vendor is better and start asking where the cut goes and how many engineer-weeks it takes to reopen it.
concepts: Exit cost, in engineer-weeks

The unit that makes vendor arguments finishable. Four lines: distinct behaviours you rely on times hours to port each, data egress, re-derivation compute (re-embedding, index builds), and eval revalidation. Quote weeks first and money second, because cash you can find on short notice and calendar you cannot. Under two weeks is not lock-in. Over ten is a strategic commitment that deserves a signature, not a procurement ticket.
Coupling points, not call sites

Exit cost scales with the number of distinct behaviours you depend on, not the number of lines that call them. Thirty-one call sites through three methods is a three-point seam. Fourteen call sites each using a different filter dialect, scoring knob, pagination rule and error convention is a fourteen-point seam. Count behaviours during the audit, or you will size a migration with find-and-replace arithmetic and be wrong by more than 4x.
The seam ladder

Four places to cut, cheapest exit first. Config seam: the vendor is a value in a file and the swap is a deploy. Protocol seam: you speak a shape more than one vendor implements (OpenAI-compatible endpoints, MCP servers) and the vendor is whoever answers. Adapter seam: your interface, their implementation, you own the translation and its upkeep. Data seam: their storage holds state you cannot re-derive, the most expensive rung and the one teams reach by accident rather than choice.
The portability test

One question, asked before signing rather than at renewal: what must I keep if I leave? An honest answer names artifacts, not intentions, golden sets, labelled traces, judge rubrics, prompt and schema history, tenant mappings, ACL snapshots. Anything on that list that lives only inside a vendor's tenancy is an exit-cost line item nobody has priced yet. The test takes ten minutes and routinely changes the answer.
The asymmetric rule, and why evals are the hinge

Buy things whose output is portable, build things whose data is yours. A managed index emits documents and vectors you already had, so buy it. Golden sets, labelled failures and domain judge rubrics encode judgments nobody else can regenerate, so build and hold them. Evals are the hinge: you cannot swap what you cannot compare, so a suite that runs only inside a vendor's platform makes substitution unmeasurable, and nobody authorises an unmeasurable swap. Eval ownership is a portability decision before it is ever a quality decision.
Carrying cost of a clean seam

Abstractions are not free and their bill arrives annually: tracking vendor features you deliberately excluded, running a conformance suite against a second implementation, explaining the indirection to every new hire. Price it in engineer-weeks per year, divide the exit saving by it, and you get the honest figure, the number of months inside which leaving repays the wrapper. Past that month, the raw call sites were the correct architecture and saying so out loud is the senior move.
The union abstraction

The characteristic failure: an interface that is the union of two vendors' feature sets. It exposes everything both of them do, so it leaks both, and it forbids nothing, so it buys no portability, you have paid carrying cost for an option that was never created. A real seam is an intersection plus an explicit decision about what you give up. If you cannot name what your abstraction forbids, it is not a seam, it is a second SDK with your logo on it.
mistakes: Arguing unit price for six weeks and never once computing engineer-weeks to leave
Sizing the port by call sites, so a fourteen-behaviour seam gets estimated as a three-day find-and-replace
Letting the vendor hold the golden set and the labelled traces, the two artifacts that make any future swap measurable
Counting re-derivation compute and forgetting revalidation, which is usually the larger half of the number
Shipping an abstraction that is the union of two vendors' features, paying carry for an option it never actually created
flags: "It's just an API call, we can swap it in a day", nobody has priced re-embedding the corpus
"We'll abstract it later", later is after the fortieth call site and the filter dialect
"Their benchmark shows parity", on whose traffic, scored by whose judge, against which of your suites?
"We're not locked in, there's an export button", an export format is not a re-derivation plan
"The wrapper is basically free", then it has no owner, and in eight months it has no tests
ask: What must we keep if we leave this vendor next year? Name the artifacts, not the intentions.
How many distinct behaviours of theirs do we depend on, and who actually counted them?
Who holds the golden set and the labelled traces, us or them?
What is this wrapper's carrying cost in engineer-weeks per year, and how many months until leaving repays it?
Have we ever run one of our own suites against a second implementation? What did that cost, in hours?

MODULES.title: State, Truth & Freshness Architecture
MODULES.tag: Where does truth live, and how long may a copy of it be wrong?
MODULES.why: Every index, embedding, cache, summary and memory file in your system is a copy of something that lives somewhere else, and every copy is wrong for some interval. Teams architect the copies carefully and the intervals not at all, which is why a large share of "the AI said something wrong" incidents are stale-mirror incidents diagnosed as model incidents, for weeks. This module makes the interval a designed, written, auditable number.
MODULES.mental: Every index, embedding, cache, summary and memory file is a mirror of some system of record, and every mirror is wrong for some interval. Architecture is choosing that interval on purpose and making it visible. You do not get to choose whether your mirrors lag. You choose the lag, you write it down, and you make the system say so when it is exceeded.
concepts: AI systems are derived-data systems

The architectural unit is not the store, it is the contract between the system of record and each derived copy. Seven fields, every time: source, maximum staleness, invalidation trigger, rebuild time, rebuild cost, tenant partition key, deletion path. A store without those seven declared is not designed, it is accumulated, and it will be discovered during an incident or an audit rather than during a review.
The freshness contract

Maximum staleness is a promise made against the spec card's freshness tolerance, and it must be measured, not aspirational. The measurement is trivial and almost nobody takes it: compare the derived store's last successful write timestamp to the source's, continuously, and emit the gap as a metric. A contract you cannot observe being violated is a comment, and comments do not page anyone at 03:00.
Invalidation trigger vs damage bound

These get conflated and the difference is the whole discipline. A change-data-capture stream or a scheduled sweep detects that a mirror is wrong. A time-to-live only bounds how long you stay wrong without ever noticing. Both are legitimate, and a TTL is often the right call, but a register that records a TTL in the invalidation column is telling you a store has no invalidation path at all.
Stale-mirror incidents

The dominant misdiagnosis in production AI. Output is wrong, the model is the interesting component, so three weeks go into prompts and retrieval tuning while an index sits nine hours behind its source. Fix the diagnostic order instead: before anyone opens a prompt, compare last-successful-rebuild to last-source-write for every store in the answer path. It is a thirty-second check that resolves a surprising share of quality regressions.
Deletion fan-out

A deletion request must arrive at the index, every cache tier, the agent memory file, the trace store and the eval fixtures. Trace one real record through the whole graph and count the survivors. That count is simultaneously a compliance finding and an architecture diagram, which is why it is the single most useful hour you can spend on this. The stores with no expiry are the ones to fix first, not the index everyone is watching.
Re-index economics set your iteration rate

Units times tokens per unit times your embedder's rate, plus index-build hours, plus the engineer-hours to verify and re-baseline, gives cost per full re-derivation. Divide your annual budget by it and you get how many times a year you are allowed to change your mind. The surprise is always the same: people expense dominates, embedding is rounding error, and the answer is two or three, one of which is spent on a mandatory model upgrade.
Dual-index cutover and resumable rebuilds

Rebuild time greater than your outage budget means you cannot rebuild in place, so you build beside and swap an alias, which creates a bounded window in which two indexes both claim to be true. Bound it, name it in the register, and make the rebuild idempotent and resumable by content hash so a crash at 80% costs minutes rather than the whole run. This is the price of being allowed to change your mind at all.
mistakes: Designing the derived stores carefully and the staleness intervals not at all, so nobody can say how wrong a copy is allowed to be
Recording a TTL in the invalidation column, which means the store has no invalidation path and the register is quietly lying
Diagnosing a stale-mirror incident as a model incident, and spending three weeks on prompts while an index sits nine hours behind
Building the deletion path to the index and stopping there, while memory files and eval fixtures keep the record forever
Discovering re-index cost during the sprint that proposed a new chunking strategy, rather than during the roadmap that promised four of them
flags: "The index updates in near real time", near what, measured how, and what does the graph look like at 09:00 Monday?
"We honour deletions, it's a delete-by-filter on the index", name the other six stores
"The cache has a 24-hour TTL so we're fine", that is a damage bound, not an invalidation path
"We'll re-chunk next quarter and see if it helps", with which of your two annual re-derivations?
"Nobody has ever complained about stale data", nobody can distinguish stale data from a wrong answer, that's the problem
ask: For every store in the answer path: what is the measured gap between its last write and the source's, right now?
Which derived stores have no invalidation trigger, and which of those never expire?
Walk me through a deletion request. How many stores does it reach, and how many hold the data afterwards?
What does one full re-derivation cost, and how many can we afford this year after the mandatory model upgrade?
How long is the two-truths window during a cutover, and what reads from the old index during it?

MODULES.title: Migration & Rollout Architecture
MODULES.tag: The model will change under you, design so that's a Tuesday, not a project
MODULES.why: In a field with quarterly turnover, the model you launched on will be deprecated, superseded, or repriced while you are still reading its release notes. Teams treat each swap as a project, budget it as a project, and are surprised every quarter. The architectural question is not how to migrate. It is what property the system needs so that migrating is configuration, and what evidence a given change is required to produce before it is allowed to be believed.
MODULES.mental: You never switch. You run both and let evidence decide. The architecture that can run two versions side by side on real traffic, and measure the difference at a stated resolution, is the one that gets to change its mind cheaply. Everything in this module is downstream of that one image: the dual-run, and the sample size that makes it mean something.
concepts: Migration capability is an architectural property

Not an ops task, not a ticket. The test is blunt: can you route 5% of traffic to a second version, and revert, without a deploy? If either half needs code, migration is a project every time and you will do it four times a year forever. Shadow, canary and instant revert belong in configuration, backfills belong in idempotent resumable jobs, and the whole capability gets exercised on a schedule whether or not you need it.
The migration ladder and its blind spots

Each rung buys evidence and each rung is blind to something specific. Offline eval only knows the cases you wrote, so it misses distribution shift entirely. Shadow runs on real inputs but nobody acts on the output, so it misses user-behaviour change while cleanly catching schema, latency and cost surprises. Canary catches both and is slow on rare failures. Choosing a rung is choosing what you have agreed not to know, so say the sentence out loud.
Sample size is the rollout plan

Given a baseline and the smallest regression you need to catch, the required sample per arm is fixed by arithmetic and the schedule falls out of it. It scales as 1 over the square of the effect, which is the fact that surprises people: halving the effect you want to detect quadruples the traffic and the days. So the minimum detectable effect is a negotiation, not an input, and when the calendar is short it is the honest lever, provided the sentence gets written down: we agreed not to detect a two-point drop, and this person signed for it. Undocumented, the same trade is just an optimistic schedule.
Rare failures need exposures, not percentages

A 1-in-2,000 failure is invisible to a canary sized for average quality. To be 95% confident of seeing at least one instance you need roughly three times the inverse of the rate in exposures, so about 6,000. A 5% canary on 40,000 tasks a day reaches that in three days and not in one. Percentages feel like coverage; only exposure counts are coverage, and the two diverge exactly where the dangerous failures live.
Rollback triggers are numbers with owners

Defined before rollout, not during: the metric, the threshold, the observation window, and the human who pulls it without convening anyone. "We'll roll back if it looks bad" is not a trigger, it is a hope with a passive voice. And rehearse it, in staging, on a schedule, because if you have never rolled back, you do not have rollback, you have a runbook nobody has executed under load.
Data migrations and the two-truths window

Index and embedding changes follow dual-write, backfill, verify, cutover, and the interesting question is how long two stores both claim to be true and who reads which one during it. Bound the window explicitly, make the backfill idempotent and resumable so a crash resumes, and verify on a sample before the alias moves rather than after the complaints.
The deprecation clock

Providers publish end-of-life dates and they do not move for you. Schedule backwards from the kill date through the ladder, the ramp and a buffer, and the start date falls out. Then run one migration per quarter whether or not you need one, because the muscle is the capability, and a team whose last swap was fourteen months ago will discover their eval set is stale exactly when the clock is shortest.
mistakes: Sizing a canary by percentage and duration that felt reasonable, rather than by the sample the detection target requires
Treating a clean shadow run as permission to go to 100%, when shadow is structurally blind to user-behaviour change
Writing rollback triggers after launch, so the first one is negotiated in a call while the metric is still moving
Letting the deprecation clock run for five weeks before starting, then buying the lost days back with resolution
Never rehearsing a rollback, so the first live execution is also the first time anyone has run the procedure
flags: "We'll canary at 5% for a few days", a few days sized against which detectable effect?
"Shadow looked clean, ship it", nobody clicked anything in shadow
"We'll roll back if it looks bad", name the metric, the number, the window and the person
"We have 60 days, plenty of time", the schedule runs backwards from the kill date, so start now
"Rollback is one flag flip", when did anyone last flip it, and was there traffic?
ask: What is the smallest quality regression this rollout is powered to detect, and what sample does that require?
How many exposures does the canary accumulate, and what failure rate does that make us blind to?
Which rung are we on, and what is that rung structurally unable to see?
What is the rollback number, what window is it measured over, and who pulls it without a meeting?
When did we last execute a rollback with real traffic, and what did it cost in minutes?

MODULES.title: Quality as an Architectural Property
MODULES.tag: Where the gates sit, what they're allowed to block, and who owns the number
MODULES.why: "We need better evals" is what every team says after being burned once, and the sentence contains no architecture: it doesn't say where a check sits, what it's permitted to stop, which budget line pays for it, or who gets woken when it fires. Quality in a running system isn't a score you possess, it's a set of places you built where something is authorized to say no, and every one of them is a line item you can price. This module turns that sentence into a diagram with numbers on it, which is the only form in which it survives a review.
MODULES.mental: Quality isn't a score your system has. It's a set of places in the system where something is authorized to say no, and architecture is choosing how many of those places exist, where they sit, and what each one is allowed to stop. Add a place and you spend milliseconds, dollars, and good answers wrongly blocked. Remove one and you buy the budget back and accept the escapes. The single most common defect in a quality design is a place that observes but cannot stop anything: a control point without an authority is a dashboard nobody reads.
concepts: Control point

A place, on the request path or beside it, where something is authorized to stop something else. You have five to choose from and a fixed budget to buy them with. The design question is never "do we have evals", it's "how many control points, sitting where, paid for out of which line?"
Authority

What a control point is permitted to do the moment it fires: block the release, block the request, block the response, open a ticket, or record only. Assign it explicitly, per control point, in writing. Record-only is a legitimate choice. It is not a legitimate accident.
Placement cost

Every control point is a line item in the latency and cost tables you built in Block 1. A synchronous check that adds 700ms against 400ms of headroom does not fit, and enthusiasm doesn't change that. Price it before you argue about it, because the argument ends the moment the arithmetic appears.
False-block rate

The share of good traffic a blocking control point wrongly stops. Rails have a cost curve in both directions: a 2% false block on a support flow is itself a support incident, paid in tickets rather than in tokens, and it's usually the larger of the two bills.
Detection lag

How long a new regression runs before anyone is paged. It's a division, not a vibe: alarm threshold over (daily volume x incidence x sampling rate x recognition rate). Choose the sampling rate by the lag it produces, never by whether the number is round.
Escaped-defect rate

The share of tasks that reach a user wrong after every blocking control point has had its chance. This is the number your spec card's quality bar is actually about. Detecting-only control points never lower it; they shorten how long it stays high, which is a different purchase.
Control-point ownership

Each control point needs a named owner, a page target, and a growth process, because checks decay in both directions. The golden set is a product artifact whose relevance expires as traffic moves, and the judge is a component that drifts, so the judge itself needs a control point watching it.
mistakes: Adding a control point without deciding its authority, so it ships as a score on a dashboard and has never stopped anything
Pricing a synchronous check in tokens when its dominant cost is false blocks, paid in support handling time
Choosing a sampling rate because the number is round (1%) instead of dividing it into the incidence rate you're trying to catch
Putting human review on the highest-volume flow, where it can't keep up, instead of the highest-blast-radius flow, where it's the only thing that works
Treating the judge and the golden set as infrastructure that stays correct on its own, with no owner, no growth process, and no control point watching them drift
flags: "We'll add an eval for that" - with no answer to where it sits, what it's allowed to block, or which budget line pays for it
"The gate is in CI" - and CI has been green on every release this year because the gate's authority is record-only
"We sample one percent" - a number chosen for its roundness and never once divided into an incidence rate
"The rail is only two percent false positives" - quoted as a small ratio, never multiplied by monthly volume or a ticket cost
"Quality is the AI team's problem" - the number has no owner on the product side, so nobody defends it when a launch date is at stake
ask: For each control point on this diagram: what is it allowed to block, and who gets paged when it fires?
How many milliseconds and how many dollars per task do our checks consume, and against how much headroom?
If quality regressed on half a percent of traffic this morning, how many days until someone is paged? Show me the division.
What is our false-block rate, and what does one false block cost us downstream?
Which failure mode on the FMEA has no control point, and which control point has no owner?

MODULES.title: Conway's Law for AI Platforms
MODULES.tag: You will ship the boundaries your org already has, so draw them on purpose
MODULES.why: You can design a beautiful set of seams and watch the org dissolve every one of them inside two quarters, because interfaces become handoffs between people and handoffs are where latency, drift and unowned artifacts live. The AI version is sharper than usual: the artifacts that decide how the system behaves - prompts, tool definitions, golden sets, judges, rails - are small, editable by anyone, and almost never appear in an ownership document. This module produces the two artifacts that fix that: a matrix naming who owns and who is paged for each, and a queue calculation giving you the quarter your central team stops being leverage and becomes the roadmap.
MODULES.mental: The seam is a team. Every interface you draw in the architecture becomes a handoff between people, so when you draw the system you have also drawn the org chart it will grow into, or the one that will quietly deform it back. The corollary is the useful part: if you don't like the org you'd get, redraw the seam, because the seam is the thing you actually control.
concepts: Drawing the seam on purpose

Conway's law is usually quoted as a warning. Treat it as a design input instead: pick the seams you want people organised around, then staff to them. The failure isn't that architecture mirrors the org, it's letting that happen by default and calling the result a strategy.
The platform/product split

Platform owns the choke points where consistency is worth a bottleneck: the model traffic choke point, key custody, the trace schema, eval infrastructure, safety rails. Product owns whatever must move at feature speed: prompts, tool definitions, retrieval tuning, golden sets, UX. Invert this and you get shadow spend on one side or a ticket queue on the other.
The ownership matrix

Ten artifacts against three columns: owner, approver, who gets paged. It fits on one page and every empty or doubled cell has a matching incident signature you can go and find in last quarter's incidents. It's the cheapest architecture document you will ever write.
Choke point

An artifact where consistency across teams is worth the cost of a bottleneck, because divergence is expensive or unrecoverable. Choke points take exactly one owner. Everything else can take several. Getting that rule backwards is the single most common org-design error in AI platforms.
Interface contract

What the platform guarantees, stated as an engineering artifact, and what a product team must supply to get it: required trace fields, a declared budget, an eval coverage threshold. Not a policy document, a schema plus a set of thresholds that a CI job can check.
Paved road

The version of the platform where the safe path is also the easy path, so nobody has to be persuaded. You measure a paved road by adoption, not compliance. 30% adoption after two quarters means the road is slower than the ditch, and that's a road problem.
The on-call split

A quality regression and an availability regression are different pages, need different skills, and usually belong to different rotations. Which rotation currently receives "the answers got worse" tells you what your ownership matrix really says, regardless of what's written in it.
mistakes: Putting the choke points in product teams (six sets of provider keys) and the fast-moving artifacts in the platform team (a prompt-change ticket queue), which is the split inverted on both axes
Writing an ownership matrix with an owner column and no paged column, so ownership means credit rather than a phone ringing
Starting a platform migration with the approval gate instead of the trace schema, which makes the platform a tax before it's ever a service
Measuring paved-road success as compliance (percentage of teams mandated) rather than adoption (percentage that would choose it)
Sending quality regressions to the availability rotation, where they arrive as a page nobody has a runbook for and everyone treats as noise
flags: "Everyone owns quality" - a sentence that has never once resulted in someone being paged
"We'll standardise later, teams need to move fast right now" - later means after six sets of keys, eleven prompt copies and no shared trace fields
"The platform team reviews every prompt change" - ask for reviews per quarter and reviewer capacity, then compute the utilisation before agreeing
"Adoption is low because teams don't understand the benefits" - adoption is low because the paved road is slower than the ditch, which is a measurable claim
"That artifact is shared" - shared means two owners, and two owners on a choke point is the shadow-spend signature
ask: For each of these ten artifacts: who owns it, who approves a change, and who gets paged when it breaks?
Which of our artifacts are choke points, and does each of those have exactly one owner?
How many reviews per quarter does the platform team absorb, against how much reviewer capacity? What utilisation is that?
When the answers get worse rather than slower, whose phone rings, and do they have a runbook?
What does a product engineer get for free by coming through the platform, stated in things they'd otherwise have to build?

MODULES.title: The Architecture Review
MODULES.tag: One page, six numbers, three diagrams, and the dissent written by you
MODULES.why: Eleven artifacts in eleven places are not an architecture. They become one when they're assembled into a single document that can be defended, attacked and revisited - and the assembling is where you find out which of them contradict each other, because almost every real review finding is two artifacts disagreeing while each looks fine alone. This is the capstone: the document, the review that stress-tests it, the ten questions that find most of the problems in someone else's system, and the discipline that keeps the document alive afterwards.
MODULES.mental: The artifact isn't the diagram, it's the argument. Given these constraints, these alternatives were considered, this one was chosen, and here is exactly what would change our mind. A review is a defense: you're not presenting a design for admiration, you're exposing it to the strongest available attack while it's still cheap to lose. If nobody in the room can articulate why you might be wrong, the review hasn't happened yet, no matter how long the meeting ran.
concepts: The eleven artifacts

Spec card, three budget tables, chosen shape with rejected alternatives, FMEA with detectability, action inventory with autonomy tiers, degradation ladder with pre-authorizers, exit memo in engineer-weeks, derived-state register, migration runbook, control points with authorities, ownership matrix. That is the document's table of contents; the check is that you can point at each one.
Constraints, not conclusions

Record the number that forced the decision and where it came from, not just the decision. "We chose the two-stage shape" is unmaintainable in twelve months because nobody can tell whether the reason expired. "Planner p95 measured 7,400ms against a 3,000ms requirement, benchmark dated March" is maintainable forever.
Cross-artifact contradiction

The characteristic finding of a real review, and the reason a linter beats a reader: budgets that don't sum to the spec card, a staleness bound exceeding the freshness tolerance three pages earlier, an action inventory granting auto-execute on the thing the blast-radius line ruled out.
Red-team role

Someone in the room is assigned, by name and in advance, the job of arguing for the rejected shape as though they believed it. Not devil's advocacy as a mood - an actual assignment, with prep time, because unassigned dissent reliably fails to appear in a room containing the author's manager.
Pre-mortem

"It's twelve months later and this failed. Why?" Asked as a fact rather than a risk, which measurably loosens tongues. Run it for ten minutes, write every answer down, and check each one against a control point in the doc. The ones with no control point are your roadmap.
Revisit trigger

A numeric condition that makes the document stale, tied to spec-card values: volume x3, a change to the cost ceiling, a provider deprecation notice on a seam. Never a calendar date, because calendar reviews get skipped by exactly the busy quarters in which the numbers actually moved.
The respected no

"This should not be built with AI" is a legitimate architectural output and needs to be made cheap to say. That means the standard is the same as for any other rejected shape - name the binding constraint and the number behind it - so declining reads as engineering rather than as a lack of ambition.
mistakes: Presenting conclusions without the numbers that forced them, which makes the document unmaintainable the moment its author changes teams
Running the review as a walkthrough where the author narrates and the room nods, instead of assigning someone the rejected shape to argue for
Reviewing the diagram rather than the arithmetic - the diagram is almost always fine, and the budgets almost never sum
Setting a calendar reminder to revisit the design instead of numeric triggers, so the review gets skipped in precisely the quarter the volume tripled
Treating "don't build it with AI" as a career-limiting conclusion, so nobody ever reaches it and the roadmap fills with features that were never going to close
flags: "We chose X" - with no number and no source anywhere near the sentence
"The eval gate covers that" - ask what the gate is allowed to block, then check whether it ever has
"We'll review it next quarter" - a calendar trigger, which is a reminder people delete during the busy quarter
"Everyone agreed in the review" - unanimity in a room containing the author's manager is a measurement of the room, not the design
"That's out of scope for this document" - said about the artifact that would have contradicted another one
ask: Which number on the spec card forced this shape, and where did that number come from?
Do the stage budgets add up to the spec card? Let's add them now, out loud.
For each control point: what is it allowed to block, and who gets paged when it fires?
For each derived store: what's the staleness bound, and what's the invalidation path within it?
What would have to become true for us to reverse this decision, and who is watching for it?

PLAIN.reqs: Most AI projects don't fail because someone picked the wrong database. They fail because the requirement was a sentence rather than a number, and everyone in the room quietly filled in the blanks differently. This module hands you a card with six blanks on it: how good the system has to be and how you will measure that, how fast, how much per task and per month, how much volume at steady state and at peak, how bad the single worst wrong answer is, and how stale the data may be. Fill all six with numbers and sources and most of the design space disappears before you draw a single box. The blank people skip is the one that matters most: what actually happens when the system is confidently wrong. That answer, more than any other, decides what you are allowed to build.
PLAIN.budgets: Think of every request as carrying three envelopes: one with milliseconds in it, one with cents, one with reliability. Every step in your system spends from all three, and none of them refill. The discipline is to start from what you promised — three and a half seconds, eight cents, ninety-nine percent — subtract the things you can't change like network time and how long the model takes to write its answer, and then allocate what's left across your steps. Two bits of arithmetic surprise almost everyone. Reliability multiplies, so five steps at 99.5 percent gives you 97.5 percent overall, not 99.5. And you cannot add up worst-case timings to get a worst-case total, because your steps don't all have a bad day at the same moment — doing so makes your system look about twenty percent slower than it really is, and talks you out of designs you could have afforded.
PLAIN.shapes: There aren't a hundred ways to build an AI system. There are about six, and they form a ladder: a single model call, a fixed chain of calls, a retrieval read path, a tool loop, an orchestrator with workers, and an offline batch pipeline. Each rung up is roughly ten times more expensive to run and look after than the one below it. The architect's actual job is to pick the lowest rung that still satisfies the numbers on your spec card, and then write down exactly which number stopped you using the cheaper one. That second half is the part teams skip, and it's why so many systems are more complicated than they need to be — nobody can prove the original reason still applies, so nobody dares simplify. Most real systems end up as two or three of these shapes joined together, and the joins are where the interesting failures live.
PLAIN.failure: Normal software tells you when it breaks. AI software often does not: the worst answers come back with a success code, a clean shape, and total confidence, so nothing in your stack raises an alarm. That means you cannot discover your failure modes by watching errors. You have to list them on purpose, before you build, and score each one three ways: how bad is it, how often will it happen, and how hard is it to notice. That third score is the one that matters most, because it decides what you are allowed to do about the row. Failures you can see inline get a blocking check. Failures you can only see later get sampled and measured. Failures nobody can see get designed out of the system entirely, because monitoring something invisible is not a plan. The output is a ranked table with a number in every cell, and it is an architecture document, not an ops document.
PLAIN.blast: Most teams think about AI safety as a defence problem: how do we stop bad instructions from reaching the model. That fight is worth having and you will not win it outright, so architects ask a different question. Suppose one turn is entirely under an attacker's control. What is the worst thing it could do? Whatever that answer is, that is your real exposure, and the way to shrink it is to shrink the set of actions the system can take at all. Sort every action into four levels: it only suggests, it drafts and a human approves, it acts but the action is easily undone, or it acts and there is no taking it back. Those levels are not a ladder to climb. They are a design choice per action, and moving one action down a level can lower the accuracy your model needs by a factor of ten or more. That is often cheaper and faster than any improvement you could make to the model itself.
PLAIN.capacity: Your system already has a behaviour at ten times normal traffic. The only question is whether you chose it or whether you will find out during an incident. For AI systems, the ceiling usually is not your servers, it is the throughput your provider has agreed to give you, measured in tokens per minute. You can work that number out in an afternoon from things you already know: how many tasks a day, how many tokens each one takes, and how much busier your busiest hour is. Then there is a second piece of arithmetic that surprises people. Queues do not create capacity. If work arrives faster than you can finish it, a queue just spreads the delay across everyone instead of refusing a few people quickly, and your typical user gets slower so that nobody gets told no. The real deliverable is a written ladder of degraded states: five steps between fully working and honestly refusing, each one saying what turns off, what the customer notices, and who agreed to it in advance. Nobody should be inventing that at three in the morning.
PLAIN.seams: Buying part of your AI system is not really a purchase decision, it is a placement decision. The moment you adopt a vendor you cut a seam into your architecture, a surface where their thing meets yours, and the position of that seam decides what it will cost you to change your mind later. Teams spend weeks comparing prices and feature lists, then discover that the number that mattered all along was how many engineer-weeks it takes to unwind the integration. This module gives you that number. You count the distinct behaviours you depend on, the data you would have to move, the embeddings and indexes you would have to rebuild, and the eval suites you would have to re-run and re-baseline. You add it up in engineer-weeks. Then you decide, deliberately and in writing, how expensive you want stopping to be.
PLAIN.statearch: Almost nothing in an AI system holds original information. The index, the embeddings, the caches, the summaries, the agent's memory notes, the eval fixtures, all of them are copies of something that really lives in a database or a document store somewhere else. Every copy is out of date for some stretch of time, and the job of architecture is to decide how long that stretch is allowed to be, write it down, and make the system tell you when it is exceeded. Most teams do the opposite: they design the copies with great care and leave the intervals to chance. That is why so many reports of the AI getting things wrong turn out to be an index running hours behind its source, and why they take weeks to find, because everyone looks at the model first. This module gives you a register of every copy, its promised freshness, and its deletion path, plus the arithmetic for how often you can afford to rebuild it all.
PLAIN.migrate: The model underneath your product will change, whether you plan for it or not. Providers retire versions on published dates, better and cheaper options appear every few months, and your own prompts and indexes need replacing as the product grows. If each of those is treated as a project, you will run a project every quarter forever. The alternative is to make changing versions a property of the architecture: you never switch, you run both at once on real traffic and let the evidence decide. That raises the only question that really matters, which is how much traffic, for how long, before the evidence means anything. That is arithmetic, not judgement, and it is the part almost everyone skips. This module covers how to pick the level of evidence a given change deserves, how to compute the sample size that makes it real, and how to write a rollback trigger as a number with somebody's name next to it.
PLAIN.quality: Most teams treat quality as a score: run some evaluations, get a number, feel better or worse. That framing quietly hides the actual design decision. Quality in a running system comes from control points, which are specific places where something is allowed to say no. A check in CI that can fail a release. A rail that can refuse a request. A sampler that can open a ticket. A reviewer who can stop a response before it goes out. Architecture is choosing how many of those you have, where they sit, and what each one is permitted to do. Every one you add costs you: milliseconds on every request, dollars per task, and good answers wrongly blocked. Every one you skip costs you differently: wrong answers reaching users, plus days of not knowing it's happening. This module is about doing that arithmetic before the meeting rather than during it.
PLAIN.orgarch: Every interface you draw in an architecture eventually becomes a handoff between people. Draw a boundary between retrieval and generation and you will, sooner or later, have two groups on either side of it with different priorities and different pager rotations. That's Conway's law, and it's usually presented as a warning. It's more useful as a design input: decide which seams you want people organised around, then staff to them deliberately. For AI systems the sharp edge is that the things which decide how the system behaves are small and easy to edit - prompts, tool definitions, golden sets, rails - so they rarely appear in any ownership document at all. This module produces two artifacts: a matrix naming who owns and who is paged for each of ten such things, and a calculation showing which quarter your central team stops being leverage and starts being the queue everyone is waiting in.
PLAIN.review: This is where the course converges. Everything you've built - the spec card, the budget tables, the shape you chose and the ones you rejected, the failure analysis, the action inventory, the degradation ladder, the exit memo, the derived-state register, the migration runbook, the control points, the ownership matrix - becomes one document that a room full of skeptical colleagues can attack for an hour. The document's job isn't to look impressive. It's to record the constraints that forced each decision, so that in twelve months someone can tell whether those constraints still hold. Most real findings in a review are two parts of the document quietly contradicting each other while each looks fine on its own page, which is why this module ends with a script that reads the whole thing as data and prints the contradictions by name. Then you decide what would change your mind, and write that down too.

GLOSSARY: The six-field artifact a feature must carry before anyone draws a box: quality bar plus the measurement that defines it, p95 latency plus interaction mode, cost per task and per month, volume with a peak multiplier, blast radius, and freshness tolerance. Every blank needs a number and a source.

A requirement that eliminates no design option and therefore constrains nothing — "accurate", "real-time", "handles anything", "as cheap as possible". The repair is always the same: a threshold on a distribution, plus the measurement that defines it.

The worst single wrong output, written as one concrete sentence about one specific user. It is the spec-card field that most often picks the architecture, because it decides whether you owe the system a verification seam, an abstention path, or a human in the loop.

The share of answers allowed to be wrong, run with the same machinery as an availability error budget: a threshold, an owner, and burn-rate alerting. A 92% quality bar is an 8% correctness budget. Its absence is why quality regressions page nobody for weeks.

What one completed unit of user-visible work costs, including every call, every retry, and the failures you paid for anyway. A task may be seven calls — per-call cost is an accounting number, per-task cost is what the unit economics actually close against.

The slack between a composed number and the budget it must fit inside, measured per envelope. Headroom is what you spend when someone proposes a new stage, which is why composing latency correctly matters: summing p95s can hide a quarter of it.
