Six reference architectures ordered by what they cost to operate: single call, prompt chain, retrieval read path, single-agent tool loop, orchestrator-worker, offline batch pipeline. Roughly an order of magnitude per rung — and the ordering is operate cost, not unit price.

The specific spec-card number that made the rung below infeasible, recorded beside the decision. It is what makes an architecture re-litigable later; without it nobody can prove that simplifying is safe, so nobody ever does.

Of all the limits a design violates, the one that actually stops it — reported so you know what to go fix first. Capability binds before latency, latency before cost, and a shape rejected on capability is never rescued by budget.

How hard a failure is to notice, scored 1-10 with higher meaning harder. A 1 is caught by a deterministic check before the response ships; a 10 is only ever reported by a customer. It is the column that decides whether a failure mode may be mitigated at all, or must be designed out.

Severity x likelihood x detectability for one failure mode, all three on 1-10 and all higher-is-worse. The absolute value means nothing; the ranking is the point. Its job is to force three judgements apart so a design review argues about the right one.

A design change that removes the surface a failure needs in order to exist — a constrained output set, a deterministic lookup replacing a generated answer, a schema, a removed capability, a human gate. It is the only legal response to a failure mode you cannot observe, because you cannot verify a mitigation you cannot measure.

The complete set of effects reachable from one model turn if that turn goes wrong — how many records, which customers, whose money, which tenants, and whether any of it can be taken back. It is a design output you shrink deliberately, not a property you discover after an incident.

Where an action sits on the scale from suggest, to draft-with-approval, to act-with-undo, to act-irreversibly. It is assigned per action path rather than per feature, and it directly sets the per-generation accuracy that action requires.

A deliberately designed operation that semantically undoes a completed action - issuing a credit rather than deleting a charge, retracting rather than un-sending. It is what moves an action path from act-irreversibly to act-with-undo, and it only counts when the failure is actually noticed, which is a detectability question.

A pre-agreed, pre-authorised sequence of reduced service states between fully working and honestly refusing. Each rung names its trigger, what gets disabled, the customer-visible effect, the quality delta, and the person who signed it — the fifth field being what makes it executable at 3am by someone who is not empowered to invent it.

The rule that decides, at the boundary, whether a request is accepted into the system at all. Without it a queue does not absorb a burst, it merely redistributes the delay from the few who would have been refused onto everyone who would have been served.

The point, around 80% utilisation, where wait time stops rising gently and turns asymptotic. Because the curve is not linear, the last few points of utilisation account for most of your tail latency, which is why utilisation above the cliff is a latency risk rather than an efficiency win.

The surface where a vendor's system meets yours. Its position, and how much of your behaviour crosses it, is what determines the cost of replacing that vendor, which is why seam placement is the actual build-or-buy decision rather than a consequence of it.

What leaving a vendor costs, expressed in engineer-weeks: distinct behaviours to port, data to move, state to re-derive, and eval suites to re-run and re-baseline. Quoted in weeks rather than money because money can be found on short notice and calendar cannot.

A boundary defined by a published request shape that more than one supplier already implements, so the supplier becomes whoever answers the call. The cheapest seam to carry, because someone else maintains the shape and conformance is somebody else's product problem.

Any store whose contents can in principle be recomputed from a system of record: indexes, embeddings, caches, summary tables, agent memory files, eval fixtures. Each one owes its source a written contract, and the ones that cannot be recomputed are the ones to worry about.

The declared maximum interval a derived store may disagree with its source, paired with the trigger that detects the disagreement and the rebuild that repairs it. A freshness contract you cannot observe being violated is a comment, not a contract.

A quality failure caused by a derived store lagging its source rather than by anything the model did. Characteristically misdiagnosed for weeks because the probabilistic component is the interesting one, and cured by a thirty-second timestamp comparison nobody thought to run.

Operating two versions concurrently on real traffic so evidence rather than opinion decides the cutover. The architectural property worth designing for, because a system that can dual-run gets to change its mind cheaply and one that cannot runs a project every quarter.

The smallest quality regression a rollout is statistically powered to catch. It sets the required sample per arm, and therefore the schedule, at one over its square, which makes it the honest lever to pull when a deadline is short and the only one worth writing down.

The published end-of-life date a supplier imposes on a version you depend on. It does not move for your roadmap, so the rollout is scheduled backwards from it and the start date is derived rather than chosen, which is how prerequisites surface while slack still exists.

A place in or beside the request path where something is authorized to stop something else. Systems have a small number of them, each costs latency, money and false blocks, and choosing how many and where is a design decision rather than a tooling one.

What a control point is permitted to do when it fires: block the release, block the request, block the response, open a ticket, or record only. Assigned explicitly per control point; a check with no assigned authority defaults to record-only and stops nothing.

The time between a regression starting and someone being paged about it. Computed as the alarm threshold divided by (daily volume x incidence x sampling rate x recognition rate). It is the number that should choose your sampling rate.

A one-page table of the artifacts that decide system behaviour (prompts, model choice, tools, golden sets, judges, budgets, rails, traces, indexes, runbooks) against three columns: owner, approver, and who gets paged. Empty and doubled cells each have a matching incident signature.

An artifact where divergence between teams is expensive or unrecoverable, so consistency is worth the cost of a bottleneck. Choke points take exactly one owner; everything else may take several. Key custody and the trace schema are the canonical examples.

A platform offering built so the safe path is also the easiest path, requiring no persuasion to adopt. Measured by voluntary adoption rather than mandated compliance: low adoption is feedback about the road, not about the teams.

A numeric condition on a spec-card value that makes an architecture document stale and requires it to be reopened: volume triples, the cost ceiling moves, a provider posts a deprecation notice on a priced seam. Deliberately never a calendar date, because calendar reviews get skipped in the quarters the numbers actually move.

A review technique that states the failure as a fact - "it is twelve months later and this failed, why?" - and asks the room to explain it. The past-tense framing produces more and more specific answers than asking for risks, because explanation is easier than forecasting.

A short, dated entry recording a decision together with the constraint that forced it and the source of that constraint, so a later reader can determine whether the reason has expired. Recording the conclusion without the constraint is what makes a design load-bearing through inertia.

reqs.worked:
The sentence: "Add AI search to our support portal." Same eleven words, two teams, two architectures that share almost nothing. The only field that differs is blast radius.

Run one — the answer is a self-serve FAQ result. Worst case: a user reads a confidently wrong answer, sees it doesn't match their situation, and opens a ticket anyway. Annoying, recoverable, no money moves. Quality bar lands at 0.92 on a 300-case golden set of real tickets, abstention allowed on 8%. Volume 4,000 tasks/day, peak multiplier 3.0. Interactive, so p95 3,500ms. Cost ceiling $0.08/task. Check the card against itself before believing it: 0.08 × 4,000 × 30 = $9,600/month against a $12,000 ceiling, so there's 20% headroom and the card is internally consistent. Now price the shapes off a measured baseline call of $0.012 and 1,400ms p95. A retrieval read path costs about 1.9× the baseline call and adds an index hop: $0.0228/task, 1.5 × 1,400 + 220 = 2,320ms. Both clear. A tool loop at roughly 5.2× latency lands at 7,680ms and is dead on latency alone. Answer: a retrieval read path, one shape, 0.8 FTE to operate.

Run two — the answer auto-closes the ticket. Same sentence. Worst case: a wrong answer closes a billing dispute, the customer doesn't get their refund, and they churn. Now do the arithmetic that changes everything. At 4,000 tasks/day and the 8% error rate the first card happily accepted, that's 320 wrong auto-closes per day, 9,600 per month. Price one at $18 of re-open handling plus goodwill and you are burning $172,800/month of damage to save $9,600 of contact-centre cost. The feature is negative value at 92%. Push the bar to 0.985 and errors drop to 60/day, 1,800/month, $32,400 — still bruising, so you also buy an abstention path at 1%, routing 40 tickets/day to a human. At four minutes each that's 160 minutes/day, roughly 0.3 FTE, and it converts the expensive failure into a cheap one.

What the second card now demands. 92% → 98.5% is not a prompt-wrangling delta; it is an error rate cut by 5.3×, and you buy that with a verification seam, not enthusiasm. Cost per task rises to $0.30, which the card immediately refuses: 0.30 × 4,000 × 30 = $36,000/month against the $12,000 ceiling. That refusal is the artifact. You carry it to finance with the $172,800 damage figure attached, and either the ceiling moves to $36,000 or the auto-close scope dies — both are good outcomes, and both happened in week one instead of month five. Latency also relaxes, because auto-close is async: p95 moves from 3,500ms to 9,000ms, which quietly re-opens two rungs that were closed a paragraph ago. Answer: a chain with a verification stage and a human queue behind an abstention signal.

Identical ask. Field five picked the architecture — not the ask, and not the enthusiasm in the room.
good: Every field on the card carries a number and the name of the person who sourced it
Quality is a threshold on a named, versioned set, with an explicit abstention allowance
Cost is stated per task and per month, and the two are multiplied to prove they agree
Blast radius is one concrete sentence about one specific wrong output, not a risk tier
The impossible triangle has a named loser, signed by whoever owns that trade-off
reqs.build: Fill the six-field spec card for a feature your team is actually shipping this quarter — not a hypothetical. Numbers only; if you catch yourself writing an adjective, stop and go find the number. Then run the falsification pass: for every field, write one line naming the evidence that would prove the number wrong and the person who owns that evidence. Multiply cost per task by volume by 30 and check it against the monthly ceiling; if they disagree, you have found your first real constraint. Then circulate it to two people — a PM, who will move the quality and freshness numbers, and the most skeptical engineer you know, who will move the latency and cost numbers. The card that survives both is the one you design against. Ninety minutes, and it will save you a quarter.
res: Google SRE Book: Service Level Objectives
Use when turning "it should be fast and reliable" into a threshold you can defend — the SLI/SLO/SLA distinction is the backbone of the whole card.
Use right now: the worked process for picking a measurement window and a target you can actually hold, applied directly to your quality and latency fields.
Use when the quality field needs a real metric — "accurate" almost always means one of these two, and stakeholders usually want the one they didn't name.
Use when filling the blast-radius field for anything regulated — it gives you shared vocabulary with legal and risk instead of an argument.

budgets.worked:
The promise: support deflection at $0.08/task, p95 3,500ms, 92% quality, 4,000 tasks/day. Allocate downward.

Step one: subtract the floors. Network in and out on an interactive surface, measured: 120ms. That is not yours to spend. Remaining: 3,380ms.

Step two: allocate the stages. Retrieval 260ms / $0.001. Rerank 300ms / $0.004. Generation 2,100ms / $0.050. Output rails 200ms / $0.002. Running totals as you go: 260 → 560 → 2,660 → 2,860ms of stage p95, and $0.001 → $0.005 → $0.055 → $0.057 per task. Generation is 73% of the milliseconds and 88% of the cents, which is the normal shape and tells you where every future argument will be.

Step three: compose properly, because 2,860 is the wrong number. Summing p95s assumes retrieval, rerank, generation and rails all have their worst day on the same request. They don't. Composing the spreads correctly (root-sum-square over each stage's p50-to-p95 gap) gives 2,467ms; a seeded simulation over 40,000 requests gives 2,520ms. So the honest end-to-end figure is 2,520 + 120 = 2,640ms against a 3,500ms budget — 860ms of headroom, 25%. Note the direction of the error: the naive sum said 2,980ms and left you believing you had 520ms. Summing p95s is conservative, and conservatism here is not free — it deletes design options you could have paid for.

Step four: the other two envelopes. Reliability: four stages at 99.9%, 99.8%, 99.5% and 99.9% composes to 99.1% raw. Add one retry to the three retryable stages and effective availability rises to 99.9%. Cost with the retry tail: mean $0.057, p95 $0.057, and 4.01 calls per task — that last number is the one to put on the slide, because "two cents a call" and "5.7 cents a task" are the same system described honestly and dishonestly. Monthly: 0.057 × 4,000 × 30 = $6,840.

Step five: someone proposes "just one more verification call." It's a good idea. It is also a subtraction, so do it. Measured on a similar stage: p50 760ms, p95 1,600ms, $0.040, 99.7% success with one retry. Re-compose: simulated end-to-end p95 becomes 3,584ms, plus the 120ms floor = 3,704ms. Over budget by 204ms. Cost becomes $0.097/task at p95 — over the $0.08 ceiling by $0.017, which at 4,000/day is $2,040/month of overrun, and lifts total spend from $6,840 to $11,640, a 70% increase. Calls per task go from 4.01 to 5.01.

That arithmetic took four minutes and it killed the proposal before the PR existed. Not because verification is a bad idea — because it costs 204ms and $4,800/month more than the promise allows, and now the conversation is the right one: which envelope do we renegotiate, or which stage do we cut to fund it? Drop rerank (300ms, $0.004) and verification nearly fits. That is a real design conversation. "Let's add a verification pass" was not.

The counter-example worth knowing. Take a pipeline of two thin stages (26ms and 20ms p95) plus generation at 2,100ms. Naive sum 2,146ms, simulated 2,133ms — 0.6% apart. When one stage owns essentially all the variance, summing p95s is fine. The rule of thumb: if the widest stage's spread exceeds the root-sum-square of every other spread, sum away and spend the saved effort elsewhere.
good: Budgets allocated top-down from the SLO, with fixed floors subtracted before anything else
End-to-end p95 composed or simulated, never summed — and the composition method written down
Availability quoted as the product across stages, and re-quoted every time a box is added
Cost tracked per task at p95 with retries and paid failures included, plus calls-per-task alongside
A correctness error budget with the same standing as availability: a threshold, an owner, and an alert
budgets.build: Build the budget table for one live feature, from real traces rather than estimates. For each stage: measured p50 and p95, actual cost per task including retries and the failures you paid for, and measured success rate. Compose them — multiplicatively for reliability, root-sum-square or simulated for latency, with the retry tail for cost. Then put the composed numbers next to the SLO you have been claiming in reviews. Most teams discover one of two things: that they have far more latency headroom than the naive sum suggested, or that their composed availability has a digit fewer nines than anyone has been saying out loud. Finish with one sentence, written down and circulated: "if this budget halved tomorrow, the first stage we would cut is ___, because ___." Deciding that in calm conditions is worth more than the table.
res: Use right now: the error-budget model this module borrows and then splits in two — read it, then ask what your correctness budget would be.
Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs
Use when a budget exists but nothing pages — burn-rate alerting is what turns a number in a doc into an operational control.
Use when you need to justify the composition math to a skeptic — it's why a p50/p95 pair is enough to model a stage and why summing p95s over-states the tail.
Use when the latency budget meets the volume field — it converts arrival rate and service time into the concurrency you must provision for at peak.

shapes.worked:
The card: internal policy answers. Quality bar 0.93, p95 3,500ms, $0.08/task, 4,000 tasks/day at 3× peak, blast radius recoverable, corpus unbounded, step count fixed. Measured baseline: one model call costs $0.012 and lands at 1,400ms p95. Now walk the ladder from the bottom and stop at the first rung that clears.

Rung 1, single call — $0.0120, 1,430ms. Cheapest and fastest by a distance. Rejected: the corpus is unbounded, and a single call cannot ground on a corpus it can't fit. Note that it wasn't cost or latency that killed it — those were comfortable. It was a capability fact.

Rung 2, prompt chain — $0.0312, 3,420ms. More steps, same problem. Rejected on the same forcing constraint: chaining calls doesn't make an unbounded corpus fit.

Rung 3, retrieval read path — $0.0228, 2,320ms. Handles the unbounded corpus. Cost is 29% of the ceiling, latency 66% of the budget. Monthly: 0.0228 × 4,000 × 30 = $2,736, and at 3× peak $8,208 — provision for the second number. Feasible. Stop here. Cheaper than rung 2, incidentally, which is a reminder that the ladder is ordered by operate cost, not unit cost.

For completeness, what's above: rung 4, tool loop — $0.0780, 7,680ms, rejected because the p95 budget of 3,500ms is under its 7,680ms floor. Rung 5, orchestrator-worker — $0.1680, 4,990ms, rejected on both cost and latency. Rung 6, batch — $0.0060, cheapest per task on the whole ladder, rejected because the mode is interactive.

The artifact is not "we chose a retrieval read path." It's: rungs 1 and 2 are unavailable because the corpus is unbounded. That sentence is a re-litigation trigger. The day someone scopes the corpus down to 40 documents, rung 1 becomes available and the system should get simpler. Without the sentence, that day never comes.

Now change one number: volume ×20, to 80,000/day. Nothing about the problem changed — same corpus, same users, same quality bar. Re-run: retrieval read path now costs 0.0228 × 80,000 × 30 = $54,720/month against a $12,000 ceiling. Rejected. Tool loop: $187,200/month, rejected. Orchestrator: rejected on per-task cost. Every rung fails. That's not a bug in the ladder, it's the card telling you a field has to move.

Which field? Two candidates. Raise the ceiling — finance signs $30,000 — and the read path still fails at $54,720. Or change interaction mode: these are policy answers, and the same questions recur, so precompute them nightly. Mode becomes async, the p95 budget relaxes from 3,500ms to four hours, and rung 6 opens: batch at $0.0060/task = $14,400/month, inside the $30,000 ceiling. Peak ×3 is absorbed by the schedule window rather than by spend, which is precisely what buys the rung.

Read that movement carefully. One number changed by 20×, and the answer moved from rung 3 to rung 6 — down the per-task cost ladder and up the operate ladder. You now own a pipeline: backfills, reprocessing, freshness monitoring, roughly 3 FTE of steady-state ownership against 0.8 for the read path. The batch pipeline is the cheapest shape per task and the most expensive shape to own, and both of those facts are load-bearing.

The real system is a composite. In practice you'd run all three: batch precompute serving 55% of traffic at $0.0060, a read path serving 42% at $0.0228, and a tool loop as an escape hatch for the hard 3% at $0.0780. Blended: $0.0152/task. And price the hatch drifting, because it will — at 10% instead of 3% the blend is $0.0191 (1.3×); at 25% it's $0.0274 (1.8×). That's why the escape hatch gets a rate cap and a dashboard, not just a trigger condition. Three shapes, two contracts: batch→read is a versioned index snapshot; read→hatch is an explicit low-confidence signal with a cap on it.
good: The chosen rung is the lowest one that clears the current card, and someone can say so out loud
Every climb has a written forcing constraint naming the exact card field that forced it
Composite systems are drawn as separate shapes with a named contract on every seam
Each shape's degraded mode is specified — what it serves on its worst day, not just its best
Operate cost is estimated in people, not just dollars, before the shape is committed to
shapes.build: Draw your current system as shapes-with-contracts on one page. Hard limit: seven boxes. If it doesn't fit, you've drawn implementation rather than architecture — zoom out until each box is one of the six shapes or a datastore. Then, for every box, write the forcing constraint that justifies it: the spec-card number that made the cheaper alternative infeasible. Do this honestly; "we already had it" is not a forcing constraint, it's a fact about history. Any box that ends up without one is a deletion candidate. Take that list of candidates to your team and defend it. You will get one of two outcomes, and both are wins: someone supplies the missing constraint and it goes into the doc where it should have been, or nobody can, and you've found real complexity to remove. Do the same exercise for the seams — for each contract, write what the consumer is entitled to assume and what happens when that assumption breaks.
res: Use when defending the lowest feasible rung against a team that wants the more impressive one — it's the canonical argument for boring, and it's written by people who ran the hard version.
Use right now: the forcing constraint needs a permanent home next to the decision, and this is the lightest format that survives team turnover.
Use when a composite means migrating off an existing blob rather than greenfielding — the pattern for adding shapes at the seams without a rewrite.
Use when someone proposes an orchestrator-worker shape for latency reasons — it tells you the ceiling on what parallelising the parallelisable part can actually buy.

failure.worked:
Thirty minutes, one whiteboard, one feature: an assistant that reads supplier invoices, extracts line items, answers questions about supplier terms, and can post the result to the ledger. Six people in the room. The rule for the session is that no one proposes a fix before the detectability score is on the board.

Eleven rows come out. Two of them get resolved in opposite directions, and the contrast is the whole lesson.

Row A: a transposed digit in an extracted amount. Severity 8 — it is money, and it posts. Likelihood 4 — it happens, not often. Detectability 2 — and here is why: the invoice carries a stated total, the extracted line items have a sum, and those two numbers either match or they do not. That is a deterministic arithmetic comparison available before anything ships. RPN = 8 x 4 x 2 = 64.

Disposition: a rail. A totals reconciliation that runs on every extraction and blocks the post on mismatch. We estimate it catches 97% of transposition errors, so the escaping likelihood drops from 4 to effectively 0.12, which we round up to 1 because pretending a control is perfect is how you get a bad table. Residual RPN = 8 x 1 x 2 = 16. A 75% reduction, from roughly forty lines of code and no model involvement at all.

Row B: an answer about supplier terms drawn from a superseded contract version. Severity 7 — someone acts on the wrong payment terms and we are in a commercial dispute. Likelihood 5 — the index holds every version of every contract, and half of them read almost identically. Detectability 9 — and this is the number that ends the discussion. The answer is fluent. It cites a real clause. The clause exists, verbatim, in a real document we really do hold. Nothing about the output is malformed. No reviewer scanning outputs would flag it. It surfaces when a supplier disputes an invoice, roughly six weeks later. RPN = 7 x 5 x 9 = 315, nearly five times Row A.

The room's first instinct is an alert: "score a sample of terms answers for staleness." Follow it one step. The scorer would have to know which contract version is current for that supplier on that date. That means resolving supplier_id plus effective_date against the contract table — a deterministic lookup. Which is the punchline: if you can build the detector, build the answer instead. The moment you can compute the right answer reliably enough to grade the model, you no longer need the model for that question.

So Row B gets an amputation. Terms questions stop being answered in free text. The assistant resolves supplier_id + effective_date to exactly one contract record and returns the clause text plus a link, generated nothing. The generative surface for that question class is deleted. Post-amputation likelihood is not reduced, it is zero, because the mode has nowhere to occur. RPN 315 -> 0. You did not mitigate it. You removed the thing that could produce it.

Two rows, two directions, one rule doing the deciding. Row A had a cheap oracle sitting right there in the document, so it earned a rail. Row B had no oracle short of building the answer, so mitigation was never on the table and the only honest move was to shrink what the system is allowed to say.

The register's totals: 1,503 RPN before controls, 928 after, of which 715 is the three structural rows. That last number is the one you take to the planning meeting. It is not a monitoring backlog. It is a design backlog, and it has to be spent before launch, because none of it gets better with a dashboard.
good: Every row on the register names a detector and what that detector compares against, or it is explicitly marked as having none
The highest-RPN rows are structural, and the structural rows are on the build plan rather than the observability plan
Severity scores trace back to the spec card's blast-radius line, so two engineers scoring the same row independently land within a point
Compounding failure modes are identified as such and answered with a step ceiling, not with a better prompt
The table has a date, an owner, and a trigger list for when it gets rescored, and the last rescore is more recent than the last capability added
failure.build: Take one feature you personally own and build the register: minimum ten rows, each scored severity, likelihood and detection-difficulty on 1-10 with all three higher-is-worse. Rank by the product. Then do the part that makes it real — circle every row with detection above 7. That circled set is your design-change backlog, and it is a different backlog from your monitoring one. For each circled row, write the specific structural move: which output gets constrained, which capability gets removed, which generated answer becomes a deterministic lookup, which step gets a human in front of it. If you cannot write one, write "accepted, revisit at X" with a real trigger — that is a legitimate answer and a dishonest silence is not. Finally, walk the table to a senior peer and let them attack your detection scores specifically. Detection is where optimism hides, and it is the column that changed what you are allowed to build.
res: Use when you want the original discipline this module adapts, including the detection-rating convention and why RPN rankings beat RPN values.
Use when someone argues for zero failures. It is the cleanest published argument for choosing a failure budget deliberately instead of pretending to have none.
Use right now: if you need a recognised vocabulary for the register when it goes to legal, risk or a customer's security review, this is the one they will already know.
Use when a failure mode has several independent contributing paths and one FMEA row is flattening a structure you need to see branch by branch.

blast.worked:
A support agent with six tools. Five are fine. One of them turns the whole system into an exfiltration channel, and the interesting part is what it costs to fix.

The tools: search_kb (internal articles), read_ticket (the customer's own words), read_crm (contract value, renewal date, contacts), create_ticket and update_ticket_status (both trivially reversible), and send_email.

Run the trifecta check. read_crm puts private data in the turn. read_ticket puts attacker-writable text in the turn — a stranger typed that, which is the entire point of a support inbox. send_email moves bytes out of the boundary to an address chosen inside the turn. Private, untrusted, egress: one turn, all three legs. No rail changes that. A rail lowers the probability; the path exists at probability greater than zero, and at 12,000 tickets a month, greater than zero is a schedule.

Three options, priced.

Option 1: remove send_email. The agent drafts, a human sends. The trifecta breaks cleanly — egress is gone. Now price it. The auto-reply path currently resolves 3,100 of 12,000 tickets a month with no human touch. Average human handling is 4.5 minutes, so removal costs 3,100 x 4.5 = 13,950 minutes, or 232.5 agent-hours a month, and it deletes the feature's headline number. Safe, and expensive enough that someone will overrule you in a quarter.

Option 2: narrow egress to an internal allowlist. send_email may only reach addresses on your own domain. The trifecta breaks — an attacker cannot name the destination. It also breaks the product: the entire use case is replying to customers, who are by definition external. Value retained: approximately zero of the 232.5 hours. This is the option that looks responsible in a slide and ships nothing.

Option 3: resolve the recipient from data that predates the untrusted content. send_email can only address participants already on the ticket when the turn began — a list built from the ticket record, not from anything the model produced. Anything else routes to a human. Measured over three months of history, 6.1% of replies went to an address not already on the ticket: 190 a month, needing 190 x 4.5 = 855 minutes = 14.3 agent-hours a month of human time.

Compare: 232.5 hours retained for 14.3 hours spent. 94% of the value, 6% of the cost, and the trifecta is genuinely broken rather than argued down — because the destination set is resolved from a source the attacker never wrote to. That last clause is the whole design, and it generalises: an allowlist is only a bulkhead when its contents are decided outside the compromised turn.

Now the tier arithmetic, which is where this stops being a story. Volume is 20,000 model-authored actions a month. In review, the business will own four bad actions a month — not zero, four, written down. The model measures 94.0% on your golden set.

Multiply out what escapes at each tier. Bad generations are 20,000 x 6% = 1,200 a month. Acting irreversibly, essentially all of them become bad actions: 1,200 against a tolerance of 4, a 300x overshoot. Act-with-undo, where perhaps 20% are noticed and reversed in time: 240, still 60x over. Approval-gated, where a reviewer catches roughly 95%: 60, still 15x over. Suggest-only, where the human authors the artifact and the model merely proposes: 3.6, which passes.

Invert it and read the requirement instead. Irreversible demands 99.98% per generation. Act-with-undo demands 99.90%. Approval demands 99.60%. Suggest demands 93.3%. Your model is at 94.0%.

Nobody is going to hand you a 99.90% model this quarter, at any price. But the gap between "unshippable" and "shipped" here was never a modelling problem — it was one line in an action inventory. A tier demotion is a five-point accuracy improvement you can deploy on Thursday.
good: Every write path in the system appears on one inventory, with its tier, its authorizing principal, its undo mechanism and its worst-case sentence
The required per-generation accuracy for each tier has been computed from real volume and a written tolerance, and compared against a measured model number rather than a vendor benchmark
Actions execute with a capability token narrower than the invoking user, scoped to the operations and records this turn actually needs
The trifecta check is a standing agenda item in design review, run again every time a tool is added rather than once at launch
Tenant identity is carried into cache keys, trace attributes and log lines, and someone has deliberately tried to make a cross-tenant cache hit happen in a test
blast.build: Write the action inventory for a system you own. One row per tool and per write path — every one, including the ones that feel too boring to list, because those are where the surprises are. Columns: action, autonomy tier, reversibility, authorizing principal, the exact undo mechanism (not "restore from backup"), and a one-sentence worst case written in plain language. Then run the trifecta check across the whole set: mark every action that can reach private data, every action that ingests text an outsider wrote, and every action that can move bytes outside the boundary. If all three sets are non-empty, enumerate the specific paths — do not summarise, name them, because "we have an injection risk" gets deferred and "read_crm to read_ticket to send_email" gets fixed. Every failing path gets one of two things written next to it: a tier demotion, or a boundary that breaks one leg. Finish by computing required accuracy per tier from your real volume and a tolerance you are willing to defend, and put that table in the design doc. It is the most persuasive page you will write all quarter.
res: Use when you need the canonical framing for why a turn's token should be narrower than the user's. The idea predates all of this by fifty years and it is still the whole game.
Use right now: it is the mental image of this module written up as an engineering pattern, and it gives you vocabulary for arguing about compartment boundaries in review.
Use when you are trying to move an action from act-irreversibly to act-with-undo and need to design the undo properly rather than hand-waving at a backup.
Use when proposing dual control on an irreversible operation and you want the precedent, the failure modes, and the reason it degrades quietly under time pressure.

capacity.worked:
The spec card says 40,000 tasks a day, Monday peak 8x, 3,200 tokens per task. Forty minutes of arithmetic turns that into a quota request, a worker count, and a ladder.

Step one: effective tokens. 3,200 splits as roughly 2,800 in and 400 out. Output tokens weigh more against a throughput meter than input tokens do — carry the weight as a parameter rather than a constant, since it is provider policy and it changes. At a weight of 4.0: 2,800 + (400 x 4.0) = 4,400 effective tokens per task. Skipping this step is how teams under-request by 35% and find out on a Monday.

Step two: throughput. 40,000 / 86,400 seconds = 0.463 tasks a second. Times 4,400 effective tokens times 60 = 122,222 TPM steady, at 27.8 RPM. Apply the 8x peak: 977,778 TPM, 222 RPM. Add 25% headroom for the peak you have not seen yet: 1,222,222 TPM. Against a tier table of 400k / 800k / 2M, the smallest tier that fits is the 2M one. That is the ask, and it has a procurement lead time measured in weeks, which is why this arithmetic belongs at design time rather than launch week.

Step three: the pool. Little's Law, L = lambda x W. At peak, lambda is 3.70 tasks a second and a task takes 9.0 seconds end to end, so L = 33.3 tasks in flight at all times. That is a floor, not a target — a pool of 34 runs at 98% utilisation.

Which is where the cliff shows up. Same load, same service time, only the worker count changing:
34 workers, 98.0% utilisation, 11.73s mean wait, 43 tasks deep.
36 workers, 92.6%, 1.86s, 7 deep.
38 workers, 87.7%, 0.64s.
40 workers, 83.3%, 0.26s.
42 workers, 79.4%, 0.11s.

Six workers separate a 0.11 second wait from an 11.73 second one — a factor of a hundred and six, from an 18% change in fleet size. Nothing else moved. This is why "we run hot for efficiency" is a latency decision disguised as a cost decision. Take 42.

Step four: the number that ruins it. 42 workers at 9 seconds is 280 tasks a minute. But procurement came back with the 800k tier, not the 2M one. 800,000 / 4,400 = 182 tasks a minute. Real capacity is min(280, 182) = 182. The fleet is not the constraint and never was.

Step five: run it at 12x and read the customer's experience. 12x is 5.56 tasks a second, 333 a minute, against 182. Demand exceeds service by 151 a minute. If you simply queue with no cap, backlog grows by 151 every minute — 9,060 an hour — and at 182 a minute of drain, the task arriving at 09:20 is waiting fifty minutes behind work that arrived while everyone was still drinking coffee. That is the counter-intuitive result stated as arithmetic: the queue did not absorb the burst, it converted a fast refusal for 45% of users into a slow one for all of them.

Now the ladder, minute by minute (the simulator in the Patterns tab prints exactly this). Rung 1, cache-only: novel queries only, effective demand drops to 227, still over. Rung 2, smaller model: capacity rises to 291, demand 227, utilisation 78% — stable. A 12x Monday is absorbed at rung 2 and the customer's experience is a slightly blunter answer nobody writes in about.

Push it to 26x, which is what the incident actually looked like. The ladder climbs: rung 3 deflects the top intents to templates, rung 4 turns on admission control and starts a bounded queue with an email, rung 5 begins refusing honestly with a retry-after. Backlog peaks at 229 tasks and drains by minute 39. Total dropped: 9 tasks. Pinned at rung 0 with no ladder at all, the same spike drops 7,433.

Nine versus seven thousand four hundred. The difference is not capacity, it is that somebody wrote five rungs down in daylight and got them signed.
good: The design doc states capacity as min(worker pool, provider quota) in tasks per minute, with both numbers shown and the binding one named
Peak utilisation for the worker pool sits below the cliff by design, and the wait time two points above the target is written down next to it
Every queue in the system has a depth cap and a stated behaviour when full, and that behaviour is a deliberate refusal rather than whatever the runtime does
The degradation ladder exists as a document with five rungs and all five fields, and the pre-authorizer column contains names rather than roles
The failover target has been run against the golden set, and the quality delta is a number in the runbook rather than an assumption in someone's head
capacity.build:
Write the degradation ladder for one real feature. Five rungs between fully working and honestly refusing, and every rung gets all five fields: the trigger that engages it (a number, not a feeling), exactly what turns off, what the customer sees and is told, the quality delta you expect, and the name of the person who pre-authorised it. Take it to that person and get the sign-off in writing — that conversation is the actual deliverable, because a rung the on-call engineer is not empowered to pull is decoration.

Then run a game day. Pick rung 3, engage it deliberately in staging with real-shaped traffic, and watch what actually happens. Expect to be wrong about at least one thing: the cache hit rate under degraded conditions is usually lower than you assumed, the smaller model's output shape often breaks a downstream parser nobody tested against it, and the customer-facing copy for the rung frequently does not exist at all. Every one of those is cheaper to discover on a Tuesday afternoon than during the event the ladder was written for.
res: Use right now: L = lambda x W is the single highest-leverage formula in this module, and this is the shortest correct statement of what it does and does not assume.
Use when you are choosing between shedding, queueing and degrading. It is the clearest published treatment of why graceful degradation has to be designed before the load arrives.
Google SRE Book - Addressing Cascading Failures
Use when your retries, queues and timeouts are interacting badly. Most capacity incidents are actually cascade incidents, and this chapter names the specific mechanisms.
Use when someone challenges the cliff numbers and you need the model behind them, including the assumptions it makes that your real traffic will violate.

seams.worked:
Same decision, two seam placements: a managed vector service holding 12M chunks for a support product. Rate assumptions, stated once and passed everywhere: 37.5 productive hours per engineer-week, 12 hours to port one distinct behaviour, 16 hours to re-baseline one eval suite.

Seam A, the thin repository. Three methods, upsert, search, delete, and every call site goes through them. Exit at 18 months: 3 coupling points x 12h = 36h, plus 9h of index-build compute (the vectors are already in your object storage, so no re-embed), plus 4 eval suites x 16h = 64h. Total 109h = 2.91 engineer-weeks.

Seam B, the raw SDK. Thirty-one call sites, but the number that matters is 14 distinct behaviours: their filter dialect in nine places, hybrid-scoring knobs in four, one pagination convention. Exit: 14 x 12h = 168h, plus the same 9h build, plus the same 64h revalidation. Total 241h = 6.43 engineer-weeks.

So Seam A saves 3.52 engineer-weeks at exit. Now price keeping it: feature-lag tracking and a quarterly conformance run against a second implementation cost about 18 engineer-days a year, 3.6 engineer-weeks annually. Over 18 months that is 5.4 weeks paid to save 3.52. Break-even is 11.7 months, and honest probability of leaving inside the horizon is 35%, so the expected saving is 0.35 x 3.52 = 1.23 weeks against 5.4 certain. Roughly 4.4 to 1 against the abstraction. The messy seam wins.

Now look at what both columns share: 64 hours of revalidation, identical, because the evals are yours either way. Make them the vendor's and that line stops being 64 hours and becomes "build an eval capability first", about six engineer-weeks, on the critical path of both options. The highest-leverage seam change here was never the wrapper. It was owning the suite, and it cuts six weeks off every vendor decision you will make afterwards.
good: Every vendor in the architecture carries a one-line exit cost in engineer-weeks, recomputed at renewal and visible in the design doc
Golden sets, labelled traces and judge rubrics live in your storage in an open format, whatever platform happens to run them
Seams are chosen per vendor rather than by habit: config where the swap is genuinely cheap, adapter where the behaviour is rich, data seams named as such and argued for
Every abstraction has a named owner and a stated carrying cost in engineer-weeks per year, reviewed against its exit saving at least annually
Once a year one real suite runs against a second implementation, so "we could switch" is a measurement with a date on it rather than a belief
seams.build:
Pick your most-embedded vendor, the one people wince about, and write the exit memo. One page.

(1) What breaks: enumerate distinct behaviours you depend on, not call sites. Filter dialects, scoring knobs, error semantics, pagination, consistency guarantees, auth model. Grep for their import outside your adapter; every hit outside is a coupling point. (2) What must be re-derived: embeddings, indexes, caches, anything you cannot copy and must recompute, with hours. (3) What must be revalidated: which suites, how many hours each to re-run and re-baseline, and be honest, most teams undercount this by 3x. (4) The tail: egress volume and remaining contract months. (5) Total in engineer-weeks, money second.

Then propose exactly one seam change that halves the number, and state its ongoing cost in engineer-weeks per year. Divide the saving by the carry to get the month inside which leaving repays it. Compare that to your honest probability of leaving.

If the current exit cost is already acceptable, the correct deliverable is do nothing, and writing that down, with the arithmetic that supports it, is the exercise. An exit memo that always recommends a refactor is a memo nobody will believe the third time.
res: Use when the exit has to happen incrementally on a live system, this is the shape a real migration off a data seam takes.
Use right now: read it before you propose a wrapper, it is the clearest statement of why union abstractions cost more than they save.
Use when you have decided an adapter seam is correct and need the standard shape and its known failure modes.
Use when evaluating whether a protocol seam is available for a category, a published shape more than one vendor implements is the cheapest seam you can get.

statearch.worked:
One customer exercises their right to erasure. You have 30 days. Follow the record.

1. Orders database (system of record). Row deleted, immediate. 2. Change-data-capture topic. Tombstone emitted, but the pre-delete image sits in the topic for the 7-day retention window. Both of these have a deletion path.

Now the seven derived stores. 3. Chunk staging bucket, 90-day lifecycle rule, no deletion path. 4. Primary index, delete-by-filter, tombstone reclaimed at the next segment merge, measured lag 6 hours. 5. Replica index in the second region, replicates the delete, +40 minutes. 6. Semantic cache, 24-hour TTL, no invalidation on tombstone, so the deleted record can still be served for 1,440 minutes against a spec-card freshness tolerance of 15 minutes, 96x over contract. 7. Agent memory files, written as free text by an extraction step with no customer identifier, so no key exists to delete by, and no expiry. 8. Trace store, 90-day retention, prompts contain the record verbatim. 9. Eval fixtures: 14 golden cases were built from this customer's tickets, and golden sets do not expire.

Count: 4 of 9 locations can receive a deletion request, and only 2 of the 7 derived stores. Two of the survivors, memory files and eval fixtures, never expire.

Price the fix. Customer-id front matter on memory files plus a delete-by-owner sweep: 3 engineer-days build, half a day per quarter to run. Provenance tags on eval fixtures plus a paraphrase-and-re-baseline procedure for the 14 affected cases: 3 days. Tombstone-driven cache invalidation replacing the TTL: 1 day, and it drops the serving-path exposure from 1,440 minutes to under 60 seconds. Staging bucket lifecycle 90 days to 7: one hour, and it lowers the storage bill. CDC retention stays at 7 days because your rebuild replays 5, so you document the exposure instead of shrinking it. Total 7.1 engineer-days, about 1.5 engineer-weeks, plus half a day a quarter.

For 1.5 engineer-weeks the exposure goes from indefinite in two stores to at most 7 days anywhere and under a minute in the answer path. The expensive part was never the work. It was that nobody had ever drawn the graph.
good: A derived-state register exists as a file in the repo, one row per store, seven columns, reviewed whenever a store is added
Staleness is measured continuously as the gap between each store's last successful write and its source's, and it is a graph somebody looks at
Every serving-path store has a real invalidation trigger; TTLs appear only as an explicitly named damage bound alongside one
Deletion is tested, not asserted: a synthetic record is erased quarterly and the sweep proves how many stores still hold it
Cost per full re-derivation is a known number, and the roadmap's chunking and embedding experiments are budgeted against it before they are promised
statearch.build:
Build the derived-state register for a system you actually run. One row per store, seven columns, no exceptions and no "n/a": store, source, maximum staleness, invalidation trigger, rebuild time, rebuild cost, tenant partition key, deletion path.

Rules that make it useful rather than decorative. Staleness must be measured, so go and measure it, do not write what the design intended. A TTL goes in a column called damage bound, never in the invalidation column. Include the stores nobody thinks of as stores: prompt caches, summary tables, agent memory files, the trace store, and the eval fixtures. If a store has no tenant partition key, say so, because it means a scoped deletion cannot even be expressed.

Then run the audit in the Patterns tab against your spec card's freshness tolerance and outage budget, and read the findings out loud in a review.

There is always one store with no invalidation path. Always. It is usually something written by a background job that somebody added in a hurry and that nothing else references by key. Find it. Then decide, explicitly, whether to give it a path, give it an expiry, or delete the store, and write the decision next to the row. The register is only worth keeping if a row can be closed.
res: Use when scoping the deletion fan-out, the obligation attaches to copies as well as originals, which is exactly what the register enumerates.
Use when designing rebuild procedures, it is the clearest treatment of restore time as a first-class requirement rather than a backup detail.
Use when a store needs a real invalidation trigger and you are weighing a stream against a scheduled sweep.
Use right now: the clearest framing of derived data as materialised views over a log, which is what your index actually is.

migrate.worked:
Monday 2026-09-01: the provider announces your model reaches end of life on 2026-10-31. Sixty days. Everyone agrees there is plenty of time, and work starts on 2026-10-05, with 26 days left.

Schedule backwards from the kill date. Buffer for the unexpected, 7 days, so 100% by 10-24. Ramp 50 to 100, 3 days, so the 50% stage ends 10-24. Canary ladder: baseline task success is 92% and you want to detect a 1.5-point drop at 80% power, alpha 0.05. Two-proportion arithmetic gives 5,570 scored tasks per arm. At 40,000 tasks/day, a 5% cohort fully scored yields 2,000/day, so 3 days; 25% and 50% clear it in a day each. Ladder = 5 days, starting 10-16. Shadow, 5 days, starting 10-11. Offline eval and re-baseline, 3 days, starting 10-08. Total 23 days against 26 available. Three days of slack. Fine.

Then on 10-05 someone opens the golden set and finds it was last refreshed in February. Since then the product shipped bulk-export summarisation and multilingual intake, which together are 22% of live traffic and 0% of the eval set. Offline eval covers 78% of what users actually do. Refreshing it: sample 400 production traces across the two new task types, two labellers for 4 days, then 3 days to write judges and baseline the current model, about 11 working days, 15 calendar days.

New total: 38 days against 26. You miss the kill date by 12 days, and the kill date does not negotiate.

What is left to sell? Resolution. Raise the minimum detectable effect from 1.5 points to 3.0 and the sample falls from 5,570 to 1,499 per arm, a 3.7x reduction, because n scales as 1/delta squared. The canary ladder compresses from 5 days to 3. Drop the shadow rung, 5 days. Cut the buffer from 7 days to 2. Total: exactly 26 days, landing on 10-31 with zero spare.

Read the bill. The 5% stage now accumulates 2,000 exposures, and seeing a 1-in-2,000 failure with 95% confidence takes about 6,000, so you are blind to rare failures at the only stage small enough to contain them. You have agreed not to detect a 2-point quality drop. You gave up the rung that would have caught a cost or schema surprise before users did. The stale eval set did not cost you time. It cost you resolution, and the invoice arrived in production.
good: Shadow, canary percentage and instant revert are configuration; nobody deploys code to change or undo a rollout
Every rollout plan states the baseline, the minimum detectable effect, the sample per arm and the resulting days at each percentage
Rollback triggers are written before traffic moves: metric, threshold, window, and one named person who pulls without a meeting
Backfills are idempotent and resumable by content hash, and the two-truths window is bounded and stated in the migration doc
One migration is rehearsed per quarter regardless of need, and the golden set is refreshed against live traffic mix on the same cadence
migrate.build:
Write the migration runbook for the next model swap you will genuinely have to do, the one with a date attached or obviously coming. One page, and it must contain numbers.

(1) Baseline: your current measured quality metric, with the sample it was measured on. (2) Minimum detectable effect: the smallest regression that would matter, stated in points, and the sample per arm the Patterns tab calculator says that requires. (3) The ladder: which rungs, at what percentages, for how many days, with the exposure count at each stage and the failure rate that count makes you blind to. (4) Rollback trigger: one metric, one number, one observation window, one named human who pulls it without convening anyone. (5) Backwards schedule: from the deadline through buffer, ramp and ladder, so the start date is derived rather than chosen.

Then rehearse the rollback in staging. Time it with a stopwatch, from the decision to traffic actually served by the old version. Write the number in the runbook. Most teams discover the revert takes four times longer than they assumed, or that it reverts the model and leaves the new prompt in place. Both are much cheaper to learn on a Tuesday afternoon than at 02:00 with the trigger already breached.
res: Use when designing the ladder, its treatment of canary sizing and evaluation windows transfers directly to quality metrics.
Use right now: it is the one-line answer to "how many exposures before I can claim I would have seen it?"
Use when someone asks why a shorter canary cannot simply be believed a bit less confidently.
Use when building the backwards schedule, a published end-of-life policy is the shape of clock every provider imposes.

quality.worked:
One feature, two placements, priced against the same spec card. The feature: a billing support assistant. Spec card says p95 3,000ms, base pipeline p95 2,400ms (so 600ms of headroom), cost ceiling $0.0120/task against a base of $0.0081, 400,000 tasks/month, quality bar under 0.5% wrong answers, blast radius "user-visible guidance, no automatic money movement".

Placement A - a synchronous grounding gate on every response. Measured p95 of the gate: 700ms. 2,400 + 700 = 3,100ms, against a 3,000ms budget. It fails on latency before you discuss anything else, and it fails by 100ms, which is the worst kind of failure because it invites people to argue about it. Cost: the gate re-reads the retrieved context, adding $0.0026/task, so $0.0107/task total, which does fit under the $0.0120 ceiling. Monthly compute: 400,000 x $0.0026 = $1,040. Now the part nobody prices: on a 3,000-response audit the gate's false-block rate came out at 2.1%. 2.1% of 400,000 is 8,400 good answers per month refused. If one in six of those users contacts support and a contact costs $0.68 in expected handling, that's 8,400 x $0.68 = $5,712/month, five and a half times the gate's compute bill. What it buys: escaped defects drop from roughly 0.25% to 0.06% of traffic, about 1,010 wrong answers a month down to 236. At $6.40 of damage per wrong answer served, that's $6,464 saved against $6,752 spent.

Placement B - a deterministic rail inline, plus 3% async sampling. The rail checks two things that need no model call: does the response match the required envelope, and does every cited document id appear in the set actually retrieved. Measured p95: 30ms. 2,400 + 30 = 2,430ms, leaving 570ms of headroom intact for the next thing that needs it. False-block rate 0.23%, or 920 answers a month, and every one of those was genuinely malformed. Async sampling at 3%: 12,000 scored tasks/month at $0.0026 = $31/month, and zero milliseconds on the request path because nothing waits for it.

The number that decides it is detection lag. Daily volume 13,333. A regression touching 0.5% of traffic produces 13,333 x 0.005 = 67 bad answers/day. At 3% sampling with a 74% recognition rate you see 67 x 0.03 x 0.74 = 1.5 of them per day, so an 8-event alarm threshold fires in 5.4 days, during which about 360 wrong answers reach users. At 1% sampling that same alarm takes 16 days. At 0.1% it takes 162 days, which is not a detection plan, it's a quarterly surprise with a spreadsheet attached.

Which spec card selects which. Placement B wins here: it fits the latency budget, its total monthly cost of being wrong is roughly $8,300 against Placement A's $10,600, and its escape rate of 0.25% still clears the 0.5% quality bar. Now change one line on the spec card, not the design: make the blast radius "applies an account credit automatically, irreversible" and the quality bar 0.05%. Placement B's 0.25% now misses the bar by 5x, and the 5.4-day blind window is 360 irreversible credits. Placement A's 700ms is also no longer a problem, because an irreversible money-moving flow gets a p95 of 8,000ms and a confirmation screen. Same two checks, same arithmetic, opposite answer. The check didn't change. The spec card did.
good: Every control point on the request diagram is labelled with its authority, its p95 and cost contribution, its false-block rate, and the rotation that gets paged
The sampling rate is derived from a target detection lag and written down as a division, so raising or lowering it is an argument about days rather than about round numbers
The false-block rate is tracked and priced in downstream cost, and reviewed with the same seriousness as the escape rate
The golden set has a named product owner and a growth rule (every escaped defect becomes a case within one week), so its relevance doesn't expire quietly
The judge has its own control point: a periodic agreement check against fresh human labels, with a threshold that pages someone when it drops
quality.build:
Take the request diagram for a system you own and mark every control point on it. For each one write five things, and refuse to move on until all five have values: (1) what it checks, in one clause. (2) Its authority, exactly one of: block the release, block the request, block the response, open a ticket, record only. (3) Its cost, as added p95 in milliseconds and dollars per task, quoted against the headroom in your latency and cost tables. (4) Its false-block rate, measured if you have the data, estimated with a stated method if you don't, multiplied by monthly volume so it's a count and not a ratio. (5) Who gets paged when it fires, and who gets paged when it stops firing.

Then do the two searches that make the hour worth it. Find the check with no owner: ask who would notice if it silently started passing everything. If the answer is nobody, give it an owner or delete it, because a check nobody maintains is worse than no check - it's a check people believe in. Find the failure mode with no check: take your FMEA table from Block 2 and, for every row with detectability 7 or higher, name the control point that would catch it. The rows where you can't are your quality roadmap, already sorted by severity. Bring both lists to your next review.
res: Google SRE Workbook - Alerting on SLOs
Use when you're choosing a sampling rate or an alarm threshold - the burn-rate arithmetic here is exactly the detection-lag math, written for availability.
Use right now: before any argument about a rail's threshold, so both sides are talking about the same two error types instead of one each.
Nancy Leveson, Engineering a Safer World (MIT Press)
Use when you want the intellectual foundation for control points - safety as a control structure rather than a component property, from the field that got there first.
Use when someone asks how many samples you need before an alarm is trustworthy, and you'd rather answer with a formula than a shrug.

orgarch.worked:
Six product teams, 34 engineers, all shipping AI features. Each team has its own provider account, prompts live inline in application code, and there is no shared trace schema. Monthly spend is $18,400 across six invoices, so nobody can attribute cost to a feature. The same support-summarisation prompt exists in 11 copies across 3 repositories. An incident in March that spanned two teams took 9 days to attribute, because neither team's logs contained a field the other could join on.

The redesign, by the choke-point rule. Platform takes what's expensive to have diverge: the model traffic choke point (one set of keys, spend attributed by team and feature tag, rate limits enforced in one place), the trace schema (seven required fields, enforced at the gateway), eval infrastructure (the runner and the storage, deliberately not the golden sets), and the rails service. Product keeps what must move at feature speed: prompts, tool definitions, retrieval tuning, their own golden sets, and UX. Note where golden sets landed. They're the thing that most encodes domain judgement, so putting them in platform is how you get an eval suite that nobody in the product team believes.

The migration order, which is the part people get wrong. Step 1, trace schema first, four weeks, additive and read-only: teams add seven fields, nothing is blocked, nothing needs approval. You cannot route or attribute what you cannot see, and this is the only step that makes every subsequent step measurable. Step 2, the traffic choke point in shadow for six weeks: teams keep their keys and mirror a copy of each call through it, so the platform proves its latency and reliability before it can hurt anyone. Step 3, key cutover team by team, highest spend first, one to two days each. Step 4, rails last, opt-in, default-on for new features only. The order that fails is the reverse: leading with "all model changes now require platform approval" makes the platform a tax before it has ever been a service, and the teams route around it inside a month.

The review-queue arithmetic, because this is where good intentions turn into a bottleneck. Suppose the platform gates every prompt change. Six teams x 9 prompt changes/month x 3 months = 162 reviews per quarter. At 45 minutes each that's 7,290 minutes of demand. Capacity: 3 platform engineers, each able to give 270 minutes a week to review before their own work suffers, over a 13-week quarter = 3 x 270 x 13 = 10,530 minutes. Utilisation today is 7,290 / 10,530 = 0.69, which feels completely fine, and that feeling is the trap. Queue wait is non-linear: at a one-day service time, the M/M/1 approximation gives 0.69 / 0.31 = 2.2 days of waiting at six teams, 4.2 days at seven, 12 days at eight, and unbounded at nine. The org adds roughly a team a quarter. So the platform team becomes the roadmap in three quarters, and product engineers start complaining in one.

The fix is not a fourth reviewer. A fourth reviewer moves break-even from 8.7 teams to 11.6, buying about three quarters. Converting 70% of those reviews into an interface contract a CI job can check moves break-even to 28.9 teams. Reviewers buy linear headroom; contracts change the slope. That single comparison is the entire argument for the paved road, and it's worth more in a staffing conversation than any diagram.
good: A one-page ownership matrix, ten artifacts by owner / approver / paged, reviewed whenever a team is added or split
Exactly one owner on every choke point, and the choke points explicitly listed rather than inferred
Owner and pager are the same team for every artifact, so mean time to repair never includes a handoff
The interface contract is a schema plus thresholds that CI checks, not a policy page in a wiki, so conformance is a build status rather than a conversation
Paved-road adoption tracked as a percentage of new features choosing the platform voluntarily, reviewed monthly against the reasons the rest didn't
orgarch.build:
Part one, the matrix. Ten artifacts down the side: prompts, model choice, tool definitions, golden sets, judges, budgets, safety rails, traces, retrieval indexes, runbooks. Three columns across: owner, approver, who gets paged. Fill in all thirty cells with team names, never with "shared" and never with a person's name (people leave, rotations don't). Then mark which artifacts are choke points. Now audit: every empty cell, every cell containing two teams on a choke point, and every row where owner and pager differ. For each finding, go and look for its incident signature in your last two quarters of incidents. You will find most of them, and that discovery is what makes the matrix credible to the people who have to sign it.

Part two, the paved-road pitch. Write one paragraph, addressed to a product engineer, that says what they get for free by coming through the platform - stated as things they would otherwise have to build themselves. Not "governance" and not "consistency"; those are your benefits, not theirs. Something closer to: spend attribution per feature without instrumenting anything, a trace you can replay, rate limits and failover already handled, and an eval runner you don't have to host. Then read it back and ask the honest question: if this were optional, would they choose it? If the answer is no, you don't have a paved road, you have a checkpoint, and adoption will only ever be as high as your ability to enforce it. Fix the paragraph by fixing the road.
res: Use when someone treats the law as a folk saying - the original framing is sharper and it's a two-minute read before a reorg conversation.
Use when you're naming your topology out loud: platform, stream-aligned, enabling, complicated-subsystem. Shared vocabulary makes the split argument much shorter.
Use right now if you're proposing a separate quality rotation - this is the load, escalation and handoff arithmetic you'll be asked about.
Use when you need to show that review wait time explodes non-linearly near capacity, rather than asserting it and hoping.

review.worked:
A review of someone else's system: a mid-size claims triage assistant, 400,000 tasks a month, five engineers, eighteen months old. Sixty minutes, ten questions asked in yield order. Three findings, each surfaced by a number rather than by an opinion.

Question 2 - "do the stage budgets add up?" Latency table: retrieval 300ms, generation 2,100ms, faithfulness gate 700ms, serialisation and egress 190ms. Spec card p95: 3,000ms. Sum: 3,290ms, over by 290ms, and that's before any queueing at the 3x peak the same spec card declares. Nobody had added the column, because each row had been added in a different week by a different person, and every individual row was justified. Ninety seconds of arithmetic, and it reframed the rest of the hour: the design as documented cannot meet its own latency requirement, so at least one control point is coming out or the requirement is wrong. That's a decision the room can make; it was not a decision anyone knew they were owed.

Question 3 - "what is each control point allowed to block?" The eval gate runs on every release and posts a score to the pull request. Asked what happens when the score drops below the stated bar, the answer was "we'd look into it". So its authority is record-only. We pulled the last 22 releases: 14 of them shipped with a score below the documented bar. Not one had been questioned, because a number appearing in a pull request comment is not a gate, it's decoration, and everyone had been reading it as a gate for four months. The fix is one line of CI config and one uncomfortable conversation about which of those 14 releases to re-examine.

Question 4 - "for each derived store, what's the staleness bound and the invalidation path?" The claim summary cache is rebuilt nightly, so its staleness bound is 24 hours. The spec card's freshness tolerance, four pages earlier, is 15 minutes. That's 96x over, and the rebuild takes 41 minutes, so a full rebuild can never satisfy the tolerance no matter how often it runs. What's missing isn't compute, it's an invalidation path: an event on claim update that invalidates one key. Both pages had been reviewed and approved separately, each by someone who never held the other one open at the same time. That is the shape of nearly every real finding.

What the yield order bought. All three findings came from questions 2, 3 and 4. Questions 5 through 10 produced one minor note between them, because this team happened to be strong there. That's the argument for a fixed order: you don't know which questions will pay, but you do know the distribution, so an hour that runs out has run out in the right place.

Then the pre-mortem, ten minutes. "It's twelve months on and this failed - why?" Five answers, three of which already had control points. Two didn't: the summarisation model gets deprecated and its replacement cites differently, and claims volume triples after the acquisition. Both became revisit triggers on the front page - deprecation notice on any seam, and volume x3 - written as numbers rather than dates, because a calendar reminder gets deleted in exactly the quarter volume actually triples.
good: One document, eleven named sections, each traceable to the module that produced it and each pointed at by name in the table of contents
Every decision states the constraint and the source, dated, so a reader in twelve months can check whether the reason expired rather than guessing
A named red-team reviewer with prep time, assigned to argue the strongest rejected shape as though they believed it
Revisit triggers stated as numeric conditions on spec-card values, with an owner watching each one, and no calendar reminders anywhere
The linter runs in CI against the document as structured data, so a contradiction introduced by an edit fails a build instead of surviving to the next review
review.build:
Assemble the document. Eleven sections, in the order the course produced them: spec card, budget tables, shape decision with rejections and binding constraints, FMEA with detectability, action inventory with autonomy tiers, degradation ladder with pre-authorizers, exit memo in engineer-weeks, derived-state register, migration runbook with its numeric rollback trigger, control points with authorities and owners, ownership matrix. Where a section is thin, write "we have not decided this" rather than leaving it out, because an absent section reads as a decided one.

Run the review, sixty minutes, two colleagues. Assign one of them, in the invitation and not in the room, to argue for the strongest rejected shape - document a day early, prepared as though they held it. Walk the ten questions in yield order, not the document in page order; page order is the author's order and it protects the author's assumptions. Spend the last ten minutes on the pre-mortem: it is twelve months later and this failed, why? Write every answer down, then check each against a control point in the document.

Record what you couldn't answer. Every question you couldn't answer with a number goes on one list, and that list is your roadmap, already prioritised - the questions a skeptical peer asks in an hour are close to the ones production asks in a quarter. Finally, write the dissent yourself, and write it in numbers: name the rejected shape you would switch to, the spec-card value that would have to move for it to win, and by how much. A dissent stated that way isn't a paragraph of fairness, it's a revisit trigger - it goes straight onto the front page with an owner attached.
res: Use when you want a lightweight, durable format for the decision-plus-constraint records this module keeps insisting on - conventions, templates and tooling in one place.
Gary Klein, Performing a Project Premortem (HBR)
Use right now, before your next review: three pages on why asking 'it failed, why?' surfaces objections that asking 'what are the risks?' never will.
Use when you're building your own review question list - a mature, ordered set of review questions to steal structure from, even though its content predates AI systems.
Use when 'we shouldn't build this with AI' needs to be a survivable conclusion in your org - the blamelessness machinery is the same machinery.

reqs.mech:
What this course assumes, stated once. You already know how retrieval, agent loops, tool schemas and eval harnesses work. This course never re-explains them. If any of those is fuzzy, the AI Engineering Mastery Hub course covers the mechanics properly and you will get far more out of this one afterwards. Here, components are things you size, place, budget, sequence and authorise — never things you learn. When a component appears below it gets one clause and then we go straight to the decision.

The mechanism is a translation, and it runs in one direction. Natural language in, thresholds out. The reason it feels hard is that stakeholders speak in outcomes ("customers should get answers") while architectures respond only to distributions ("92% of a defined case population, measured this way, within this many milliseconds"). Nobody hands you the second form. Producing it is the job.

Start with the three questions, because they are answerable without technical vocabulary. Who is harmed by a wrong answer? This produces blast radius directly, and it produces the quality bar indirectly — the harm severity is what makes 92% acceptable or catastrophic. What does the user do in the next ten seconds? This produces interaction mode and therefore the latency budget: a person staring at a spinner tolerates one number, a person who fired off a request and went to lunch tolerates a different one by three orders of magnitude. What does the status quo cost per task today? This produces the cost ceiling, and it produces it in the only form finance respects — a comparison. If a human handles the task for $4.20, a ceiling of $0.30 is not a constraint you invented, it is a 93% saving you're offering.

Then derive, don't guess. Quality: name the measurement first, the set second, the threshold third, in that order, because a threshold without a measurement is decoration. Add the abstention allowance in the same breath — a bar of 0.92 with no abstention path means the system must answer every time, and "must answer" is a far more expensive requirement than "must be right when it answers." Latency: always p95, never mean, and say which mode it applies to. Cost: two numbers, per task and per month, and multiply one into the other in front of the room. Volume: steady plus a measured peak multiplier — measured, because a 3× guess against a real 12× is a launch-day outage with your name on it. Freshness: minutes, or the explicit token for a static corpus.

The unarchitectable catalogue. Four requirements recur, and all four are refusals dressed as asks. "Accurate" without a measurement — you cannot eliminate an architecture with it, so it eliminates nothing and constrains nothing. "Real-time" without a number — every architecture claims it. "Handles anything" — an unbounded scope, which is the only requirement that makes every rung of the ladder simultaneously feasible and inadequate. "As cheap as possible" — an optimisation direction, not a ceiling, and a direction cannot fail a design review. When you meet one, do not translate it privately. Hand it back with a reformulation attached: that is what the validator in the Patterns tab does, and doing it on paper is the same move.

The impossible triangle is the closing move. Quality, latency and cost cannot all be maximised, and the honest artifact is a sentence naming the loser: "we are optimising quality and cost, and formally accepting a p95 of nine seconds on this surface." Get a name against it. This feels like an awkward meeting and it is — but the alternative is that the trade-off gets made anyway, silently, by whoever writes the code, and then gets discovered by a customer.

Finally, falsify. Walk each of the six numbers and write what would prove it wrong. A quality bar falsified by a labelling review. A latency budget falsified by an abandonment curve. A cost ceiling falsified by a finance model. A peak multiplier falsified by last Black Friday's traffic. Numbers with a falsification test attached behave like constraints under pressure. Numbers without one behave like opinions, and opinions move.
trade: Tight quality bar vs a generous abstention allowance
Coverage against correctness
A high bar with no abstention path forces a shape you can't afford; full coverage at a low bar ships the errors to customers
Numbers sourced from users vs numbers invented by the team
Elicitation effort now against renegotiation later
Invented numbers get overturned by the first stakeholder who finds them inconvenient, usually mid-build
One p95 budget vs per-mode budgets
Simplicity against honesty
A single budget spanning interactive and async work either strangles one surface or flatters the other into a lie
Refusing a requirement in writing vs quietly under-delivering
Short-term friction against long-term trust
An unspoken refusal resurfaces as a quality incident, and the incident review finds your diagram
scale: Cards are per-surface, not per-company — one card per user-visible surface, or you average two products into one impossible spec
Measure the peak multiplier from your own traffic history; a guessed 3× against a real 12× is an outage, not a rounding error
Re-run the card at every order of magnitude of volume: the same six numbers select a different shape at 4K/day and at 80K/day
Version the card next to the design doc, so when a number changes the diff tells you exactly which decisions must be re-litigated
sec: Blast radius has a twin: "the worst single wrong output" and "the worst single leaked output" are different sentences and you need both written down
A quality bar with no abstention allowance forces the system to answer when it should decline — refusal is a safety control you must budget for explicitly
Freshness tolerance is a compliance field: "answers may be 24 hours stale" is also a statement about revoked permissions and deleted records
Name who is authorised to change each number; a cost ceiling that anyone can raise in a thread is not a ceiling, it's a suggestion
reqs.interview: I don't start with a diagram, I start with an index card that has six blanks on it: quality bar and the measurement that defines it, p95 latency and interaction mode, cost per task and per month, volume with a measured peak multiplier, blast radius, and freshness tolerance.
