Until every blank has a number and a source, there's nothing to architect — you're just guessing with vocabulary. I get five of those six from three questions anyone can answer: who's harmed by a wrong answer, what does the user do in the next ten seconds, what does the status quo cost per task. The field that does the most work is blast radius, because it's what actually picks the shape — the same sentence, "add AI search to the portal," gives you a retrieval read path if a wrong answer is an annoyance, and a verified chain with a human queue if a wrong answer auto-closes a billing dispute. And I always name which of quality, latency and cost we're refusing to optimise, and get someone to sign it. The requirement you decline in writing is cheaper than the one you decline silently in production.

budgets.mech:
A budget is an allocation, and allocation runs downward. You begin with the SLO, because that is the only number that came from outside the engineering team and therefore the only one you cannot quietly edit. Everything else is derived from it by subtraction.

First subtract the floors. Three costs are not available for clever design: the network round trip, the index or datastore lookup, and the time the model spends actually emitting output tokens. That last one is the one people forget, and it dominates. Generation time scales with output length, so "make the answer more thorough" is a latency decision wearing a quality costume. On a typical interactive surface these floors consume 40-60% of the budget before you have designed anything. What remains after the subtraction is your entire allowance for cleverness — for reranking, verification, routing, rails, and every other box you would like to draw. Architects who skip this step spend money they never had and discover it in staging.

Then compose, and compose correctly, because the three envelopes compose by three different rules.

Reliability multiplies. Five stages at 99.5% each is 0.995^5 = 97.5% end to end. Eight stages at 99.9% is 99.2%. This is the arithmetic that makes box count a first-class design constraint rather than an aesthetic preference, and it is almost never done out loud in a review, where people quote the per-stage number because it sounds better. Retries buy availability back — one retry on a 99.5% stage takes it to 99.9975% for that stage — but retries cost latency and money, and they buy back only availability. Nothing buys back correctness.

Cost adds, with a tail. Sum the per-stage costs, multiply each by its expected attempt count, and include the stages you pay for on requests that ultimately fail. Then look at the p95, not the mean, because retries and variable output length give cost a genuinely fat right tail. A mean of $0.057 sitting under a p95 of $0.097 means one task in twenty costs 70% over model. At 120,000 tasks a month that gap is real money, and it is the gap that shows up as "the bill was higher than the forecast."

Latency composes serially or in parallel, and you may not sum p95s. This is the one worth slowing down for. Serial stages add their distributions, not their percentiles. Summing p95s assumes every stage has its worst day on the same request, which is exactly as likely as it sounds. Model each stage from its measured p50/p95 pair and combine the spreads by root-sum-square: end-to-end p95 ≈ sum of p50s + sqrt(sum of squared p50-to-p95 gaps). In the worked example that's 2,467ms where naive summing said 2,860ms — a 14% over-statement. Parallel stages contribute the maximum of the group, not the sum, which is why fan-out costs money rather than time: two 300ms stages run concurrently cost two stages' worth of cents and roughly one stage's worth of milliseconds. And know when the shortcut is fine: when one stage owns nearly all the variance — generation usually does — naive summing lands within a percent or two, and you should take the shortcut and spend the effort somewhere it matters.

Now the part classic systems don't need: two reliability budgets. Availability asks did the system answer. Correctness asks was the answer right. A conventional service only has the first, so the whole SRE apparatus — error budgets, burn-rate alerts, freeze policies — attaches to it by default and nothing attaches to the second. That is the single clearest reason quality regressions in AI systems drift for weeks: the availability dashboard is green, the pager is silent, and the product is wrong. Give correctness the same machinery. A 92% quality bar is an 8% correctness error budget — at 4,000 tasks/day, 320 wrong answers a day is the budget you agreed to spend. Set a threshold, name an owner, alert on burn rate, and treat exhausting it exactly as you would treat exhausting an availability budget. Note also that the two multiply into what the user experiences: 99.9% available and 92% correct is 91.9% of requests that actually worked.

Price and quota anchors — as of August 2026. This is the one dated table in the course. Refresh it against your provider's current rate card and nothing else in these twelve modules changes, because every other module and every calculator takes prices as parameters. These are planning ratios, not quotes: output tokens cost roughly 3-5× input tokens, so verbosity is a cost lever before it is a quality one. A frontier tier costs roughly 10-20× a small fast tier per token, which is what makes routing worth building. Caching a stable prompt prefix returns up to ~90% of that prefix's input cost, which is why long fixed context is cheaper than it looks and long variable context is not. Asynchronous batch processing runs around 50% of synchronous pricing, the single easiest discount available and the reason interaction mode belongs on the spec card. Reranking a candidate set costs one to two orders of magnitude less than generating over it, and embedding a document costs about two orders of magnitude less than generating over it — which is why retrieval read paths are cheap and agent loops are not. Generation throughput in the tens of output tokens per second means time-to-last-token is roughly linear in answer length. Every one of those is a ratio, and ratios rot far more slowly than prices.

The output is a table, and the table is the artifact. Stage, p50, p95, cost, success rate, retries. Composed row at the bottom. SLO row beneath that. Headroom row beneath that, with PASS or FAIL per envelope. Anyone can read it, anyone can check it, and any proposal to add a box is now a subtraction that has to survive it.
trade: Retries to buy availability vs failing fast
Nines against latency and cost tail
Retries on a slow stage blow the p95 budget to protect an availability number nobody was missing
Fan-out in parallel vs running stages serially
Milliseconds against cents
Parallel work costs full price for every branch — you buy latency with money, and at high volume that trade inverts
Budgeting p95 cost vs mean cost
Forecast accuracy against modelling effort
Mean-cost budgets under-forecast by the size of the retry tail, which is exactly the gap finance notices
One combined reliability budget vs separate availability and correctness budgets
Operational simplicity against detecting quality drift
A single budget means the green dashboard keeps paging nobody while the answers get worse
scale: Peak concurrency comes from Little's Law, not intuition: arrival rate × service time. At 4,000/day bursting 3× with a 2.6s task, that's the number you provision and the number you negotiate quotas against
Rate limits are a fourth envelope in disguise — a per-minute token or request quota is a latency budget with a queue attached, and it binds first at peak, not at steady state
Re-derive the budget table at every 10× of volume; stages that were rounding errors at 4K/day become the binding constraint at 400K/day
Publish the composed table, not the stage numbers — teams optimise whatever number is on the dashboard, and stage p95 is the number that lets everyone pass while the product fails
sec: Retries on non-idempotent stages don't just cost money, they can duplicate side effects — budget retries only where the stage is safe to repeat
A correctness error budget is a security control on any surface with a costly blast radius: burning it should be able to disable the automated path, not just file a ticket
Timeouts are a containment mechanism, not a latency tweak — an unbounded stage converts a slow dependency into an availability incident across every caller
Cost budgets need per-tenant attribution, or one abusive tenant spends the whole month's envelope and the alert fires against the aggregate long after
budgets.interview: I treat every request as carrying three envelopes — milliseconds, cents and nines — and every stage debits all three. Budgets get allocated top-down from the SLO, never summed bottom-up from what we happened to build, because a bottom-up number is a description of the system and a description can't fail. First I subtract the fixed floors: network, index lookup, and output-token generation time, which on an interactive surface is usually about half the budget. What's left is the allowance for cleverness. Then I compose by the right rules: reliability multiplies, so five stages at 99.5% is 97.5% end-to-end and box count is a reliability decision; cost adds with a retry tail, so I budget p95 cost, not mean; and latency you compose or simulate, never sum, because stages don't have their bad day simultaneously and summing p95s over-states the tail by fifteen to twenty-five percent — which quietly deletes designs you could have afforded. The AI-specific piece is that we need two reliability budgets, not one: availability, did it answer, and correctness, was it right. Conflating them is why quality regressions have no error budget and no pager. And the practical payoff is that "let's add a verification call" becomes a subtraction anyone can check — in our case 204 milliseconds and $4,800 a month, which ended the debate before the PR existed.

shapes.mech:
The ladder has six rungs and they are ordered by operate cost. Not by capability, not by fashion, and specifically not by per-task price — a batch pipeline is the cheapest rung to run a task through and the most expensive one to own, and if you order by unit cost you will make exactly the wrong decision. What follows is a profile per shape. How each of these works internally is the Mastery course's job; here you get one clause and then the facts you allocate against.

1. Single call. One request, one response. Latency shape: one call, essentially all of it generation, so the p95 is your model's p95. Cost: 1× baseline. Failure modes introduced: none you didn't already have. Observability: 1× — one span, one cost line. Operate: ~0.1 FTE. Degrades to: a canned response. Realistic quality ceiling around 0.88 on non-trivial tasks, because there's no seam to check anything.

2. Prompt chain / workflow. A fixed sequence of calls with deterministic control flow. Latency: serial, roughly 2.4× a single call. Cost: ~2.6×. Introduces: partial-completion states and inter-step format drift. Observability: 2× — you now need per-step traces or debugging is guesswork. Operate: ~0.3 FTE. Degrades to: the last good step's output, which is genuinely useful. Quality ceiling ~0.93, because a fixed chain gives you somewhere to put a check.

3. Retrieval read path. A lookup feeding a call. Latency: index hop plus generation, ~1.5× plus a fixed 200-250ms floor. Cost: ~1.9× — cheaper than a chain, note. Introduces: staleness, permission drift between index and source, and a whole second system that can be down. Observability: 2.5× — you're now debugging two subsystems and the join between them. Operate: ~0.8 FTE, most of it index freshness. Degrades to: keyword results with no synthesis, which is a real product rather than an error page. Quality ceiling ~0.94.

4. Single-agent tool loop. A call that decides its own next step until it stops. Latency: the killer — an unbounded step count means a p95 driven by the tail of the step distribution, ~5× and highly variable. Cost: ~6.5×, also variable. Introduces: non-determinism in the execution path itself, which means two identical requests can cost and take wildly different amounts. Observability: 6× — every step needs a span or you cannot answer "why did this one take nine seconds." Operate: ~1.5 FTE. Degrades to: hand off to a human with the trace attached. Quality ceiling ~0.95.

5. Orchestrator-worker. Independent subtasks fanned out and rejoined. Latency: better than a loop for the same work — parallel, so ~3× — but with a fixed coordination floor around 650ms. Cost: ~14×, the steepest jump on the ladder, because every branch is paid in full. Introduces: partial-failure semantics, result-merge conflicts, and a coordination layer that is itself a system. Observability: 9×. Operate: ~2.5 FTE. Degrades to: partial results from the workers that finished. Quality ceiling ~0.96.

6. Offline batch pipeline. Work done ahead of time, served from storage. Latency: not a request-path shape at all — hours. Cost: ~0.5×, the cheapest on the ladder, because you can use async pricing and spend more compute per item. Introduces: staleness as a permanent condition, backfill complexity, and reprocessing whenever anything upstream changes. Observability: 10× — pipeline health, freshness lag, per-run diffs. Operate: ~3 FTE and a schedule that pages someone. Degrades to: yesterday's run, which is often perfectly fine. Quality ceiling ~0.97, because offline you can afford the compute nobody would pay for in a request path.

The forcing-function catalogue is how you traverse it. Each of these is a capability fact that no amount of budget fixes, and each forces exactly one climb. Unbounded corpus → retrieval. If the knowledge doesn't fit and won't fit, no chain of calls solves it. Unknown step count → tool loop. If you genuinely cannot enumerate the steps in advance, a fixed chain will be wrong on the cases that matter. Be strict with yourself here: "we haven't enumerated the steps" and "the steps cannot be enumerated" are different claims, and the first one is usually what's true. Independent subtasks under context pressure → orchestrator-worker. Both halves are required; independent subtasks that fit comfortably do not justify a coordination layer. Non-interactive plus volume → batch. When the mode field says async and the volume field is large, batch is not a compromise, it's the correct answer and the cheapest one.

Composites are the normal case, and the seams are the architecture. A production system is typically a batch pipeline feeding a read path with an escape hatch behind it. Draw that as three shapes and two contracts, never as one blob, because the blob hides exactly the things that will page you. Each contract needs a written answer to three questions: what the consumer is entitled to assume, how it's versioned, and what happens when the assumption breaks. Batch→read is usually a versioned index snapshot with an explicit freshness guarantee. Read→hatch is usually a low-confidence signal with a rate cap — and the cap matters, because the escape hatch is a budget line whose cost is set by how often it fires. At 3% of traffic a 6.5× shape is a rounding error; at 25% it has doubled your blended cost per task while everyone was looking at the dashboard for the cheap path.
trade: Lowest feasible rung vs one rung of headroom
Operate cost against future flexibility
Headroom you never use is permanent operate cost; no headroom is a rewrite when one card number moves
Composite of three shapes vs one general-purpose shape
Seam complexity against blended cost
One shape for everything means the hard 3% sets the cost and latency for the easy 97%
Batch precompute vs serving live
Per-task cost against staleness and operate burden
Batch is cheapest per task and most expensive to own — teams buy the unit price and inherit the pipeline
Tool loop vs orchestrator-worker for the same workload
Latency variance against coordination cost
A loop's unbounded step count makes p95 unpredictable; an orchestrator makes it predictable and roughly doubles the bill
scale: Re-run the ladder at every 10× of volume — the same card selected rung 3 at 4K/day and rung 6 at 80K/day, and nothing about the problem changed

Per-task cost and operate cost move in opposite directions at the top of the ladder; at low volume operate cost dominates, at high volume unit cost does, and the crossover is worth computing explicitly
Escape-hatch share is the number to alert on — blended cost is roughly linear in it, and it drifts upward silently as inputs get harder
Each shape has a different scaling bottleneck: read paths hit index capacity, loops hit rate limits, orchestrators hit coordination, batch hits the schedule window
sec: Each rung climbed widens the authorisation surface: a shape that can take actions needs an explicit permission boundary per action, sized before it's built
Retrieval introduces permission drift between the index and the source of truth — the index must carry access decisions, not just content
Composite seams are trust boundaries: a contract between shapes needs validation on the consuming side, because the producing side will eventually be wrong
Degraded modes need their own threat model — falling back to a cheaper shape must not fall back to a weaker authorisation check
shapes.interview: I think about AI architecture as a ladder of six shapes — single call, prompt chain, retrieval read path, tool loop, orchestrator-worker, offline batch — ordered by what they cost to operate, roughly an order of magnitude per rung. My job is the lowest rung that clears the spec card, plus a written forcing constraint naming which card number made the rung below infeasible. That second part is what most teams skip, and it's why systems never get simpler: nobody can prove the original reason still holds, so nobody's allowed to touch it. A concrete example: unbounded corpus killed rungs one and two, so we built a read path at two point three cents a task. Then volume went up twentyfold and every rung failed on the monthly ceiling — so we changed the interaction mode to async, which opened the batch rung at six tenths of a cent. Cheapest shape per task, most expensive to own, about three FTE versus zero point eight. Both facts matter. And in practice it ended up a composite: batch serving fifty-five percent, read path forty-two, an expensive escape hatch for the hard three percent, blended at a cent and a half. That hatch gets a rate cap, because at twenty-five percent instead of three it nearly doubles the blend.

failure.mech:
The mechanism behind the silent 200 is worth being precise about, because the imprecise version leads people to the wrong fix.

A traditional service has a type system, a schema, a transaction boundary and an exception mechanism, and those four things collectively encode a huge number of correctness assumptions. When one is violated, something raises. The raise is not a courtesy — it is a structural property of the system, and it is why observability for classic services can be mostly generic: count the raises, time the requests, alert on both.

A generative call has almost none of that. The output is a string. Every string is a valid string. If you constrain the output to a schema you recover shape validity, which is real and worth having, but shape validity is orthogonal to being right. A perfectly-typed {"amount": 4310.00} is indistinguishable at the transport layer from a perfectly-typed {"amount": 3410.00}. The runtime has no opinion. The status code is 200 in both cases because in both cases the transport did its job.

So the entire correctness signal has to be manufactured. And manufacturing it requires an oracle: something outside the model that can say whether this particular output is acceptable. This is the load-bearing idea of the module. Every detector is an oracle plus a comparison, and the cost and feasibility of a detector is entirely determined by which oracle is available.

Some oracles are free and sitting in the payload. An invoice states its own total; line items sum. That is an oracle. A schema is a weak oracle. A step counter is an oracle for stuck loops. A token meter is an oracle for cost runaway. These give you detection scores of 1 to 3 and they earn inline rails, because the check is cheap, deterministic and can run before the response leaves.

Some oracles exist but only cheaply in aggregate. Whether abstention rate has crept up, whether faithfulness scores drifted after a version bump, whether latency's tail fattened — these need a sample, a scorer and a few days of data. Detection 4 to 7. These earn samplers: you learn the rate, not the instance, and you learn it late.

And some failure modes have no oracle short of computing the correct answer. Which contract version was current. Whether the summary the agent passed to step three quietly dropped the constraint that mattered. Whether this cache entry belongs to this tenant. Detection 8 to 10. Here the arithmetic turns on you: the moment an oracle becomes cheap enough to run as a detector, it is cheap enough to run as the answer — so either you build it and use it directly, or you accept that no detector exists and the only remaining move is to shrink the surface.

That is the whole ordering rule, and it is why detectability goes in the first column. It is not a property of how much you care about the failure. It is a property of what oracles your architecture happens to make available, and you can change that — by adding a structural check, by constraining an output set, by keeping a deterministic record alongside a generated one. Architecture is the act of manufacturing oracles for the failures you are not willing to be blind to.
trade: Rail (inline gate) vs sampler (async scorer)
Per-request latency and cost vs how late you learn
Rail everything and you pay a check on every request and add a blocking dependency to the hot path; sample everything and every individual bad answer still ships, you only learn the rate
Structural amputation vs keeping the capability and gating it
Product surface vs residual risk
Amputate too eagerly and you ship a system so narrow nobody wants it; gate instead and you have inherited a control whose effectiveness you have to keep proving forever
Rescore the whole register vs patch the row that just bit you
Consistency vs speed after an incident
Patch-only and the scores drift into folklore within two quarters; full rescore every time and it becomes a ceremony people schedule around and then skip
Score detection optimistically vs pessimistically when unsure
Build cost now vs discovery cost later
Optimism moves rows out of the structural quadrant and into a monitoring plan that will not work; pessimism costs you real design effort on failures that a cheap check would have caught
scale: Detection scores are volume-dependent and this surprises people: a mode you catch by eyeballing outputs at 200 requests a day is detection 4, and the identical mode at 200,000 a day is detection 9, because the human oracle silently vanished when you were not looking

Rail cost scales with every request while sampler cost scales with the sample, so the rail/sampler line moves as volume grows and a rail that was obviously correct at launch can become the single largest line item in the feature's budget

Compounding modes cap your shape choices: if the register says context pollution is your top structural row, the step ceiling that follows is a hard constraint on how deep an agent loop you are allowed to design, and it belongs in the shape decision rather than being discovered afterwards

Rescore triggers that actually work in practice: any new capability added to the action surface, any order-of-magnitude change in volume, any provider version change, and any failure mode observed in the wild that is not already a row
sec: Cross-tenant leak is the row people score wrong most often: severity is always near 10 because it is a reportable event, and detectability is near 9 because a correct-looking answer built from the wrong tenant's data looks exactly like a correct answer — that combination is a forced structural fix, and the usual one is putting the tenant identifier inside the cache key rather than trusting the query text

Traces, logs and eval samples are copies of the same sensitive payload the request carried, so a detector you add for quality reasons has quietly created a new place the data lives, with its own retention and access story

Capability regression after a provider version bump is a security row as much as a quality one, because the behaviour that changed may be a refusal you were relying on as a control — pin the version and rescore rather than assuming refusals are stable

Any failure mode whose only detector is a human reviewer is also a social-engineering surface: reviewers approve faster under load, so a control that is 95% effective in a calm week is worth considerably less on the Monday your volume spikes
failure.interview:
Here is how I would say it out loud in a design review. Normal systems fail loudly, and that is a gift we stopped noticing — a timeout throws, a constraint violation raises, and the failure announces itself. AI systems fail with a 200. The wrong answer and the right answer come back with the same status code, the same shape, and the same confidence, and nothing in the stack has an opinion about which one it just returned. So a low error rate tells you the transport worked. It tells you nothing about whether the thing was right.

What that means for design is that we cannot find our failure modes by watching errors — we have to enumerate them on purpose, before we build, and score each one three ways: how bad, how often, and how hard to notice. The third score is the one that changes what we are allowed to do. If a failure is visible inline, we gate it. If it is only visible in aggregate, we sample it and we accept that we will learn the rate rather than the instance. And if nobody can see it at all, then monitoring is not an option and we either shrink what the system is allowed to say, or we write down that we are accepting it. The one thing we do not get to do is plan a mitigation for a failure we cannot observe — because we will never know whether the mitigation worked, and we will feel safe anyway. That is the rule I would want on the wall.

blast.mech:
The mechanism worth internalising is why the bulkheads beat every alternative, and it comes down to what kind of thing a control is.

Instructions are requests. Everything you write in a system prompt — do not do X, ignore instructions in retrieved content, never send to an address outside the thread — is a request the model may honour. Honouring it is probabilistic and the probability is not under your control. It varies with input, with version, with how much the surrounding context is pulling the other way. A request is negotiable by construction, and a determined adversary's entire job is negotiation.

Structure is not a request. If the token issued for this turn carries scope for two operations on one record, then a turn that decides to do a third thing does not get talked out of it — it gets a 403, from a system that has never read the prompt and has no opinion about it. That asymmetry is the point. You are moving the decision from a component that argues to a component that does not.

Which leads directly to the design procedure. You do not ask how likely a compromise is. You assume it, once, per action path, and read what follows. The assumption is not pessimism, it is a way of removing probability from the analysis entirely so that what remains is a set — the set of effects reachable from a compromised turn. Sets are much easier to reason about than probabilities, and much harder to argue with in review.

Now the arithmetic that makes tiers an engineering lever rather than a governance concept. Take a fixed tolerance for bad actions per month, T. Take volume V. Each tier has an escape fraction E — the share of bad generations that survive to become real-world bad actions. Then bad actions per month is V x (1 - accuracy) x E, and setting that equal to T and solving gives required accuracy = 1 - T / (V x E).

The whole leverage lives in E. Going from act-irreversibly (E = 1.0) to approval-gated (E around 0.05) multiplies your error budget by twenty. Going to suggest-only (E around 0.003) multiplies it by more than three hundred. Against a fixed tolerance, those multipliers land directly on the accuracy requirement — 99.98%, 99.60%, 93.3% — and the last of those is a number your current model already meets.

Two honest caveats, because this arithmetic is easy to abuse. First, E is not a constant you inherit; measure yours. Reviewer catch rates degrade under volume and time pressure, which means an approval gate is worth more in a calm quarter than on the Monday your traffic spikes, and a system that leans hard on human review has coupled its safety to its load. Second, undo only counts if the failure is noticed. An undo mechanism nobody triggers because nobody knew is a reversibility class you claimed and do not have — which is exactly the seam where this module hands back to the failure register, because "noticed" is a detectability score.

Then there is the trifecta, which is a reachability question and nothing more. Private data reachable, attacker-writable content reachable, egress present. Three legs, one turn. Break any leg and the path is gone: don't put the private read in the same turn as the untrusted read, resolve egress destinations from data that predates the untrusted content, or remove the egress. Notice that none of those three moves is a filter, a classifier or a better prompt. They are all walls.
trade: Demote a tier vs invest in accuracy
Product capability now vs a model improvement you may never get
Chase accuracy and you may spend two quarters closing a gap the tier change closes on Thursday; demote reflexively and you ship a product whose whole value was the automation you just removed
Human approval gate vs structural containment
Flexibility of judgement vs a control that holds under load
Approval handles cases no rule anticipates, and its catch rate quietly collapses exactly when volume spikes; structural containment holds under any load and refuses the legitimate exception too
Narrow capability tokens vs one service identity
Containment vs operational simplicity

Per-turn scoped tokens mean a compromised turn does almost nothing, and they add issuance, rotation and debugging surface; a single broad identity is simple right up until one turn inherits everything the service can do
Allowlist resolved from pre-turn data vs allowlist checked at call time
Real containment vs the appearance of it
An allowlist the turn can influence is not a boundary, it is a suggestion with extra steps; resolving it from data that predates the untrusted content is what makes it structural
scale: Blast radius grows with tenancy, not with traffic: a per-user mistake at a thousand users is a support ticket, and the same mistake behind a shared cache or a shared index is one event affecting everyone, which is a completely different severity row

Approval-gate economics invert as volume rises - at 200 actions a day a reviewer is thorough and E stays low, at 20,000 a day the reviewer is a rubber stamp and E drifts toward the ungated number while your design doc still claims the old one

Every new tool multiplies the reachability graph rather than adding to it, so the trifecta check has to be re-run on tool addition, not on release - the sixth tool is what turned five safe ones into an exfiltration channel

Compensating actions need designing at the same time as the action, because retrofitting undo onto a write path that already ran a million times means reconciling a million rows you no longer have the inputs for
sec: The turn's token should be narrower than the invoking user in both scope and lifetime: the operations this task needs, on the records already in scope, expiring in minutes - a token that merely impersonates the user has contained nothing

Egress is broader than it looks. Email, webhooks, outbound HTTP, a URL rendered into a response the browser will fetch, an image source, a link a user is likely to click - each of those moves bytes outward, and each belongs on the inventory with the same scrutiny as an API call

Cross-tenant cache hits are leaks and they are invisible by construction, because the wrong tenant's answer is a perfectly plausible answer - put the tenant identifier in the cache key and write the test that proves a miss, from both directions

Dual control degrades under time pressure in an entirely predictable way, so it belongs on operations that are rare and consequential, never on the hot path - a second approver who approves everything within four seconds has cost you latency and bought you a log line
blast.interview:
The framing I would use in a review is this. We are not going to win the argument about whether bad instructions can reach the model. They can — anything the system reads is something someone can write, and that includes tickets, documents, emails and web pages. So instead of asking how we stop it, I want to ask what happens if we lose. Assume one turn is entirely attacker-authored. What is the worst thing that turn can do? If the answer makes people uncomfortable, we have a design problem, and no prompt is going to fix it, because you cannot patch away a capability you granted.

The way out is bulkheads. A ship survives a breach because the compartments are sealed, not because the hull is strong, and our version is the same: bound the set of actions reachable from a turn by structure rather than by instruction. A token that carries less authority than the person who triggered it. A recipient list resolved from the ticket record before any untrusted text arrived. A second human on anything irreversible.

And the part that usually changes the meeting is the arithmetic. If we act irreversibly at our volume, we need 99.98% per generation to stay inside our tolerance. If we put a human on it, we need 99.6%. If we demote to suggest, we need 93.3%, and we are already at 94. A tier demotion is a model upgrade we cannot buy, and it ships this week.

capacity.mech:
The mechanism behind the brownout ladder is worth taking apart, because two separate pieces of arithmetic drive it and people usually only know one.

The first is the capacity ceiling, and its shape is unfamiliar. In a classic service you scale out until CPU stops being the constraint. Here your fleet is rarely the constraint at all — the provider's tokens-per-minute and requests-per-minute grants are, and those do not scale by adding machines. They scale by a conversation with a lead time. So the capacity number you carry in your head has to be min(fleet, quota), expressed in the same unit both ways, and the second term is the one that moves on someone else's schedule. This is why capacity work is a schedule dependency and not an operational chore: a quota you need in March is a request you make in January.

The second is the queueing curve, and this is the piece that produces genuinely counter-intuitive results. Mean wait in an M/M/c system is governed by the gap between servers and offered load, and as that gap closes, wait rises asymptotically rather than linearly. Concretely, at 33.3 erlangs of offered load: 42 servers is 79% utilisation and 0.11 seconds of wait; drop to 36 and you are at 93% and 1.86 seconds; drop to 34 and you are at 98% and 11.73 seconds. Six servers, a hundredfold change. Nothing about the load moved.

Two consequences follow that are worth stating plainly. Utilisation above roughly 80% is a latency decision, not an efficiency win — the last few points buy you very little cost and most of your tail. And a small fleet reduction that looks harmless on an average-latency dashboard can be catastrophic at p95, because the average is dominated by the fast path and the tail is where the queue lives.

Now the part that most systems get backwards. A queue does not create capacity. It converts refusal into waiting. If arrivals exceed service rate, the backlog grows without bound — at 333 arrivals a minute against 182 of service, it grows by 151 a minute, 9,060 an hour — and every request that joins inherits the entire accumulated delay. The user who would have been served instantly at 09:03 is now waiting behind everything that arrived since. So an unbounded queue does not protect p95, it destroys it, and it does so for everyone rather than for the subset who would have been refused. A queue is a lever only when it has a depth cap and an admission rule: accept while there is room, refuse honestly and immediately when there is not. Admission control is what turns a queue from a way of hiding overload into a way of managing it.

Which brings you to the four levers, and the reason they are four rather than one. Shed refuses some so the rest stay fast — you have chosen who loses. Queue makes everyone wait so nobody is refused — you have chosen that everyone loses a little, which is not obviously better. Degrade serves everyone worse — you have spent quality instead of latency. Borrow moves traffic to another provider or a smaller model — you have spent money, or quality you have not measured. Four different currencies, and no ordering between them that holds across products. That is precisely why the choice cannot be made during the incident: it is a product decision wearing an infrastructure costume, and the person qualified to make it is asleep.

Hence the ladder, and hence the fifth field. The trigger, the disabled feature, the customer-visible effect and the quality delta are all engineering. The pre-authorizer is not, and it is the one that makes the other four executable at 3am. An on-call engineer is not empowered to decide that every support answer gets worse tonight. They are entirely empowered to execute rung 3, which the VP of Support signed in March. The ladder's real function is converting a judgement call under pressure into an execution step.

One last piece: failover is a capacity lever, and it is the one that lies to you. Moving traffic to a second provider preserves availability and says nothing about quality, so an un-evaluated failover target turns a capacity incident into a quality incident that nobody detects — a silent 200 at fleet scale. Run the failover target against your golden set before you need it, write the delta in the runbook, and now it is a rung with a known quality cost rather than a save with an unknown one.
trade: Shed vs queue at saturation
Who absorbs the loss

Shedding refuses a subset and keeps everyone else fast, and you have to defend choosing who loses; queueing spreads the delay across everyone and quietly destroys p95 for users who would have been served instantly
Degrade to a smaller model vs reject honestly
A worse answer vs no answer

Degrading keeps the product working at a quality delta you should have measured, and risks shipping answers below your quality bar without saying so; rejecting is honest, costs you the interaction, and is far easier to explain afterwards
Headroom vs utilisation target
Cost per task vs tail latency
Running at 90% looks efficient on a cost dashboard and puts you a few points from the cliff; running at 70% is visibly wasteful and is what buys you a p95 that survives a peak nobody predicted
Multi-provider failover vs a single provider with a deeper ladder
Availability vs quality certainty and operational surface

Failover preserves uptime and imports a second quality profile, a second quota to negotiate and a second thing to evaluate; a deeper ladder keeps one known quality profile and accepts that a provider outage is visible to customers
scale: Quota is a schedule dependency with a lead time measured in weeks, so the peak-TPM number belongs in the design doc rather than the launch checklist - a quota you need in March is a conversation you start in January

Peak multipliers are usually larger than teams remember, because memory averages over the hour while the queue experiences the minute - derive the multiplier from per-minute data and expect it to be roughly double the number people quote from feel

The cliff moves as service time moves, so anything that lengthens a task (a longer chain, a bigger context, a slower model tier) raises offered load in erlangs and silently pushes a comfortable pool toward the edge without a single extra request arriving

Batch and interactive traffic must not share a quota pool without priority, or the nightly job will eat the interactive envelope at exactly the wrong moment - separate keys, separate limits, or an explicit priority scheme
sec: Rate limits are a security control as much as a capacity one: per-tenant admission caps stop one compromised or malformed account from consuming the envelope everyone else depends on, which is a denial of service you inflicted on yourself

Degraded rungs must not degrade authorisation - a smaller model, a template path or a cache-only mode still has to carry tenant scoping, and the rungs are exactly where that gets forgotten because they were written under time pressure

An unbounded queue is a resource-exhaustion surface, since anything that can enqueue cheaply can push the backlog past the point where legitimate traffic is unrecoverable; the depth cap is the control

Failover targets need their own security review, not an inherited one - a second provider means a second data-handling agreement, a second retention policy and a second place your customers' text now lives
capacity.interview:
The way I would put it in a planning meeting is that our behaviour at ten times load already exists — we just have not read it yet. And the first thing to get straight is that our ceiling probably is not our fleet. It is the tokens-per-minute our provider has agreed to, which does not scale by adding machines, it scales by a conversation with a lead time. So real capacity is the smaller of the two, and I want that number in the doc.

Then there is one result that always surprises people, so I would put it up front. Adding a queue to absorb bursts does not add capacity. It converts refusing a few people quickly into making everybody wait. If work arrives faster than we finish it, the backlog just grows and every request inherits the whole accumulated delay, so our median user gets slower in order that nobody gets told no. A queue only helps when it has a depth cap and an admission rule that refuses honestly at the boundary.

And then the actual deliverable, which is the ladder. Grids never go from on to off — they shed load in pre-agreed rungs, decided in daylight by people with the authority to decide them. We need the same: five rungs between working and honestly refusing, and each one has to say what turns off, what the customer sees, what the quality cost is, and who signed it. That last field is the whole point. At 3am the on-call engineer is not authorised to decide that support answers get worse tonight, but they are absolutely authorised to pull rung 3 that the VP signed in March.

seams.mech:
Exit cost is an arithmetic object with four terms, and every argument about lock-in is really a disagreement about one of them.

Term one, coupling. Distinct behaviours you depend on, times hours to port each. The word doing the work is distinct. A codebase with 31 call sites all going through one interface has three behaviours to port; a codebase with 14 call sites, each using a different corner of the vendor's filter language, has fourteen. This is why estimates made by counting call sites are wrong in both directions and why the audit that produces this number should be a grep for the vendor's import outside the adapter, not a story someone tells in standup.

Term two, egress. The one everyone remembers and the one that almost never dominates. Volume times a published per-gigabyte rate, plus the wall-clock to move it. Include it, then stop thinking about it.

Term three, re-derivation. The state you cannot copy and must recompute. Re-embedding a corpus, rebuilding an index, recomputing summaries. This is compute hours and it is usually cheap in money and awkward in calendar, because the rebuild has to happen while the old system is still serving.

Term four, revalidation. Number of eval suites times hours to re-run and re-baseline each. This is the term teams forget and it is frequently the largest. It is also the term with the interesting property: it is identical across every seam placement, because it depends on what you own rather than how you integrated. That structural fact is why eval ownership outranks abstraction design. Moving your suite in-house cuts the same number of hours off the wrapper option and the raw option, and it does it once for all future vendors.

Against exit cost stands carrying cost, and the comparison is deliberately asymmetric. Exit cost is probabilistic, you pay it only if you leave. Carrying cost is certain, you pay it every year regardless. So the correct comparison is expected saving against certain carry, and the derived quantity worth quoting is the break-even month: exit saving divided by annual carry, times twelve. If that lands at eleven months and your contract runs three years, the wrapper loses on arithmetic and you should say so plainly rather than building it because clean code feels responsible.

The last mechanism is the portability test, which converts all of this into a purchasing question. What must I keep if I leave? Whatever the answer names, golden sets, labelled traces, judge rubrics, tenant mappings, must be in your storage in a format you can read without them. Everything else is a rental, and rentals are fine. The mistake is not renting. The mistake is renting the one thing that makes substitution measurable.
trade: Config seam vs adapter seam for a model provider
Swap speed vs behavioural fidelity
A config-only swap ships a different personality to production and calls it a deploy
Owning the eval suite vs living on the vendor's platform
Portability vs a year of platform work you get to skip
The suite you don't own turns every substitution into an unmeasurable one, so nobody signs it off
Thin wrapper vs raw call sites
Certain annual carry vs probabilistic exit saving
Carrying a wrapper for three years to save four weeks once, at 35% probability
Protocol seam vs the vendor's proprietary edge
A live second option vs the 8% they genuinely do better
Standardising on the intersection, then quietly reaching around it in nine places
Multi-year term for a discount vs month-to-month
Unit price vs a contract tail inside the exit number
Finding out the exit cost includes eleven months you cannot cancel
scale: Exit cost grows with corpus size only through re-derivation; it grows with behaviours, and is nearly flat in call sites, which is exactly why teams mis-size it
Below roughly ten call sites the raw seam usually wins the arithmetic; past forty the wrapper wins on comprehension long before it wins on exit
Multi-region and multi-tenant deployments multiply the data seam, not the code seam, one egress bill per region and one deletion path per tenant boundary
Recompute the number at every renewal, corpus growth quietly doubles re-derivation while everyone in the room is still quoting last year's figure
sec: Data residency and subprocessor terms are part of the seam, a vendor who cannot honour a region constraint has already set your exit date for you
Termination clauses: how long do they hold data after notice, in what format, and who pays the egress, all three belong in the exit number
Key custody at the seam, if their SDK holds your provider credentials then the swap is also a rotation, with its own blast radius
Audit rights and log export, an exit you cannot evidence is an exit your compliance function will not approve regardless of the engineering estimate
seams.interview: The way I think about buying is that every vendor decision cuts a seam into the system, the surface where their thing meets ours, and where I put that seam and how much of our behaviour crosses it is our exit cost. There isn't another number. So before I look at pricing I count coupling points, distinct behaviours we'd depend on rather than call sites, because thirty-one calls through three methods is a three-point seam and fourteen calls each using a different filter dialect is a fourteen-point seam. Then I add egress, re-derivation, re-embedding and index builds, and eval revalidation, and I express the total in engineer-weeks, because money we can find on short notice and calendar we can't. My default is asymmetric: buy things whose output is portable, build things whose data is ours. In practice that means we hold the golden sets, the labelled traces and the judge rubrics no matter whose platform runs them, because you cannot swap what you cannot compare. And I price abstractions honestly, a wrapper has an annual carrying cost, so I divide the exit saving by it and get the number of months inside which leaving actually repays the indirection. Sometimes that number tells me to keep the mess, and I'd rather say that than build something tidy that loses on arithmetic.

statearch.mech:
Treat the system as a log and a set of materialised views over it, because that is what it is. The system of record accepts writes. Everything else, the index, the embeddings, the summary tables, the caches, the agent's memory file, the trace store, the eval fixtures, is a view that was correct at some past moment and has been drifting since. The design work is not choosing the stores. It is writing the contract each one owes the source.

The seven fields. Source. Maximum staleness. Invalidation trigger. Rebuild time. Rebuild cost. Tenant partition key. Deletion path. Every field is a decision someone is making whether or not they write it down, and the register exists so that the decision happens in a review rather than in an incident.

Staleness must be measured. The metric is the gap between a store's last successful write and its source's last write, sampled continuously. That single time series turns "the index is roughly current" into a number you can put next to the spec card's freshness tolerance, and it converts a class of quality regressions from mysteries into one-line diagnoses. The alternative is the stale-mirror incident: output goes wrong, the model is the suspicious component because it is the probabilistic one, and three weeks disappear into prompt archaeology while an index sits nine hours behind. The countermeasure is a diagnostic order, not a tool. Before anyone opens a prompt, compare last-rebuild to last-source-write for every store in the answer path.

Invalidation is not the same as a damage bound. A capture stream or a sweep detects that a view is wrong. A TTL merely limits how long you remain wrong without ever noticing. Both are legitimate engineering, and TTLs are often correct, but a register that records a TTL under invalidation is describing a store nothing will ever tell you about. The distinction matters most on deletion, because a TTL will eventually expire a deleted record while an invalidation trigger removes it now, and only one of those satisfies an erasure obligation with a deadline.

Re-index economics are a people bill, not a compute bill. Take a real corpus: 1.2M documents at roughly 1,400 tokens each is 1,680 million tokens. At any current embedding rate that is tens of dollars. Nine hours of index build is tens more. Then 60 engineer-hours to run the migration, verify the output and re-baseline the suites, and that term is 99% of the total. Divide your annual re-derivation budget by the result and you get the number of times a year you may change your mind about chunking or embedding. It is usually two or three, one of which is consumed by a mandatory model upgrade. That number, not enthusiasm, is what governs how fast the pipeline can improve, and it should be stated before the roadmap promises four experiments.

Rebuild time versus outage budget decides the cutover shape. If a full rebuild exceeds what you may be down, you cannot rebuild in place, so you build beside and swap an alias, and you accept a bounded window in which two indexes both claim to be true. Bound it, write it in the register, and decide what reads from the old one meanwhile. Make the rebuild idempotent and resumable, keyed by content hash, so a crash at 80% resumes rather than restarts. An unresumable nine-hour rebuild is a nine-hour rebuild you will avoid doing, and a rebuild you avoid doing is a mind you have stopped being able to change.

A rebuild that outruns the outage budget, so it never gets scheduled and the strategy never changes
Tenant partition key on every store vs filters at query time
Deletion and isolation you can express vs slightly less plumbing
A store where a scoped erasure literally cannot be written, discovered during the audit
Fewer derived stores vs a store per access pattern
Fan-out you can hold in your head vs local performance wins
Nine mirrors, four deletion paths, and nobody who can draw the graph from memory
scale: Rebuild time grows with corpus while the outage budget stays fixed, so every system eventually crosses into needing a dual-index cutover, plan the crossing before it arrives
Deletion fan-out grows with the number of stores, not with data volume, which is why adding a cache is a compliance change as well as a latency change
Per-tenant rebuild is the scaling escape hatch, a full corpus rebuild is unaffordable monthly while a per-tenant one is routine, if every store has the partition key
Capture-stream lag is bimodal, fine at the median and dreadful during bulk imports, so measure staleness at p99 and alert there rather than on the average
sec: Erasure obligations attach to derived copies, so the register is the evidence artifact, an auditor asks how many stores hold the record and the honest answer should be written down already
Access-control changes propagate exactly like deletions and are usually slower, a revoked permission that reaches the index in six hours is a six-hour leak with a metric attached
Trace stores are the quietest exposure in the system, they hold verbatim prompts including whatever was retrieved, under a retention policy nobody chose deliberately
Agent memory files are usually written without a tenant key or provenance, which makes them both undeletable and unattributable, fix the key before you fix the content
statearch.interview: The way I frame state in an AI system is that everything except the system of record is a mirror, the index, the embeddings, the caches, the summaries, the agent's memory file, the eval fixtures, and every mirror is wrong for some interval. Architecture is choosing that interval deliberately and making it visible. So I keep a derived-state register: one row per store, seven columns, source, maximum staleness, invalidation trigger, rebuild time, rebuild cost, tenant partition key, deletion path. Staleness has to be measured rather than intended, it's the gap between the store's last write and the source's, as a live metric, because otherwise a stale-mirror incident gets diagnosed as a model incident and you lose three weeks to prompt archaeology while an index sits nine hours behind. I'm strict about one distinction: a capture stream detects that a mirror is wrong, a TTL only bounds how long you stay wrong, and a TTL in the invalidation column means the store has no invalidation at all. Then I price re-derivation, corpus times tokens times the embedder rate, plus build hours, plus the engineer-hours to verify and re-baseline, and that last term is almost all of it. Dividing the annual budget by that gives the number of times a year we're allowed to change our mind about chunking. It's usually two, and one of them is spent on a model upgrade we didn't choose.

migrate.mech:
The dual-run is the whole mechanism. You never switch; you run both and measure. Everything else is a question about what evidence the dual-run produces and how much it costs to obtain.

The ladder, and what each rung cannot see. Offline eval runs the new version against cases you already wrote, so it is fast, cheap, repeatable, and blind to distribution shift by construction, it can only be wrong in the ways you anticipated. Shadow sends real production inputs to both versions and discards the new one's output; it catches schema changes, latency regressions and cost surprises on real input distribution, and it is structurally blind to user behaviour because nobody ever saw the output and therefore nobody clicked, abandoned, retried or escalated. Canary exposes real users and catches both classes, and pays for it in exposure time, which makes it slow precisely where failures are rare. Choosing a rung is choosing an ignorance, so name the ignorance in the plan.

Sample size is the plan. For a quality rate you can score, comparing new against control is a two-proportion test. Given baseline p, a minimum detectable effect delta, alpha and power, the required n per arm is fixed. The property that governs schedules is that n scales as 1/delta squared: at a 92% baseline, detecting a 1.5-point drop needs about 5,570 scored tasks per arm, and detecting a 3.0-point drop needs about 1,499, a 3.7x difference for a factor of two in resolution. Days at each percentage follow from that number divided by the scored volume that percentage yields, which is why the canary percentage and the scoring fraction are the same decision. During a rollout, score the entire canary cohort rather than your usual production sample, it is 5% of traffic and it is the only period where the sample rate is on the critical path.

Rare failures are a different calculation entirely. Average quality can look untouched while a 1-in-2,000 catastrophic path is live. To be 95% confident of observing at least one instance you need roughly 3/rate exposures, about 6,000 for that rate, which a 5% canary on 40,000 daily tasks reaches in three days and misses in one. Report exposures alongside percentages in every rollout plan, because percentages create a feeling of coverage that exposure counts flatly contradict.

Rollback is a number and a person. Metric, threshold, window, owner, all written before traffic moves, because a trigger negotiated while the metric is moving is not a trigger. Rehearsal is what converts the runbook into a capability: schedule it, run it with real traffic in staging, time it, and write the number down. If the last rehearsal was never, you have documentation, not rollback.

Data migrations follow the same logic with a longer tail: dual-write to both stores, backfill history, verify on a sample, then move the alias. The design question is the two-truths window, how long both stores claim to be correct and who reads which. Idempotent, resumable backfills keyed by content hash are what keep that window bounded, because a job that restarts from zero after a crash extends it by its entire runtime. And underneath all of it is the deprecation clock: providers publish kill dates, the dates do not move, so schedule backwards from them and start on the derived date rather than when the calendar feels comfortable.
trade: Shadow before canary vs going straight to canary

Automated rollback on threshold vs a human decision
Seconds to revert vs flapping on a noisy metric
Auto-rollback triggered by a scoring outage, or a human waiting for consensus at 02:00
One migration per quarter by policy vs migrating only when forced
Standing capability vs the work you skip
The first swap in fourteen months, run against an eval set that is fourteen months stale
scale: Higher traffic buys resolution for free, the same three-day canary detects a much smaller effect, so large systems should tighten the detectable effect rather than shorten the ladder
Low-traffic and long-tail surfaces cannot reach the sample at any percentage, so they migrate on offline eval plus a longer soak, and the plan should say that outright
Judge cost during rollout is bounded by cohort size, scoring 100% of a 5% canary costs 5% of traffic, which is why full canary scoring is affordable exactly when it matters
Backfill duration grows with corpus while the two-truths window should not, so resumability and per-tenant batching are what keep the window flat as you grow
sec: Shadow traffic duplicates real inputs into a second system, so it inherits every data-residency, retention and subprocessor constraint the primary path has
A rollback that reverts the model but leaves a new prompt or tool schema live is a configuration split-brain, version the behaviour bundle and revert it as one unit
Canary cohorts assigned by user identity leak the experiment across tenants in a shared workspace, partition on the tenant boundary rather than the user
Dual-write windows double the write surface, an access-control change during the window must reach both stores or the older one serves a revoked permission
migrate.interview: My starting position is that you never switch, you run both and let evidence decide, so the property I care about architecturally is whether shadow, canary and instant revert are configuration rather than code. If either half needs a deploy, every model change is a project and you'll run one every quarter forever. Then the real question is what evidence a given change has to produce. I think of it as a ladder where each rung is blind to something specific: offline eval only knows the cases we wrote, shadow misses user-behaviour change because nobody clicked anything, and canary catches both but is slow on rare failures. Picking a rung means picking what we've agreed not to know, so I say that out loud. And I insist the sample size lives in the rollout plan, not the retro. At a 92% baseline, detecting a point and a half needs about 5,570 scored tasks per arm; three points needs about 1,500, because n scales as one over delta squared. That's also the honest lever when a deprecation clock is short, you buy days with resolution, and you write down the drop you agreed not to detect and who signed for it. Rollback is a metric, a number, a window and a named person, rehearsed quarterly, because if you've never rolled back you don't have rollback.

quality.mech:
You have five control points, each with fixed properties you cannot design around. The offline CI gate is cheap and blocks releases, the strongest authority here because it stops the change rather than the response - and it is structurally blind to production distribution, because it scores a fixed set that stops resembling live traffic the day after you freeze it. The input rail is cheap, sits before the expensive work, and blocks requests, so its false positives reach the user as a refusal to try. The output rail blocks responses and taxes the latency budget of every single response, including the 99.7% that were fine, which is why a deterministic output rail is worth a great deal and a model-call one usually isn't. Async online sampling costs zero milliseconds and sees real traffic, but detects hours or days late and prevents nothing. Human review has the highest fidelity on the list and does not scale, which isn't a flaw but a placement instruction: maximum blast radius, minimum volume.

The composition rules follow from that. Only blocking control points change the escaped-defect rate, and they compose multiplicatively on the residual: three blocking checks catching 22%, 18% and 10% of the defect stream leave 0.78 x 0.82 x 0.90 = 57.6% of it, not 50%. Detecting-only control points leave the escape rate exactly where it was and buy you a shorter blind window instead, which is a real purchase but a different one, and conflating the two is the most common modelling error in these designs. Deterministic rails and semantic checks also don't catch the same things: a well-formed, correctly-cited, confidently wrong answer passes a schema rail and a citation-existence rail at 100%, every time, by construction. That's why a design made entirely of cheap rails has a great p95 and no ability to see the failure mode that actually damages trust.

The budget arithmetic is the whole conversation. Every control point contributes added p95 (zero for anything off the request path), dollars per task equal to its per-invocation cost times the share of traffic it inspects, and a false-block count equal to volume times coverage times false-positive rate. Sum the first against your latency headroom, the second against your cost ceiling, and price the third in whatever a blocked good answer costs you downstream. Combinations that break either envelope are not options, no matter how much anyone likes them, and saying so with a number ends the debate in about forty seconds.

Detection lag is a division you should do out loud. Events per day equals daily volume times the regression's incidence times your sampling rate times the recognition rate of whatever is doing the scoring. Days to alarm is your alarm threshold divided by that. Run it once for your real numbers and the sampling-rate argument resolves itself, because most teams discover their round 1% produces a two-to-three week lag on the regressions they're most afraid of.

And the control points themselves decay. The judge drifts when the provider ships a new version or when traffic moves somewhere the rubric never anticipated, so it needs a control point of its own: a periodic agreement check against fresh human labels, with a threshold and a page target. The golden set decays the same way, which makes it a product artifact with an owner and a growth rule rather than a file in a repo. A quality system with no control point on its own control points will pass every check on the day it stops working.

Escapes prevented vs latency headroom and false blocks
A p95 you can't meet plus a false-block bill larger than the damage you prevented
Deterministic rail vs model-based check
Cost and speed vs the class of defect it can see at all
A fast, cheap wall of rails that is structurally blind to confidently wrong answers
Offline CI gate vs online sampling
Blocks the change vs sees real traffic
Green releases all quarter while production quality slides, or detection with nothing to block
Higher sampling rate vs lower scoring spend
Detection lag vs cost per task
A round sampling number that produces a three-week blind window on your worst regression
Human review on volume vs on blast radius
Examples seen vs damage prevented
Reviewers drowning in low-stakes traffic while the irreversible flow goes unwatched
scale: Rails scale with traffic, human review does not: past roughly a few hundred reviews a day you are choosing what humans see, so choose by blast radius and write the rule down
At 3x peak an output rail's p95 contribution doesn't change, it's just charged 3x as often - what breaks first is the scoring queue behind async sampling, so give it its own degradation rung
Tier the sampling rate by route rather than globally - 100% on the money-moving route, 1% on the browse route - which buys detection lag where it matters at a fraction of the cost
Escape count and false-block cost both grow linearly with volume, so the crossover between two placements is itself a volume number - compute it once and record it as a revisit trigger
sec: An input rail is a security control and a quality control at once with a single authority, so decide whether a suspected-malicious request is blocked or logged before an incident forces it
False blocks are a denial-of-service surface: if a rail can be reliably triggered by user-supplied content, someone can lock a competitor's tenant out of your product
Control-point logs hold the raw inputs and outputs that failed, making them the highest-sensitivity store in the system and the one most often exempted from retention policy
A record-only control point on a compliance-relevant behaviour is a documented, dated record that you knew and chose not to stop - assign real authority or don't build the check
quality.interview: I don't think about quality as a score, I think about it as a set of places in the system where something is authorized to say no. There are five to choose from: a CI gate that can block a release, an input rail that can block a request, an output rail that can block a response, async sampling that can open a ticket, and human review that can stop something outright but doesn't scale. Architecture is picking how many of those you have, where they sit, and what each one is allowed to stop, and then paying for every one of them out of the latency and cost budgets. So when someone says we need better evals, my first two questions are what is it allowed to block and who gets paged, and my third is what it costs in milliseconds and dollars against the headroom we actually have. If the answer to the first question is nothing, it's a dashboard, not a control point. And I always do the detection-lag division out loud, because a one percent sample against a half-percent regression means you find out next quarter, and nobody realises that until you divide it in front of them.

orgarch.mech:
The split, as a rule you can apply rather than a philosophy. An artifact belongs to platform when divergence across teams is expensive or unrecoverable, and to product when speed of change is worth more than consistency. That one test resolves nearly every case. Model traffic: divergence means six sets of keys, no aggregate rate limiting, and unattributable spend, so platform. Key custody: divergence means a credential in a repository somewhere, so platform. Trace schema: divergence means you cannot join two teams' logs during an incident, so platform - and it is the one genuinely irreversible artifact, because every trace already written stays in its old shape. Eval runner and storage: commodity, so platform. Golden sets and judges encode domain judgement, and a suite the product team doesn't believe is one they route around, so product. Prompts, tool definitions, retrieval tuning and UX are product, always.

The matrix is three columns because ownership without paging is a fiction. Owner means the team whose backlog the change lands in. Approver means the team that must agree before an irreversible change happens. Paged means whose phone rings at 2am. Each degenerate cell has a signature you can go and find. No owner: the artifact decays silently, you hear about it from a user, and the fix lands in whichever team happened to notice, which is how golden sets rot. Two owners on a choke point: divergent configuration, shadow spend, and an incident nobody can roll back in one place. Owner and pager differ: mean time to repair permanently includes a handoff, because the paged team can only mitigate and the owning team has to fix it the next morning. Approver equals owner on an irreversible artifact: the change that cannot be undone receives the least scrutiny in the whole system.

Four topologies, each with a team count where it stops working. One central team owning everything is right at one to three product teams and becomes a queue at roughly five. Fully embedded engineers with no platform work up to four or five teams, then produce duplicate infrastructure faster than anyone consolidates it, and you end up paying for three vector stores and two gateways. Platform plus product is stable from about four teams to about twenty, which is where most organisations should land. A guild - a cross-team forum with no dedicated staff - works below three teams and fails the moment anything needs a single owner, because a guild is structurally incapable of owning a choke point.

The interface contract is what stops the platform becoming a review queue. State what the platform guarantees numerically: a p99 gateway overhead ceiling, an availability target, a spend report by feature tag, failover behaviour. Then state what a product team must supply to get it: the required trace fields, a declared latency and cost budget per route, and an eval coverage threshold before a route may take production traffic. All three are machine-checkable, which is the entire point - a contract a CI job enforces scales with team count, and a contract a human enforces scales with reviewer count. That difference is the slope change in the bottleneck estimator, and it's why the paved road is an engineering artifact rather than an advocacy campaign.

Finally, the rotation split, which is the highest-signal question in this module. "The API is slow" and "the answers got worse" are different pages: different symptoms, different diagnostics, different fixes, and usually different people. Availability pages go to the rotation that owns the infrastructure. Quality pages should go to a rotation that owns the model behaviour and has runbooks for it - roll back the prompt version, check judge agreement, compare canary quality scores against control. Send quality pages to the availability rotation and they arrive as an alert nobody can act on, get acknowledged and ignored twice, and then get tuned into silence. Ask an organisation which rotation receives "the answers got worse" and you learn what their ownership matrix actually says, whatever the document claims.

Separate quality rotation vs one combined rotation
Right skills on the page vs on-call load per person

Mandating the platform vs making it the easy path
