High compliance, low adoption, and a shadow stack that appears the quarter after the mandate lapses
scale: The bottleneck quarter is computable: reviews per team per quarter times team count against reviewer capacity, with the queue biting at about 80% utilisation rather than at 100%
Team growth is the input people forget - run the estimator forward four to eight quarters at your real hiring rate, because the answer arrives sooner than anyone's intuition
Platform headcount scales sub-linearly with team count only if the contract is machine-checked; if humans check it, platform headcount scales linearly and you have built a services org
Past roughly twenty product teams the platform itself needs an internal split - traffic, data, quality - and the same choke-point rule applies one level down
sec: Key custody is the clearest choke point in the whole matrix: one owner, one rotation, one revocation path, and no product team holding a raw provider credential
An unowned artifact is an unpatched artifact - the row with an empty owner cell is where a disclosed vulnerability sits for a quarter because nobody's backlog it lands in
Approver equal to owner on an irreversible artifact defeats separation of duties, which is both a security control and the reason your auditor asks for this matrix
Paved-road adoption is a security metric, not just an engineering one: every team outside the road is a set of credentials, rails and logs outside your controls
orgarch.interview: The way I think about it is that the seam is a team: every interface I draw becomes a handoff between people, so when I draw the system I've drawn the org chart it's going to grow into, and I'd rather do that on purpose. The rule I use for splitting is that platform owns the places where divergence is expensive or unrecoverable - model traffic, key custody, the trace schema, eval infrastructure, the rails - and product owns whatever has to move at feature speed, which is prompts, tools, retrieval tuning and the golden sets, because a suite the product team doesn't believe is a suite they route around. Then I write a one-page matrix, ten artifacts against owner, approver and who gets paged, and I audit it: unowned cells, two owners on a choke point, and any row where the owner isn't the one being paged. Each of those has an incident signature I can usually find in the last two quarters. And I always compute the bottleneck quarter, because reviews per team times team count against reviewer capacity tells you the date the platform stops being leverage, and hiring another reviewer just moves that date, while turning the review into a contract CI can check changes the slope.

review.mech:
The document is eleven artifacts and a contradiction check. Assembly isn't clerical work: it's the first time the artifacts sit where they can be compared, and comparison is where the findings are. Nearly every real finding is two artifacts disagreeing while each is individually defensible - budgets that don't sum to the spec card, a staleness bound four pages from the tolerance it violates, an action inventory granting auto-execute on the thing the blast-radius line ruled out. Humans miss these because the two halves are read on different days by different people: a mechanical problem with a mechanical fix, which is why the Patterns tab ships a linter rather than a template.

Record constraints and their sources, not conclusions. "We chose the two-stage shape" is dead prose within a year: nobody can tell whether the reason still holds, so the design becomes load-bearing by inertia. "Rejected the agentic planner: measured p95 7,400ms against a 3,000ms requirement, benchmark dated March, rerun when the requirement or the model changes" stays alive indefinitely, because a reader can check every clause. The test for your own document: could a competent stranger determine whether each reason has expired, using only what's on the page? If not, you recorded an outcome and threw away the reasoning.

Running the review. Assign the red-team role by name, in the invitation, with the document a day early - unassigned dissent does not appear in a room containing the author's manager, and pretending otherwise is how designs get approved unanimously and fail predictably. Ask the ten questions in yield order rather than walking the document in page order, because page order is the author's order and defends the author's assumptions by construction. Close with a pre-mortem: "it is twelve months later and this failed, why?" The past-tense framing produces more and more specific answers than "what are the risks?", because it asks for explanation rather than speculation.

The ten questions, ordered by yield. 1. Which number on the spec card forced this shape, and where did it come from? 2. Do the stage budgets sum to within the spec card - latency, cost per task, cost per month at peak? Add them out loud. 3. For each control point, what is it allowed to block, and who is paged when it fires? 4. For each derived store, what is the staleness bound and the invalidation path inside it? 5. Which actions are irreversible, and who approves each one? 6. Show me the degradation ladder and the name that pre-authorised each rung. 7. Which failure modes have low detectability, and is the control for each one structural rather than an alert? 8. What's the exit cost in engineer-weeks for each vendor seam? 9. What's the migration's rollback trigger as a number, and who owns pulling it? 10. Who owns each artifact and who gets paged for it? Questions 2 through 4 produce most findings in most reviews, which is exactly why they're not at the end, where an hour that overruns would drop them.

Saying it shouldn't be built with AI. This is a legitimate architectural output and it needs to be cheap to reach, which means holding it to the same standard as any other rejected shape: name the binding constraint and the number behind it. "The bar implied by this blast radius is 99.95% task success; our best measured shape reaches 96.5%; closing that requires human review on 100% of traffic at $0.42 per task against a $0.03 ceiling" is an engineering conclusion. "It feels risky" is a career risk. Building the number is what makes declining respectable in a room that's excited.

Keeping it alive. Revisit triggers are numeric conditions on spec-card values, each with an owner watching it: volume triples, the cost ceiling moves, the p95 target moves, the freshness tolerance moves, or a provider posts a deprecation notice on a seam you priced an exit for. Never a calendar date - calendar reviews get skipped in busy quarters, and busy quarters are precisely when the numbers move.

A revisit trigger on provider deprecation is also a supply-chain control, because a deprecated model version is an unmaintained dependency with your traffic running through it
review.interview: The way I think about an architecture review is that the artifact isn't the diagram, it's the argument: given these constraints, these alternatives were considered, this one was chosen, and here's exactly what would change our mind. So the document records the constraint and its source rather than the conclusion, because a doc that says we chose X without the number that forced it is unmaintainable in twelve months - nobody can tell whether the reason expired. When I review someone else's system I ask ten questions in yield order, and the first four find most of it: which number forced this shape, do the stage budgets actually sum to the spec card, what is each control point allowed to block and who's paged, and for each derived store what's the staleness bound and the invalidation path. Almost every real finding is two artifacts contradicting each other while each looks fine alone, so I'd rather run a linter over the document as structured data than trust a room to hold eleven pages open at once. Then I assign someone to argue the rejected shape, run a ten-minute pre-mortem, and set revisit triggers on numbers rather than on a calendar - because the calendar review is the one that gets skipped in the quarter the volume tripled.

reqs.intro: A spec card you can't validate is a wish list. This is the card as a dataclass with a validate() that refuses — it names the offending field, says why it's unarchitectable, and hands back a reformulation you can paste into the ticket. Then feasible_shapes() filters the architecture table by what's left, printing what's already eliminated and by which number. Run it on the real ticket you were handed this week; the refusals are your elicitation agenda.
reqs.code:
"""SPEC CARD - the six numbers that turn an AI ask into a design constraint.

Stdlib only. Deterministic. No network. Run: python spec_card.py

Prices and per-call latency are PARAMETERS, not facts baked into this file.
Refresh unit_call_cost_usd / unit_call_p95_ms from your own traces and every
verdict below moves with them. The shape names match the shape ladder.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Any, List, Tuple

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- vocabulary

VAGUE = (
    "accurate", "accuracy", "real time", "real-time", "realtime", "instant",
    "fast", "snappy", "cheap", "cheapest", "anything", "everything", "asap",
    "high quality", "world class", "best in class", "scalable", "always",
    "fresh", "up to date", "reasonable", "good enough", "seamless",
)

FIX = {
    "quality_bar": "a pass rate on a named set, e.g. 0.92",
    "quality_metric": "the measurement AND the set: exact-match on 300 labelled tickets",
    "golden_set_size": "an integer count of cases you have actually labelled (>= 50)",
    "abstain_allowed": "the share of cases the system may refuse, e.g. 0.08",
    "p95_latency_ms": "a p95 in milliseconds, e.g. 3500",
    "interaction_mode": "one of: interactive, async, batch",
    "cost_per_task_usd": "dollars per completed task, retries included, e.g. 0.08",
    "monthly_ceiling_usd": "the monthly number finance actually signed, e.g. 12000",
    "tasks_per_day": "steady-state completed tasks per day, e.g. 4000",
    "peak_multiplier": "peak-over-steady ratio measured from traffic, e.g. 3.0",
    "blast_radius": "one of: cosmetic, recoverable, costly, unrecoverable",
    "worst_output": "one sentence naming the worst single wrong output",
    "freshness_max_age_min": "max tolerable staleness in minutes, or -1 for a static corpus",
}

MODES = ("interactive", "async", "batch")
RADII = ("cosmetic", "recoverable", "costly", "unrecoverable")

NUMERIC = {
    "quality_bar": (0.0, 1.0),
    "abstain_allowed": (0.0, 0.5),
    "golden_set_size": (50, 10 ** 7),
    "p95_latency_ms": (50, 60 * 60 * 1000),
    "cost_per_task_usd": (0.0, 1000.0),
    "monthly_ceiling_usd": (1.0, 10 ** 9),
    "tasks_per_day": (1, 10 ** 9),
    "peak_multiplier": (1.0, 100.0),
    "freshness_max_age_min": (-1, 10 ** 7),
}


@dataclass
class SpecCard:
    """Six fields. Every blank needs a number AND a source."""
    name: str = "unnamed feature"
    # 1 - quality bar and the measurement that defines it
    quality_bar: Any = None
    quality_metric: Any = None
    golden_set_size: Any = None
    abstain_allowed: Any = None
    # 2 - latency budget and interaction mode
    p95_latency_ms: Any = None
    interaction_mode: Any = None
    # 3 - cost ceiling, per task and per month
    cost_per_task_usd: Any = None
    monthly_ceiling_usd: Any = None
    # 4 - volume, steady and peak
    tasks_per_day: Any = None
    peak_multiplier: Any = None
    # 5 - blast radius
    blast_radius: Any = None
    worst_output: Any = None
    # 6 - freshness tolerance
    freshness_max_age_min: Any = None


Problem = Tuple[str, str, str, str]  # field, found, why unarchitectable, fix


def _is_number(v: Any) -> bool:
    return isinstance(v, (int, float)) and not isinstance(v, bool)


def _vague_hit(v: Any) -> str:
    if not isinstance(v, str):
        return ""
    low = v.lower()
    for w in VAGUE:
        if w in low:
            return w
    return ""


def validate(spec: SpecCard) -> List[Problem]:
    """Refuse any spec containing a field you cannot design against."""
    out: List[Problem] = []

    for name, (lo, hi) in NUMERIC.items():
        v = getattr(spec, name)
        if v is None:
            out.append((name, "blank",
                        "no number, so no architecture can be eliminated", FIX[name]))
        elif not _is_number(v):
            hit = _vague_hit(v)
            why = ("the word %s is not a threshold on a distribution" % hit) if hit \
                else "a string where a number belongs"
            out.append((name, repr(v), why, FIX[name]))
        elif not (lo <= v <= hi):
            out.append((name, repr(v),
                        "outside the plausible range %s..%s" % (lo, hi), FIX[name]))

    for name, allowed in (("interaction_mode", MODES), ("blast_radius", RADII)):
        v = getattr(spec, name)
        if v not in allowed:
            out.append((name, repr(v),
                        "must be one of %s" % (", ".join(allowed)), FIX[name]))

    for name in ("quality_metric", "worst_output"):
        v = getattr(spec, name)
        if not isinstance(v, str) or len(v.strip()) < 12:
            out.append((name, repr(v), "unstated, so nobody can falsify it", FIX[name]))
        else:
            hit = _vague_hit(v)
            if hit:
                out.append((name, repr(v),
                            "%s names a feeling, not a measurement" % hit, FIX[name]))

    # Cross-field arithmetic: the card must not contradict itself.
    if _is_number(spec.cost_per_task_usd) and _is_number(spec.tasks_per_day) \
            and _is_number(spec.monthly_ceiling_usd):
        implied = spec.cost_per_task_usd * spec.tasks_per_day * 30.0
        if implied > spec.monthly_ceiling_usd:
            out.append((
                "monthly_ceiling_usd",
                "$%.0f/mo vs implied $%.0f/mo" % (spec.monthly_ceiling_usd, implied),
                "per-task cost x volume x 30 already exceeds the monthly ceiling",
                "cut cost per task to <= $%.4f, or raise the ceiling to $%.0f"
                % (spec.monthly_ceiling_usd / (spec.tasks_per_day * 30.0), implied),
            ))

    if _is_number(spec.quality_bar) and _is_number(spec.abstain_allowed):
        if spec.quality_bar + spec.abstain_allowed > 1.0:
            out.append((
                "abstain_allowed",
                "%.2f + %.2f > 1.00" % (spec.quality_bar, spec.abstain_allowed),
                "you cannot answer correctly and abstain on the same case",
                "quality_bar + abstain_allowed must be <= 1.0",
            ))

    return out


def report(spec: SpecCard) -> bool:
    probs = validate(spec)
    print("SPEC CARD: %s" % spec.name)
    if not probs:
        print("  ACCEPTED - all six fields carry a number you can design against.")
        return True
    print("  REFUSED - %d unarchitectable field(s):" % len(probs))
    for f, found, why, fix in probs:
        print("    %-22s found %-30s %s" % (f, found[:30], why))
        print("    %-22s   ->  %s" % ("", fix))
    return False


# ---------------------------------------------------- archetype feasibility
# cost_mult / lat_mult are multiples of ONE baseline model call, which you pass
# in. Nothing here rots when prices change.

ARCHETYPES = (
    # id,              label,                    cost_mult, lat_mult, fixed_ms, verifiable
    ("single_call",    "single call",                  1.0,      1.0,       30, False),
    ("prompt_chain",   "prompt chain/workflow",        2.6,      2.4,       60, True),
    ("retrieval_read", "retrieval read path",          1.9,      1.5,      220, True),
    ("agent_loop",     "single-agent tool loop",       6.5,      5.2,      400, True),
    ("orchestrator",   "orchestrator-worker",         14.0,      3.1,      650, True),
    ("batch_pipeline", "offline batch pipeline",       0.5,    900.0,    60000, True),
)


def feasible_shapes(spec: SpecCard, unit_call_cost_usd: float,
                    unit_call_p95_ms: float) -> list:
    """Filter the ladder by the card. Print what is already eliminated, and why."""
    print("\nFEASIBLE SHAPES for: %s" % spec.name)
    print("  parameters: unit call = $%.4f, p95 %dms  (refresh from your traces)"
          % (unit_call_cost_usd, unit_call_p95_ms))
    print("  %-24s %10s %9s   %s" % ("shape", "cost/task", "p95", "verdict"))
    survivors = []
    for sid, label, cmult, lmult, fixed, verifiable in ARCHETYPES:
        cost = cmult * unit_call_cost_usd
        p95 = lmult * unit_call_p95_ms + fixed
        reasons = []
        if cost > spec.cost_per_task_usd:
            reasons.append("cost $%.4f > ceiling $%.4f" % (cost, spec.cost_per_task_usd))
        if p95 > spec.p95_latency_ms:
            reasons.append("p95 %.0fms > budget %.0fms" % (p95, spec.p95_latency_ms))
        if spec.interaction_mode == "interactive" and sid == "batch_pipeline":
            reasons.append("batch cannot serve an interactive mode")
        if spec.blast_radius in ("costly", "unrecoverable") and not verifiable:
            reasons.append("blast radius %s needs a verification seam" % spec.blast_radius)
        verdict = "FEASIBLE" if not reasons else "rejected: " + "; ".join(reasons)
        print("  %-24s %10s %9s   %s"
              % (label, "$%.4f" % cost, "%.0fms" % p95, verdict))
        if not reasons:
            survivors.append((sid, label, cost, p95))
    if survivors:
        sid, label, cost, p95 = survivors[0]
        print("  --> lowest feasible rung: %s ($%.4f, %.0fms). Climbing higher needs a"
              % (label, cost, p95))
        print("      written forcing constraint naming which card field forced the climb.")
    else:
        print("  --> nothing on the ladder clears this card. The card is the bug.")
    return survivors


# --------------------------------------------------------------------- demo

def main() -> None:
    ticket = SpecCard(
        name="Add AI search to our support portal (as written)",
        quality_bar="should be accurate",
        quality_metric="users like the answers",
        golden_set_size=None,
        abstain_allowed=None,
        p95_latency_ms="real-time",
        interaction_mode="fast",
        cost_per_task_usd="as cheap as possible",
        monthly_ceiling_usd=None,
        tasks_per_day=None,
        peak_multiplier=None,
        blast_radius=None,
        worst_output="a bad answer",
        freshness_max_age_min="always fresh",
    )
    report(ticket)

    print()
    faq = SpecCard(
        name="Support search - self-serve FAQ",
        quality_bar=0.92,
        quality_metric="human-graded correct on a 300-case golden set of real tickets",
        golden_set_size=300,
        abstain_allowed=0.08,
        p95_latency_ms=3500,
        interaction_mode="interactive",
        cost_per_task_usd=0.08,
        monthly_ceiling_usd=12000,
        tasks_per_day=4000,
        peak_multiplier=3.0,
        blast_radius="recoverable",
        worst_output="a confidently wrong answer the user sees and escalates anyway",
        freshness_max_age_min=1440,
    )
    if report(faq):
        feasible_shapes(faq, unit_call_cost_usd=0.012, unit_call_p95_ms=1400)

    print()
    auto = SpecCard(**dict(faq.__dict__,
                           name="Support search - auto-closes the ticket",
                           quality_bar=0.985,
                           abstain_allowed=0.01,
                           blast_radius="costly",
                           worst_output="a wrong answer auto-closes a billing dispute and the customer churns",
                           cost_per_task_usd=0.30,
                           p95_latency_ms=9000,
                           interaction_mode="async"))
    if not report(auto):
        # The card caught the contradiction before anyone drew a box. Take the
        # refusal back to finance, get the ceiling raised, then re-run.
        print("  (ceiling renegotiated to $36000 on the strength of that arithmetic)")
        auto = SpecCard(**dict(auto.__dict__, monthly_ceiling_usd=36000))
    if report(auto):
        feasible_shapes(auto, unit_call_cost_usd=0.012, unit_call_p95_ms=1400)

    print()
    print("Same sentence, two blast radii, two ladders. Field 5 picked the")
    print("architecture - not the ask, and not the enthusiasm in the room.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
notes: Prices and per-call latency are parameters, never constants. Refresh unit_call_cost_usd and unit_call_p95_ms from your own traces and every verdict moves with them — that is the only way a tool like this survives a year.

The cross-field check earns its keep: cost per task × volume × 30 versus the monthly ceiling catches a contradiction that survives most design reviews, because the two numbers usually come from two different people who never met.

Note what the demo does with the refusal — it doesn't shrug and continue, it takes the arithmetic to finance and re-runs with a renegotiated ceiling. A refusal is an input to a conversation, not a dead end.
The archetype table deliberately uses the same six shape names as the shape ladder. Keeping one vocabulary across your calculators is what makes their outputs composable in a design doc.
Verifiability is a hard gate, not a cost: a blast radius of "costly" or worse rejects any shape with no seam to check the output before it lands, regardless of how cheap or fast that shape is.
