failure.exp: To grade the answer, the scorer must resolve supplier and effective date against the contract table. That deterministic lookup is the correct answer. If you can build the detector, build the answer instead and delete the generative surface for that question class.

blast.q: An agent can read CRM records, read customer-written tickets, and send email. Rails are in place. What is the correct architectural read?
o: Acceptable, since the injection classifier reduces the risk to a manageable residual level
An escalation path exists in every turn, and one of the three legs has to be broken
Acceptable, provided outbound email is logged and reviewed by a human within the hour
A monitoring problem, since the risk only materialises when an actual payload arrives
blast.exp: Private data, attacker-writable content and egress in one turn is the lethal trifecta, and rails only lower the probability of a path that structurally exists. At meaningful volume, a non-zero probability is a schedule. Break a leg or accept it in writing.

blast.q: Volume is 20,000 actions a month, tolerance is 4 bad actions, and the action is irreversible. What per-generation accuracy does that demand?
o: 99.98%, because essentially every bad generation becomes a bad action at this tier
99.20%, since the tolerance of four spreads across the full month's action volume
96.00%, which is a realistic target for a well-tuned model on a narrow task domain
99.60%, matching the standard reliability bar for any customer-facing write path
blast.exp: Required accuracy is 1 - T / (V x E). At the irreversible tier E is 1.0, so it is 1 - 4/20,000 = 99.98%. Compare that to the same tolerance behind an approval gate, where E drops to about 0.05 and the requirement falls to 99.60%.

blast.q: Why should the token an agent action executes with be scoped narrower than the user who triggered the turn?
o: Narrow tokens are cheaper to rotate, which lowers the operational cost of key management
Provider rate limits are applied per token, so narrower scopes spread load more evenly
A compromised turn should not be able to do everything its human is permitted to do
Audit logs are easier to read when each action carries its own dedicated credential
blast.exp: Impersonating the user contains nothing: the turn inherits everything the human could do. A token scoped to the operations and records this task needs turns containment into a structural fact enforced by a system that has never read the prompt.

blast.q: A semantic cache keyed on question text serves tenant A's stored answer to tenant B. Why is this scored as a severe and near-undetectable row?
o: Cache hits skip the guardrails, so the answer is never checked before it is returned
The answer is plausible and correct-looking, so nothing downstream flags it as wrong
Cache entries have no trace attached, making post-incident reconstruction impossible
Cross-tenant reads are logged as errors, but the logs are sampled at too low a rate
blast.exp: The leaked answer looks exactly like a correct answer, so no rail, reviewer or user reports it. That combination of high severity and high detectability score forces a structural fix: the tenant identifier belongs inside the cache key, with a test proving the miss.

blast.q: Removing send_email costs 232 agent-hours a month. Narrowing recipients to ticket participants costs 14 hours. What makes the second option a real bulkhead?
o: The recipient list is resolved from data that existed before the untrusted content arrived
The allowlist is checked at call time, immediately before the outbound request is issued
The remaining volume is small enough that a human can review each outbound message
The model is instructed to only address participants already present on the ticket record
blast.exp: An allowlist is only a boundary when the compromised turn cannot influence its contents. Resolving recipients from the ticket record as it stood before the turn began means the attacker never had a write to the destination set. Checking at call time against a list the turn produced is theatre.

blast.q: An agent times out mid-way through a non-idempotent write and the harness retries. What has that retry actually accomplished?
o: It has recovered cleanly, since the original write never committed before the timeout
It has converted an ambiguous outcome into a confirmed duplicate side effect
It has doubled the latency budget for this request but left the data model consistent
It has triggered the compensating action, which will reconcile both writes on the next pass
blast.exp: A timeout tells you nothing about whether the write landed. Retrying without an idempotency key turns "maybe once" into "probably twice". Idempotency keys plus a designed compensating action are what let a retry be safe and a mistake be undone.

blast.q: Where does dual control belong on a system with a mix of high-volume and consequential operations?
o: On the highest-volume path, where the greatest number of bad outcomes can be prevented
On every write path, since a uniform policy is far simpler to audit and to explain
On rare irreversible operations, because it degrades badly when applied under load
On the read paths that touch private data, where a leak cannot be undone afterwards
blast.exp: A second approver who clears everything in four seconds has cost you latency and bought a log line. Dual control works where the operation is rare enough that the reviewer stays engaged, and irreversible enough that the delay is obviously worth it.

blast.q: Your model measures 94.0%. Required accuracy is 99.90% at act-with-undo and 93.3% at suggest. What is the honest recommendation?
o: Ship at act-with-undo and close the gap with prompt work over the following two sprints
Ship at suggest now, since a tier demotion is an accuracy gain you cannot otherwise buy
Hold the launch until an evaluation harness can verify the model reaches 99.90% reliably
Ship at act-with-undo behind a feature flag while a larger model is procured and tested
blast.exp: Nobody is delivering a 99.90% model this quarter at any price, and the gap was never a modelling problem. Demoting the tier multiplies the error budget by more than three hundred and lands the requirement below what you already measure.

capacity.q: 40,000 tasks a day at 4,400 effective tokens each, with an 8x Monday peak. What throughput do you request, before headroom?
o: About 978,000 TPM, from 122,000 steady multiplied by the peak factor of eight
About 122,000 TPM, since the daily average is what a provider quota is sized against
About 293,000 TPM, using a blended factor that averages peak hours against quiet ones
About 176,000,000 TPM, which is the daily effective token total across all tasks
capacity.exp: 40,000/86,400 = 0.463 tasks a second; times 4,400 tokens times 60 gives 122,222 TPM steady; times 8 gives 977,778. Quotas are enforced per minute, so you size against the peak minute, not the daily average, and then add headroom on top.

capacity.q: Arrivals are 3.7 tasks a second and each task takes 9.0 seconds end to end. What does Little's Law tell you?
o: Peak throughput is 33 tasks a second once the pool has fully warmed up under load
Mean queue wait will be 33 seconds at the utilisation the current pool is running at
33 tasks are in flight at all times, which is the floor on concurrency, not a target
33 workers is the right pool size, giving a comfortable margin above the arrival rate
capacity.exp: L = lambda x W = 3.7 x 9.0 = 33.3 tasks in flight. That is a floor: a pool of 34 runs at 98% utilisation, which is deep past the cliff. You size above it — 42 workers puts you at 79% and a 0.11 second wait.

capacity.q: At fixed load, 42 workers gives 79% utilisation and 0.11s of wait; 34 gives 98% and 11.73s. What is the design lesson?
o: Wait rises asymptotically near saturation, so utilisation past ~80% is a latency risk
Wait scales roughly linearly with utilisation, so trimming the pool has a predictable cost
The pool should be sized to the arrival rate, since service time is what drives the wait
Utilisation is an efficiency metric, and the extra workers are unused capacity to reclaim
capacity.exp: Six workers, a hundredfold change in wait, with load and service time unchanged. Above roughly 80% the queueing curve turns asymptotic, so the last few points of utilisation buy little cost saving and account for most of your tail latency.

capacity.q: Demand is 333 tasks a minute against 182 of capacity, and someone adds an uncapped queue to absorb the burst. What happens?
o: Throughput improves, because work is smoothed across minutes instead of arriving in bursts
Backlog grows 151 a minute and every arriving request inherits the accumulated delay
p95 improves for most users, while the slowest 45% of requests absorb the added waiting
The system stabilises once the queue reaches its natural depth at the current arrival rate
capacity.exp: A queue converts refusal into waiting; it creates no capacity. With arrivals above service rate the backlog grows without bound — 151 a minute, 9,060 an hour — and the user who would have been instant at 09:03 waits behind all of it. Depth cap plus admission control is what makes a queue a lever.

capacity.q: Four saturation levers: shed, queue, degrade, borrow. Why must the choice be made before the incident rather than during it?
o: The levers must be applied in a fixed order, and getting that sequence wrong cascades
Only one lever can be active at a time, so picking wrongly means a costly rollback
They spend different currencies, so choosing is a product decision, not an ops one
Three of the four require a config deploy, which is unsafe to attempt during a spike
capacity.exp: Shed picks who loses, queue makes everyone lose a little, degrade spends quality, borrow spends money or unmeasured quality. There is no ordering that holds across products, so the person qualified to choose is a product owner — who at 3am is asleep.

capacity.q: A rung has a trigger, a disabled feature, a customer-visible effect and a quality delta. What is missing, and why does it matter?
o: A rollback procedure, without which the rung cannot be safely disengaged afterwards
A named pre-authorizer, without which the on-call engineer is not empowered to pull it
A cost estimate, without which finance cannot approve the degraded operating mode
A dashboard panel, without which nobody can confirm the rung actually took effect
capacity.exp: The first four fields are engineering; the fifth is authority. An on-call engineer is not empowered to decide that every support answer gets worse tonight, but is entirely empowered to execute a rung the VP of Support signed in March. That field is what makes the ladder executable.

capacity.q: Failover to a second provider is configured, but that provider has never been run against your golden set. What have you actually built?
o: A capacity save whose quality cost is unknown, so it converts one incident into another
A reasonable v1, since availability failures hurt customers more than quality drops do
A latency risk, because the failover target's response times have not been characterised
A cost exposure, since traffic will shift to a provider whose rates were never negotiated
capacity.exp: Failover preserves availability and says nothing about quality. An un-evaluated target turns a visible capacity incident into an undetected quality incident — a silent 200 at fleet scale. Run it against the golden set first and record the delta in the runbook.

capacity.q: Your pool of 42 workers serves 280 tasks a minute; the granted quota supports 182. What is the system's capacity?
o: 280 a minute, with the quota acting as a soft limit that throttles rather than blocks
231 a minute, since sustained throughput settles between the two competing ceilings
182 a minute, and adding workers changes nothing except how many of them are blocked
462 a minute, because the fleet and the quota constrain different stages of the pipeline
capacity.exp: Capacity is min(fleet, quota), and here the quota binds. That matters operationally because autoscaling cannot fix it: the remedy is a quota negotiation with a lead time measured in weeks, which is why the number belongs in the design doc, not the launch checklist.

seams.q: A service has 31 call sites into a vendor SDK, all going through three shared helper methods. For the exit memo, coupling points =
o: 31, because every call site must be visited, tested and re-reviewed during the port
3, because exit cost scales with distinct behaviours you depend on, not with call sites
34, the call sites plus the helpers, since both layers need rewriting on a vendor swap
0, since the helpers already form an adapter and the vendor is fully hidden behind them
seams.exp: Porting 31 mechanical call sites behind three methods is find-and-replace. The expensive work is reproducing distinct behaviours, filter dialects, scoring knobs, error semantics. Count behaviours. Note the inverse case is the dangerous one: 14 call sites each using a different corner of the vendor's API is a 14-point seam.

seams.q: A wrapper would save 3.5 engineer-weeks at exit and costs 3.6 engineer-weeks a year to carry. Your contract runs 3 years. Build it?
o: Yes, because a clean seam also improves testability and onboarding for every new hire
Yes, but only after the vendor has been in production for a full year without incident
No, break-even is under 12 months and you are committed for 36, so carry beats saving
No, wrappers are always the wrong call when a vendor offers a stable versioned interface
seams.exp: Exit saving divided by annual carry, times twelve, gives the break-even month: 3.5/3.6 x 12 is about 11.7. You would pay roughly 10.8 weeks of carry over the term to save 3.5 once. The other reasons may be real, but they are not this argument, and D overreaches into a rule.

seams.q: Your eval suite runs only inside the vendor's platform. In an exit memo this shows up as:
o: A data export task, sized in gigabytes and priced against the published egress rate
A minor line item, since eval definitions are usually short and easy to re-key by hand
A blocker, because substitution becomes unmeasurable until you can compare on your data
A contract negotiation, since the vendor is obliged to hand back derived artifacts on exit
seams.exp: You cannot swap what you cannot compare. The cost is not moving files, it is that no one can authorise a substitution nobody can measure. Building the capability lands on the critical path of every vendor decision you make afterwards, which is why owning evals outranks abstraction design.

seams.q: Two seam placements for the same vendor produce exit costs of 2.9 and 6.4 engineer-weeks. Both include 64 hours of eval revalidation. That shared line tells you:
o: Revalidation is fixed overhead and should be excluded when comparing the two placements
The eval suite is over-sized and ought to be trimmed before either migration is attempted
Evals are yours regardless of seam, so moving them in-house pays down both columns at once
The two estimates were produced from the same template and one of them was not re-derived
seams.exp: A term identical across placements is invariant to integration and therefore depends on ownership. That makes eval ownership the higher-leverage change: it cuts hours off every option and every future vendor, while the wrapper only ever helps against this one.

seams.q: Which is the clearest sign you have built a union abstraction rather than a seam?
o: The interface has grown to more than a dozen methods across several vendor capabilities
You cannot name a single vendor capability the abstraction deliberately refuses to expose
New vendor features take about a sprint to surface through the abstraction to callers
Two different teams disagree about which layer a given retry policy properly belongs in
seams.exp: A seam is an intersection plus an explicit decision about what you give up. If it forbids nothing it constrains nothing, so it buys no portability while still charging carry. Size, feature lag and layering arguments are symptoms at most; the naming test is diagnostic.

seams.q: Your corpus tripled since the vendor was chosen. Which term of the exit-cost model moves most?
o: Coupling, since a larger corpus tends to pull in more of the vendor's query surface
Revalidation, because a larger corpus makes each golden-set run take proportionally longer
Egress, which scales linearly with stored bytes and dominates at any meaningful scale
Re-derivation, the term that scales with corpus, re-embedding and index build hours
seams.exp: Re-derivation is the only term corpus size drives directly. Coupling tracks behaviours, revalidation tracks suite count, and egress scales but rarely dominates. The practical consequence: recompute the exit number every renewal, because growth changes it while everyone quotes last year's figure.

seams.q: You want a live second option for a model provider with the least ongoing carry. The seam to reach for is:
o: An adapter seam with your own interface and a maintained translation layer per vendor
A data seam, keeping prompts and outputs in your storage rather than in their workspace
A protocol seam, standardising on a request shape several vendors already implement
A config seam, with the model name promoted to an environment variable per deployment
seams.exp: A protocol seam costs least to carry because someone else maintains the shape and multiple vendors already conform. A config seam is cheaper still to build but swaps behaviour without validating it. An adapter is yours to maintain forever. A data seam is a different concern entirely.

seams.q: Honest probability of leaving a vendor within 18 months is 35%. The wrapper saves 3.5 weeks at exit and carries 5.4 weeks over that window. The correct framing is:
o: Expected saving 1.2 weeks against 5.4 certain weeks, so roughly 4 to 1 against building
Saving 3.5 weeks against 5.4 weeks of carry, close enough that either decision is defensible
Probability applies to both sides equally, so the 35% cancels and 3.5 versus 5.4 stands
Carry should also be discounted by 35%, giving 1.9 weeks against 1.2 weeks of saving
seams.exp: Exit saving is contingent, you collect it only if you leave. Carry is certain, you pay it every year either way. Weighting only the contingent side is the whole point of the comparison; discounting both, or neither, hides the asymmetry that makes the decision.

statearch.q: A register lists a semantic cache with invalidation "24h TTL". The spec card's freshness tolerance is 15 minutes. The finding is:
o: Acceptable, since a 24-hour TTL bounds staleness and the cache is only a performance layer
Two findings: no invalidation path at all, and a staleness bound running 96x over contract
One finding: the TTL should be lowered to 15 minutes so it matches the spec card exactly
Not a finding yet, because cache staleness only matters once a deletion request arrives
statearch.exp: A TTL bounds how long you stay wrong; it never detects that you are wrong, so the invalidation column is empty. And 1,440 minutes against a 15-minute tolerance is 96x over. Lowering the TTL to 15 minutes would destroy the hit rate and still leave no invalidation path.

statearch.q: Answer quality dropped on Tuesday. No prompt, model or retrieval change shipped. What do you check first?
o: Sample fifty recent traces and score them against a judge to characterise the regression
Check whether the provider silently moved an alias, since that is the usual cause of drift
Compare each serving store's last successful write against its source's last write
Diff last week's retrieval results for the golden set to see which documents stopped ranking
statearch.exp: The stale-mirror check takes thirty seconds and rules out the most commonly misdiagnosed cause. The others are all legitimate investigations, and all of them cost hours or days. Order matters more than technique: cheap eliminations first, and the model is the expensive place to look.

statearch.q: You trace a deletion through nine locations. Four can receive it. Two of the five survivors never expire. Where do you start?
o: The primary index, because it is the store users read from on every single request
The two stores that never expire, since bounded exposure is a schedule and unbounded is not
The trace store, since it holds verbatim prompts and therefore the richest personal data
The change-data-capture topic, because it is upstream and fixes propagate from there down
statearch.exp: The index already has a path. A 90-day retention is an exposure with an end date; a store with no expiry and no key is an obligation you cannot ever discharge. Fix unbounded before bounded, then shorten the bounded windows that exceed the deadline.

statearch.q: Full re-derivation: embedding costs $34, index build $29, and 60 engineer-hours of migration, verification and re-baselining. The design implication is:
o: Batch the embedding calls, since the embed line is the only variable cost in the whole run
Iteration rate is set by engineer-hours, so the embedder price cannot buy another experiment
The corpus is too small for the run to be worth optimising along any of the three dimensions
Move the index build to cheaper hardware, as compute is the largest controllable line here
statearch.exp: People are roughly 99% of the run. That is why re-index economics govern how often you may change chunking or embedding models, and why teams who optimise the embedding bill are surprised to still get two runs a year. Cut verification effort, or accept the rate.

statearch.q: A full index rebuild takes 9 hours. Your outage budget is 30 minutes. The consequence for architecture is:
o: Rebuilds must be scheduled overnight, when a longer outage window is generally available
The index must be sharded so that each shard rebuilds inside the thirty-minute allowance
In-place rebuild is impossible, so you build beside and accept a bounded two-truths window
The outage budget should be renegotiated upward, since nine hours is normal at this corpus size
statearch.exp: Rebuild time exceeding the outage budget is what forces dual-index cutover, and the cost of that pattern is a window where two indexes both claim to be true. Bound it, name it in the register, and decide what reads the old index meanwhile. Overnight windows are still outages.

statearch.q: Which store in a typical AI system is most often found to have no invalidation path at all?
o: The primary vector index, since delete-by-filter leaves tombstones until the next merge
The replica index in the second region, which lags the primary by a replication interval
The agent memory files, written by an extraction step with no key anything else references
The change-data-capture topic, which retains the pre-delete image for its retention window
statearch.exp: Memory files are written as free text by a background step, usually with no tenant key and no provenance, so nothing can address them for invalidation or deletion, and they do not expire. The other three all have a path, imperfect but real, and a measurable lag.

statearch.q: A rebuild crashes at 80% after seven hours. Rerunning starts from zero. The architectural defect is:
o: Insufficient compute provisioning, which made the total run long enough to be fragile
Missing checkpointing, so the job is neither idempotent nor resumable by content hash
The absence of a dual-index cutover, which would have kept the old index serving throughout
Poor observability, since the failure should have alerted well before the seven-hour mark
statearch.exp: Resumability is what makes rebuilds routine. An unresumable nine-hour job is one you quietly stop scheduling, and a rebuild you avoid is a chunking or embedding decision you can no longer revisit. Key work by content hash and skip what is already done.

statearch.q: Your register has a store with no tenant partition key. Beyond deletion, the sharpest consequence is:
o: Query performance suffers, because scans cannot be pruned to a single tenant's partition
Rebuild cost rises, since the whole store must be rebuilt rather than one tenant at a time
Per-tenant rebuild is impossible, and scoped erasure cannot even be expressed as a request
Access-control propagation slows, as permission changes must fan out across every partition
statearch.exp: The partition key is what makes both a scoped delete and a per-tenant rebuild expressible at all. Losing per-tenant rebuild is what turns re-derivation from routine into an annual event, which is the same constraint that caps your iteration rate.

migrate.q: Baseline task success is 92% and you need to detect a 1.5-point drop at 80% power. You now decide 0.75 points matters. The sample per arm:
o: Doubles, since required sample scales linearly with the effect size you want to detect
Roughly quadruples, because required sample scales as one over the effect size squared
Stays flat, as sample size is driven by the baseline rate rather than the effect size
Rises about 40%, following the square root relationship between sample and precision
migrate.exp: n scales as 1/delta squared, so halving the detectable effect is a 4x cost in traffic and days. This is the single fact that decides whether a rollout schedule is honest, and the reason resolution is the lever people reach for when the clock is short.

migrate.q: A shadow deployment ran five days on live inputs with no anomalies. What is it structurally unable to tell you?
o: Whether the new version's latency profile holds up under real production input distribution
Whether output token growth has pushed cost per task above the budgeted figure per route
Whether users behave differently, since nobody ever saw or acted on the shadow output
Whether the response schema still validates against every downstream consumer's expectations
migrate.exp: Shadow is excellent at latency, cost and schema because those are properties of the call itself. It is blind to abandonment, retries, escalation and satisfaction because no human was ever exposed. Clearing shadow is permission to canary, never permission to ship.

migrate.q: You fear a 1-in-2,000 catastrophic failure. A 5% canary on 40,000 tasks/day. How long before you can claim you would have seen it?
o: One day, since 2,000 exposures already equals the reciprocal of the failure rate itself
Three days, about 6,000 exposures, roughly three times the inverse of the rate
Seven days, since a full week is required to cover weekday and weekend traffic patterns
It cannot be established at 5%, because rare failures require a full production rollout
migrate.exp: Rule of three: about 3/rate exposures gives 95% confidence of seeing at least one. 2,000 exposures leaves a roughly 37% chance of seeing nothing even though the failure is live. Report exposure counts, not percentages, or the plan will feel safer than it is.

migrate.q: A provider announces a 60-day deprecation. The correct first move is:
o: Book the migration into the next planning cycle, which comfortably precedes the kill date
Start the offline eval immediately, since the ladder can be compressed later if needed
Schedule backwards from the kill date through buffer, ramp and ladder to derive a start date
Ask the provider for an extension, as published end-of-life dates are frequently negotiable
migrate.exp: The start date is derived, not chosen. Working forwards is how a team spends five of eight weeks feeling comfortable, then buys the lost days back with resolution. Working backwards also exposes prerequisites, like a stale eval set, while there is still slack to absorb them.

migrate.q: Deadline pressure means the ladder must shorten by five days. The most honest lever is:
o: Raise the minimum detectable effect and write down the drop you have agreed not to detect
Increase the canary percentage so the required sample accumulates over noticeably fewer days
Reduce the scoring fraction, which cuts judge cost and lets more stages run in parallel
Skip the offline eval rung, since the canary supersedes everything offline eval could show
migrate.exp: Raising the MDE is a real trade made explicit. Raising canary percentage does shorten days but widens blast radius, and is a fine second lever if stated. Cutting the scoring fraction lengthens the schedule. Offline eval is the cheapest rung and the wrong one to drop.

migrate.q: Your rollback runbook exists, is reviewed annually, and has never been executed with real traffic. You have:
o: Rollback capability, provided the runbook has been reviewed by more than one engineer
Documentation, since an unrehearsed procedure has no measured duration and no proof
Partial capability, sufficient for low-severity regressions but not for a full outage
Adequate coverage, as long as the feature flag it depends on is exercised in other flows
migrate.exp: An unrehearsed rollback has no measured time-to-revert, and rehearsals routinely reveal that the model reverts while the prompt or tool schema does not. Rehearse quarterly, time it with a stopwatch, and put the number in the runbook.

migrate.q: During an index migration you dual-write to old and new stores while a backfill runs. The design question that matters most is:
o: Which store receives writes first, so that ordering guarantees hold across both destinations
How the backfill is parallelised, since throughput sets the total duration of the migration
How long both stores claim to be true, and which of them reads serve during that window
Whether the new store's schema is a strict superset of the old, to keep rollback available
migrate.exp: The two-truths window is the risk. Bound it explicitly, state who reads which store during it, and make the backfill idempotent and resumable so a crash at 80% does not extend the window by a whole runtime. The others are real concerns, one rung down.

migrate.q: Traffic grows 10x. Your standing three-day canary at 5% now yields ten times the sample. The right response is:
o: Shorten the canary proportionally, since the required sample now accumulates in far less time
Reduce the canary to 0.5%, keeping sample constant while shrinking the blast radius sharply
Tighten the detectable effect, converting the surplus sample into resolution you did not have
Leave the plan unchanged, as the extra sample simply raises confidence in the same conclusion
migrate.exp: Extra traffic is resolution you can now afford, and the smaller regressions it exposes are the ones that used to reach production unnoticed. Shrinking the cohort or the window is defensible for blast radius, but it spends the gain rather than banking it.

quality.q: Your p95 budget leaves 600ms of headroom. The proposed grounding check measures 700ms at p95. What is the correct move?
o: Ship it now and renegotiate the p95 target with product afterwards
Keep it inline but run it on the slowest five percent of requests
Move it off the request path, or swap it for a cheap inline rail
Keep it inline and buy the time back by trimming the retrieval stage
quality.exp: 700ms against 600ms of headroom is an arithmetic failure, not a philosophical one. Running it on the slowest requests inverts the logic - those are the ones with the least room. Trimming retrieval to fund a check trades a known quality contribution for an unknown one, and you'd have to prove that trade with numbers you don't have yet.

quality.q: 13,000 requests a day, a regression touching 0.5% of traffic, 1% async sampling, and you need 8 flagged samples before anyone is paged. When do you find out?
o: Within a day, since one percent of thirteen thousand is ample signal
In about twelve days, most of an incident's useful lifetime
Within an hour, because the sampler runs continuously on traffic
In about three days, once the daily rollup crosses the alert line
quality.exp: 13,000 x 0.005 x 0.01 = 0.65 flagged samples per day, and 8 / 0.65 is about 12 days. The sampler does run continuously, which is exactly why people assume it's fast - continuity isn't the same as volume. Do this division before choosing a sampling rate, not after the incident review.

quality.q: A rail wrongly blocks 2% of good answers on a flow doing 400,000 tasks a month. Which number belongs in the review?
o: The two percent figure, which sits inside the normal band for rails
The rail's added compute per task, the marginal spend it introduces
The share of blocked users who retried and succeeded on their own
Eight thousand blocked good answers a month, priced in support cost
quality.exp: Ratios hide magnitude, counts don't. 2% of 400,000 is 8,000 refusals a month, and at a modest expected support cost per refusal that bill routinely exceeds the rail's entire compute cost. Retry-success data is genuinely useful, but it adjusts the price of a false block rather than replacing the count.

quality.q: Your eval suite runs on every release, posts a score to the pull request, and has never failed a build. What authority does it have?
o: Record only, which means it has stopped precisely nothing all year
Block release, because a poor score is visible to every reviewer
Open ticket, since reviewers file follow-ups whenever scores drop
Block response, as the score governs what the release may do live
quality.exp: Visibility is not authority. If no configuration in the system causes the check's verdict to stop anything, its authority is record-only, whatever the team believes. That's a legitimate choice when made deliberately - and a very expensive accident when it isn't.

quality.q: One flow can move money irreversibly and carries 0.4% of your volume. Where does human review belong?
o: On a random three percent sample across all flows, for coverage
On the flow with the most traffic, where reviewers see most cases
On every request that already tripped a rail, since those look bad
On that flow alone, because review buys fidelity and not coverage
quality.exp: Human review is the highest-fidelity control point you have and it does not scale, so its placement rule is maximum blast radius, minimum volume. Sampling for coverage is what async scoring is for. Reviewing only rail-tripped requests reviews the cases a machine already caught.

quality.q: Why can an offline CI gate stay green all quarter while production quality falls?
o: Because CI runs a cheaper model than production for cost reasons
Because thresholds in CI are usually set below production targets
Because it scores a fixed set that no longer matches live traffic
Because the gate runs after the deploy, so its verdict lands late
quality.exp: A CI gate is structurally blind to production distribution: it scores what you froze, and traffic keeps moving. That's not a flaw to fix, it's a property to plan around - which is precisely why online sampling exists alongside it rather than instead of it.

quality.q: You add async sampling at 5%. Which number on the spec card does that change?
o: The escaped-defect rate, since sampled failures are never served
None of them; it shortens how long a bad rate lasts, not the rate
The p95 latency, because scoring runs alongside each live response
The quality bar, which the new coverage lets you tighten right away
quality.exp: Only blocking control points change the escape rate. A sampler observes what already went out, so it buys a shorter blind window, not fewer wrong answers. Conflating detection with prevention is the single most common modelling error in these designs.

quality.q: Your provider silently updated the judge model and scores shifted by four points. What was missing from the architecture?
o: A contract clause barring vendor version changes without any notice
A larger golden set, so the shift would have surfaced in the scores
A second judge from a different family, averaged to damp variance
A control point on the judge itself, with an owner and a page target
quality.exp: The judge is a component, and components drift. A periodic agreement check against fresh human labels, with a threshold and a rotation attached, is the control point that catches this. Bigger sets and ensembles change the variance, not your ability to notice a shift.

quality.q: Where does a new output rail's cost belong in the design document?
o: In the latency and cost tables, as a line item against the headroom
In the eval plan, beside the other quality work planned this quarter
In the risk register, since rails exist to reduce residual risk
In the platform backlog, because rails are shared infrastructure
quality.exp: A rail taxes every response's latency and every task's cost, so it's a budget line item first and everything else second. Putting it in a plan or a register is how checks get approved that the budget was never going to accommodate.

quality.q: Two designs: a synchronous gate on everything, or a cheap rail plus 3% sampling. What decides between them?
o: Team maturity, since sampling demands more operational discipline
Your provider, because gate cost varies sharply between vendors
The spec card: blast radius, latency headroom, and the quality bar
The volume, because sampling only pays off beyond a certain scale
quality.exp: The same two checks flip which one wins the moment the blast radius becomes irreversible or the quality bar tightens by 10x. Volume and vendor move the numbers, but the selection is made by the requirement, which is why the spec card sits at the front of the document.

orgarch.q: Six product teams each hold their own provider keys, and the platform team reviews every prompt change. What is wrong with this split?
o: Nothing structural; it needs clearer documentation and better tooling
It is inverted on both axes: choke point devolved, fast artifact gated
The platform team is understaffed for the review volume it has taken on
Prompt review should be automated before any key consolidation happens
orgarch.exp: Keys are a choke point, where divergence costs you attribution, rate limiting and revocation, so they belong to platform. Prompts must move at feature speed, so they belong to product. This org gated the fast thing and devolved the expensive-to-diverge thing, which is both errors at once.

orgarch.q: Your ownership matrix lists an owner for every artifact but has no 'who gets paged' column. What does that cost you?
o: Very little, since ownership already implies operational responsibility
Slower onboarding, because new engineers can't tell who to ask first
Ownership becomes credit rather than a phone ringing at three in the morning
Audit friction, because separation of duties can't be demonstrated cleanly
orgarch.exp: Owner and pager are different claims. Without the paging column, ownership degrades into attribution, and mean time to repair quietly includes a handoff on every row where the two differ. The column is one word wide and it's the honest one.

orgarch.q: 6 teams x 9 reviews/month, 45 minutes each, against 3 reviewers giving 270 minutes a week over 13 weeks. What is utilisation?
o: About 0.69, which is comfortable and needs no action this quarter
About 0.69, and the queue is one added team away from getting painful
About 0.42, since reviewers also absorb work outside the review queue
About 1.15, which is why the current backlog keeps growing every week
orgarch.exp: 7,290 minutes of demand against 10,530 of capacity is 0.69. The trap is that 0.69 feels fine: wait time is non-linear, so one more team pushes it to 0.81 and roughly doubles the wait, and the team after that takes it to 0.92 and roughly triples it again.

orgarch.q: Adoption of your paved road is 30% after two quarters. What does that number mean?
o: Teams don't yet understand the benefits, so the rollout needs advocacy
The mandate isn't being enforced, so compliance reporting needs teeth
The road is slower or harder than the ditch, which is a road problem
The rollout is on track, since platform adoption is slow by its nature
orgarch.exp: Adoption is the measurement precisely because it's a judgement made by people with alternatives. Low adoption is feedback about the road: onboarding friction, latency overhead, or missing capability. Reaching for enforcement converts an engineering problem into a political one and buries the signal.

orgarch.q: You're migrating six teams onto a shared gateway. What ships first?
o: An approval gate on model changes, to stop divergence getting worse
The trace schema, additive and read-only, blocking nothing for anyone
Key cutover for the highest-spend team, to prove the value fastest
The rails service, since safety is the strongest justification you have
orgarch.exp: You can't route, attribute or measure what you can't see, and the trace schema is the only step that blocks nobody while making every later step measurable. Leading with an approval gate makes the platform a tax before it's ever been a service, and teams route around it inside a month.

orgarch.q: Who should own the golden sets in a platform/product split?
o: Platform, so that scoring methodology stays consistent across teams
A central quality guild, so no single team can lower its own bar
Whichever team has the most eval experience, regardless of the surface
Product, because a suite the product team doesn't believe gets routed around
orgarch.exp: Platform owns the runner and the storage, which are commodity. The set encodes domain judgement, and judgement doesn't survive being centralised: a standardised suite the feature team doesn't trust becomes a formality they satisfy rather than a control they use.

orgarch.q: Your platform team is at 92% review utilisation. What actually changes the trajectory?
o: Hiring a fourth reviewer, which raises capacity by a third immediately
Prioritising the queue better so the important reviews clear faster
Turning most reviews into a contract that a build job can check
Batching reviews into a twice-weekly slot to cut context switching
orgarch.exp: A reviewer buys linear headroom and moves break-even by about three teams. A machine-checked contract changes the slope, moving break-even by twenty. Prioritising and batching change who waits and for how long, not whether the queue exists.

orgarch.q: "The answers got worse" pages the infrastructure on-call rotation. What happens next?
o: It gets acknowledged, has no runbook, and is eventually tuned to silence
It gets escalated correctly, because on-call escalation paths exist for this
It gets fixed slowly, since infra engineers can read model traces too
It gets triaged into the backlog and reviewed at the next sprint planning
orgarch.exp: A page nobody can act on is a page that gets ignored, then adjusted until it stops firing. Quality and availability regressions need different diagnostics and different runbooks, which usually means different rotations. Which rotation currently receives this page tells you what your matrix really says.

orgarch.q: A guild - a cross-team forum with no dedicated platform staff - stops working at roughly what point?
o: Around twelve teams, when meeting size makes decisions impractical
When the first artifact appears that needs exactly one accountable owner
When the organisation adopts more than one model provider concurrently
Around six teams, when review volume exceeds volunteer time available
orgarch.exp: A guild is structurally incapable of owning a choke point, because its whole design is shared consent rather than single accountability. The failure isn't about size; it arrives the day something has to have one owner, which is usually key custody or the trace schema.

orgarch.q: Which artifact in an AI platform is genuinely irreversible, and therefore needs an approver who isn't the owner?
o: The model choice, given how much prompt behaviour is tuned to one family
The rails service, since removing a rail exposes traffic that was screened
The trace schema, because every trace already written stays in its old shape
The budget tables, since committed spend is hard to claw back mid-year
orgarch.exp: Model choice sits behind a choke point and is config. Rails and budgets are reversible by editing them. Historical traces cannot be rewritten into a new shape, so a schema change silently splits your incident history - which is exactly the kind of change that shouldn't be self-approved.

review.q: A design document states "we chose the two-stage retrieval shape" with no number attached. What is the cost of that omission?
o: Very little, since the choice is recorded and the team can explain it
Reviewers can't verify the choice, so approval takes an extra round trip
In twelve months nobody can tell whether the reason for it has expired
New engineers onboard slowly, because the rationale isn't written down
review.exp: A conclusion without its constraint is unmaintainable. The design becomes load-bearing through inertia rather than through a reason anyone can check. Record the number and its source, dated, so a stranger can evaluate whether it still holds.

review.q: Latency stages read 300 + 2,100 + 700 + 190 ms and the spec card says p95 3,000ms. What is the finding?
o: 3,290ms: it misses by 290ms before any queueing at the declared peak
It fits, since stage p95 values don't compose by simple addition anyway
It's within tolerance, given that 290ms is under ten percent of budget
It depends on the shape of the distribution across the four stages
review.exp: Composed p95 is at least the sum of stage p95s and usually worse, so addition is the optimistic case and it already fails. It's true that percentiles don't add cleanly - that argument makes the finding stronger, not weaker. Ninety seconds of arithmetic, and it's the finding most reviews skip.

review.q: You are reviewing someone else's AI architecture with sixty minutes. What do you ask after "which number forced this shape?"
o: Which model and provider they selected, and what the fallback path is
How the retrieval layer is chunked and what the reranking strategy is
Whether they've load-tested the system at the declared peak multiplier
Whether the stage budgets actually sum to within the spec card's numbers
review.exp: The budget question takes ninety seconds and fails startlingly often, because each row was added in a different week by a different person and nobody added the column. Model choice, chunking and load tests all matter, but none of them yields findings at that rate per minute.

review.q: A derived store rebuilds nightly. The spec card's freshness tolerance is 15 minutes and a rebuild takes 41 minutes. What's the fix?
o: Rebuild hourly instead, cutting the worst-case staleness by a factor of 24
An event-driven invalidation path, since no rebuild cadence can beat 41 min
Raise the freshness tolerance to 24 hours to match what's actually delivered
Cache with a 15-minute expiry so entries can never exceed the tolerance
review.exp: A rebuild taking 41 minutes cannot satisfy a 15-minute bound at any cadence, so frequency is the wrong lever. You need targeted invalidation on the event that makes a key stale. Raising the tolerance is legitimate only if you can defend the new number, and a blanket short expiry just trades staleness for a rebuild storm.

review.q: Your review ends with unanimous approval and no objections raised. What has that measured?
o: The design's quality, since experienced reviewers found nothing to object to
The room, not the design - dissent doesn't appear unless it's assigned
Review fatigue, meaning the document was too long to engage with properly
That the pre-read worked, since objections were resolved before the meeting
review.exp: Unassigned dissent reliably fails to appear in a room containing the author's manager. That's why the red-team role is assigned by name, in the invitation, with the document a day early - so someone arrives prepared to make the strongest case for the shape you rejected.

review.q: Why is a pre-mortem phrased as "it's twelve months later and this failed, why?" rather than "what are the risks?"
o: It's shorter, so more objections fit into the time the meeting has left
It assigns blame in advance, which raises the stakes and sharpens focus
It asks for explanation rather than speculation, which people do far better
It moves the discussion to concrete dates, making mitigations schedulable
review.exp: Stating the failure as a fact and asking why converts the task from forecasting into explaining, and explaining is something people are markedly better at. The output is more answers and more specific ones. It is emphatically not about blame - that framing shuts the room down.

review.q: Which revisit trigger keeps an architecture document alive?
o: A quarterly calendar reminder assigned to the document's original author
A standing agenda item at the monthly architecture review for the group
Volume x3, a cost-ceiling change, or a deprecation notice on a priced seam
A review whenever the team changes ownership or the on-call rotation shifts
review.exp: Calendar triggers get skipped in busy quarters, and busy quarters are exactly when the numbers moved. Numeric triggers tied to spec-card values fire when reality changes, which is the only time the document was worth reopening anyway.

review.q: You conclude a feature shouldn't be built with AI. How do you make that a respected outcome?
o: Frame it as a delay, so the option stays open when models improve later
Hold it to the same standard as a rejected shape: the number that forced it
Escalate the decision so the accountability sits above the design team
Present it alongside a non-AI design so there's still something to approve
review.exp: "96.5% measured task success against a 99.95% bar, closable only with human review at $0.42 a task against a $0.03 ceiling" is an engineering conclusion. "It feels risky" is a career risk. Building the number is what makes declining read as rigour rather than as timidity.

review.q: Why express the architecture document as structured data and lint it, rather than as prose?
o: Prose is slower to write and harder to keep consistent across many authors
Structured data renders into diagrams automatically, which reviewers prefer
Linting removes the need for a human review, freeing the hour for building
Cross-artifact contradictions sit pages apart, so a reader can't hold both
review.exp: The characteristic real finding is two artifacts disagreeing while each looks fine alone, and prose guarantees they're read on different days by different people. As data, they're one comparison apart. The linter checks consistency, which is the floor - the human hour is still where correctness gets argued.

review.q: During a review you can't answer four of the ten questions with a number. What is that list?
o: A sign the review was scheduled too early in the design process
Follow-up work for the reviewers, who raised the questions in the first place
Your actual roadmap, already prioritised by a skeptical peer in one hour
Evidence the question list needs tailoring to your particular system
review.exp: The questions a skeptical peer thinks to ask in an hour are close to the ones production will ask within a quarter, and they arrive already ordered by yield. Write them down as they occur, don't answer them in the room, and take the list away as the plan.

CARDS.f: Requirement reads "it should be accurate." What's missing?
CARDS.b: A measurement, a set, a threshold, and an abstention allowance. "92% on a 300-case golden set, abstaining on 8% or less" eliminates three architectures. "Accurate" eliminates none, which is why it isn't a requirement.

CARDS.f: $0.08/task, 4,000 tasks/day, $12,000/month ceiling. Consistent?
CARDS.b: Yes — 0.08 × 4,000 × 30 = $9,600, so 20% headroom. Always do this multiplication out loud: the two ceilings usually come from two people who never spoke to each other.

CARDS.f: Identical ask, two teams, two architectures. Which field diverged?
CARDS.b: Blast radius. A wrong FAQ answer is an annoyance → retrieval read path. A wrong answer that auto-closes a billing dispute is churn → verified chain plus a human queue. Field 5 picks the shape.

CARDS.f: Quality bar 0.92, abstention allowance left blank.
CARDS.b: You just required the system to answer every single time. "Right when it answers" and "must always answer" are different price tags, and the second one climbs a rung to buy back the same quality.

CARDS.f: 5-stage pipeline, 99.5% per stage. End-to-end?
CARDS.b: 97.5%. Reliability composes multiplicatively — quote the product, never the per-stage number. This is the arithmetic that makes box count a reliability decision instead of an aesthetic one.

CARDS.f: Stage p95s: 260, 300, 2,100, 200ms. End-to-end p95?
CARDS.b: About 2,520ms, not 2,860ms. Compose the spreads by root-sum-square or simulate. Summing p95s over-states by ~14% — conservative, but it deletes designs you could have afforded.

CARDS.f: "Just one more verification call": +1,600ms p95, +$0.040. Budget 3,500ms / $0.08.
CARDS.b: 3,704ms and $0.097 — over by 204ms and $0.017, which is $4,800/month. Now name what gets cut to fund it. Dropping rerank (300ms, $0.004) nearly does. That's the real conversation.

CARDS.f: 99.9% available, 92% correct. What share of requests actually worked?
CARDS.b: 91.9% — the product. Answering and being right are two independent ways to fail, so you need two error budgets. Availability has a pager by default; correctness has to be given one.

CARDS.f: The corpus is unbounded. Which rungs die, and on what grounds?
CARDS.b: Rungs 1 and 2, on capability — no chain of calls makes a corpus fit that doesn't fit. Note what didn't kill them: cost and latency were both comfortable. Check capability first; budget never rescues it.

CARDS.f: Volume ×20. Read path at $0.0228/task against a $12,000/month ceiling.
CARDS.b: $54,720/month — and every rung fails. So move a card field: async mode opens the batch rung at $0.0060/task = $14,400/month. One number moved the answer from rung 3 to rung 6.

CARDS.f: Composite: 55% batch $0.0060, 42% read path $0.0228, 3% loop $0.0780.
CARDS.b: $0.0152 blended. At 25% hatch instead of 3% it's $0.0274 — 1.8×. Alert on hatch share, not total spend: the blend is linear in the share, and spend is the lagging indicator.

CARDS.f: A box in the diagram with no recorded forcing constraint.
CARDS.b: A deletion candidate. Take it to the team — either someone supplies the constraint and it finally goes in the doc, or nobody can and you've found real complexity to remove. Both outcomes are wins.

CARDS.f: Severity 9, likelihood 3, detectability 9. Disposition?
CARDS.b: Structural. RPN 243, but the number is not what decides it — detectability above 7 removes mitigation from the menu. Constrain the output, remove the capability, or gate it. Never plan a mitigation for a failure you cannot observe.

CARDS.f: Row A is 8/4/2 with a 97% catch-rate rail. Residual RPN?
CARDS.b: 16, down from 64. Escaping likelihood 4 x 0.03 = 0.12, rounded up to 1 (never to zero), so 8 x 1 x 2 = 16. A 75% reduction from forty lines of deterministic arithmetic.

CARDS.f: 4% per-step error, 35% growth per step, 8 steps. Chance of at least one bad step?
CARDS.b: 72%, against 28% if the steps were independent — a 2.6x inflation. Compounding modes get a step ceiling; only linear modes can be budgeted for with a per-step control.

CARDS.f: Someone proposes a scorer to check whether a cited clause is from the current contract version.
CARDS.b: Notice that the scorer needs supplier_id + effective_date resolved against the contract table — which is the answer. If you can build the detector, build the answer instead.

CARDS.f: 20,000 actions/mo, tolerance 4 bad. Required accuracy at act-irreversibly?
CARDS.b: 99.98%. Required = 1 - T/(V x E), and E is 1.0 when nothing catches it. Behind an approval gate (E about 0.05) the same tolerance needs only 99.60%.

CARDS.f: Model is 94.0%. Act-with-undo needs 99.90%, suggest needs 93.3%.
CARDS.b: Demote the tier. Suggest multiplies your error budget by 300x against the same tolerance — a five-point accuracy gain you can deploy on Thursday, not a model you can buy.

CARDS.f: Agent reads CRM, reads customer tickets, sends email. Rails are in place. Verdict?
CARDS.b: Fail. Private + untrusted + egress in one turn is an escalation path regardless of rail quality. Break a leg: resolve recipients from pre-turn data, split the turns, or remove the egress.

CARDS.f: An allowlist the model populates at call time. Bulkhead or theatre?
CARDS.b: Theatre. A boundary the compromised turn can influence is a suggestion with extra steps. Resolve the allowlist from data that predates the untrusted content and it becomes structural.

CARDS.f: 40k tasks/day, 4,400 effective tokens each, 8x Monday peak. Quota to request?
CARDS.b: 122,222 TPM steady, 977,778 at peak, about 1.22M with 25% headroom. Size against the peak minute, never the daily average — and start the conversation weeks early, because quota has a lead time.

CARDS.f: 42 workers gives 0.11s wait. 34 gives 11.73s. Same load. What moved?
CARDS.b: Utilisation, from 79% to 98%. The queueing curve is asymptotic near saturation, so an 18% fleet cut bought a hundredfold wait. Above ~80%, utilisation is a latency decision wearing a cost costume.

CARDS.f: 333 arrivals/min, 182 capacity, uncapped queue added to absorb the burst.
CARDS.b: Backlog grows 151/min — 9,060/hour — and everyone inherits it. The queue converted a fast refusal for 45% into a slow one for 100%. A queue is a lever only with a depth cap and admission control.

CARDS.f: Your rung says: trigger, what's disabled, customer effect, quality delta. Ship it?
CARDS.b: No — the fifth field is missing. Without a named pre-authorizer, the 3am engineer has a runbook they are not empowered to execute. Authority is what makes a rung a rung.

CARDS.f: 31 raw call sites, 11 distinct behaviours. Which number goes in the exit memo?
CARDS.b: 11. Exit cost scales with behaviours you depend on, not call sites, mechanical replacement is cheap and semantic differences are not. Sizing by call sites is how a fourteen-behaviour seam gets estimated as a three-day job.

CARDS.f: Wrapper saves 3.5 engineer-weeks at exit, costs 3.6 engineer-weeks a year to carry. Contract runs 3 years.
CARDS.b: Don't build it. Break-even is 11.7 months against a 36-month commitment. Saving divided by annual carry, times twelve, is the only number this argument needs.

CARDS.f: The vendor hosts your golden set. What is the real exit-cost line?
CARDS.b: Not a data export. An eval capability you don't have, roughly six engineer-weeks, sitting on the critical path of every vendor decision you make afterwards. You cannot swap what you cannot compare.

CARDS.f: P(leave within 18 months) = 35%. Wrapper carry 5.4 weeks. Exit saving 3.5 weeks.
CARDS.b: Expected saving 1.2 weeks against 5.4 certain, about 4 to 1 against building. Weight the saving by probability; never weight the carry, because you pay carry whether you leave or not.

CARDS.f: Nine locations, four can receive a deletion. Two survivors never expire.
CARDS.b: That fraction is a compliance finding and an architecture diagram at once. Start with the two that never expire, not the index everyone is watching, because bounded exposure is a schedule and unbounded is an obligation.

CARDS.f: Spec card freshness tolerance 15 minutes. Cache TTL 24 hours, no tombstone wiring.
CARDS.b: 96x over contract, and two findings not one: the staleness breach, and an empty invalidation column. A TTL bounds how long you stay wrong, it never detects that you are wrong.

CARDS.f: Re-index run: $34 embedding, $29 compute, 60 engineer-hours.
CARDS.b: People are 99% of it. Optimising the embedder buys you nothing, iteration rate is set by verification and re-baselining effort. Budget divided by run cost is how many times a year you may change your mind, and one is already spent.

CARDS.f: "The AI started getting things wrong on Tuesday." First check?
CARDS.b: Mirror lag, not the model. Compare each serving store's last successful write to its source's. Thirty seconds, and it resolves a surprising share of regressions that otherwise eat three weeks of prompt archaeology.

CARDS.f: Baseline 92%, detect a 1.5-point drop, 80% power, alpha 0.05. Sample per arm?
CARDS.b: About 5,570 scored tasks. Halve the detectable effect and it quadruples, n scales as one over delta squared. The rollout schedule is a power calculation, not a calendar preference.

CARDS.f: 5% canary, 40,000 tasks/day, 3 days. Can it see a 1-in-2,000 failure?
CARDS.b: 6,000 exposures, just clearing the 3/rate floor for 95% confidence. Run it for one day instead and you have 2,000 exposures and roughly a 37% chance of seeing nothing while the failure is live.

CARDS.f: 26 days to the kill date, 38 days of plan. What do you sell?
CARDS.b: Resolution, not hope. MDE 1.5 to 3.0 points cuts the sample 3.7x and compresses the ladder. Then write the sentence: we agreed not to detect a 2-point drop, and this person signed for it.

CARDS.f: Shadow ran five days on live inputs, completely clean. Ship to 100%?
CARDS.b: No. Shadow is blind to user behaviour because nobody saw the output, so nobody abandoned, retried or escalated. It clears schema, latency and cost. Quality on real users needs a canary sized by sample.

CARDS.f: A synchronous check adds 700ms. Your headroom is 600ms.
CARDS.b: It doesn't fit. Move it off the request path or make it deterministic. A check you can't pay for isn't a plan, it's a preference.

CARDS.f: 1% sampling, a regression on 0.5% of traffic, 13,000 requests/day, 8 events to alarm.
CARDS.b: 0.65 events/day, so about 12 days to page. Choose the sampling rate from the lag you're willing to accept, not from the roundness of the number.

CARDS.f: 2% false-block rate on 400,000 tasks/month.
CARDS.b: 8,000 good answers refused. Priced at even a modest support cost per refusal, that exceeds the check's entire compute bill. Quote the count, never the ratio.

CARDS.f: Your eval runs in CI and posts a score to the PR.
CARDS.b: That's authority record-only. It has stopped nothing. Assign a real authority or delete the check, because a check people believe in is worse than no check.

CARDS.f: 6 teams x 9 reviews/month at 45 min, against 3 reviewers x 270 min/week x 13 weeks.
CARDS.b: 0.69 utilisation, about 2 days of wait. At 7 teams it's 4 days, at 8 it's 12, at 9 it's unbounded. Compute the bottleneck quarter before you agree to the gate.

CARDS.f: A choke point with two owners.
CARDS.b: That's the shadow-spend signature: divergent config and an incident nobody can roll back in one place. Choke points take exactly one owner; features take several.

CARDS.f: Artifact owned by the product team, paged to platform.
CARDS.b: MTTR now permanently includes a handoff - platform mitigates, product fixes tomorrow. Owner and pager should be the same team, or you've priced a delay into every incident.

CARDS.f: Paved-road adoption sits at 30% after two quarters.
CARDS.b: The road is slower than the ditch. Adoption is the metric, not compliance - reaching for enforcement converts an engineering problem into a political one and buries the signal.

CARDS.f: The document says "we chose the two-stage shape."
CARDS.b: Missing the number that forced it. Record the constraint and its source, dated - otherwise nobody in twelve months can tell whether the reason expired.

CARDS.f: Stage p95s: 300 + 2,100 + 700 + 190. Spec card says 3,000ms.
CARDS.b: 3,290ms, over by 290 before any queueing at peak. Adding the column takes ninety seconds and is the finding most reviews never get to.

CARDS.f: Revisit trigger: "review this quarterly."
CARDS.b: Calendar triggers get skipped in busy quarters, which are the quarters the numbers moved. Tie it to spec-card values: volume x3, cost ceiling change, deprecation notice on a seam.

CARDS.f: The review ended with unanimous approval.
CARDS.b: That measured the room, not the design. Assign the red-team role by name in the invitation, with the doc a day early, or dissent will not show up.

SCENARIOS.title: The two-week estimate
SCENARIOS.sit: Your engineering manager has told the VP that the internal engineering-docs assistant is "about two weeks of work." The estimate came from a prototype one engineer built over a weekend: a single model call with a chunk of the handbook pasted into the prompt, and it demoed beautifully. The real corpus is roughly 40,000 documents across six systems, updated continuously. Expected traffic is 2,500 queries/day. A baseline model call measures $0.010 and 1,300ms p95 on your infrastructure. The commitment meeting is Thursday and nothing has been signed yet.
SCENARIOS.task: What do you tell the VP on Thursday, and what number do you put next to it?
SCENARIOS.model:
The two-week estimate is real, and it prices the wrong thing. Start with the ladder. Rung 1, single call: $0.0100/task, 1,330ms — comfortably inside any sane budget, and rejected anyway, because 40,000 continuously-updated documents is an unbounded corpus and no prompt makes it fit. That is a capability fact, not a budget fact, so no amount of money rescues rung 1. The prototype demoed well because it was asked questions the pasted chunk happened to cover.

Rung 3, retrieval read path: 1.9× baseline = $0.0190/task, 1.5 × 1,300 + 220 = 2,170ms p95. Monthly inference: 0.019 × 2,500 × 30 = $1,425. That number is small enough to be a rounding error, and it is not the number that matters.

The number that matters is operate cost. A read path is roughly 0.8 FTE steady state — index freshness across six systems, permission drift, re-embedding on document change, and the on-call that comes with a second subsystem. At a loaded $200K/year that's about $13,300/month, which is 9.3× the inference spend. The two-week estimate has no operate line in it at all, and the operate line is where 90% of the cost lives at this volume.

So: tell the VP two weeks is a fair build estimate for rung 1, which we cannot ship, and that the shape the corpus forces is five to six weeks plus roughly 0.8 FTE ongoing. Then offer the cheap alternative honestly — if we scope the corpus to the 400 documents that cover 80% of queries, rung 1 becomes available again and the two-week estimate is real. That's a scope decision for the VP, made with both numbers visible, on Thursday rather than in month four.
pts: Identifies that the unbounded corpus is a capability constraint that kills rung 1 regardless of budget
Prices the read path with actual arithmetic ($0.0190/task, $1,425/month) rather than asserting it's more expensive
Surfaces operate cost as the dominant term and quantifies it against inference spend (~9×)
Names that the estimate covered build only, and separates build estimate from ongoing ownership
Offers a scope alternative that would make the cheap rung genuinely available, and leaves the choice with the VP

SCENARIOS.title: The "just make it accurate" ticket
SCENARIOS.sit: The ticket says: "Add AI answering to the customer help widget. It should be accurate and fast, and handle anything customers ask." The PM who wrote it is capable and busy, and genuinely believes she has given you a requirement. Support currently handles 1,200 contacts/day at a fully-loaded $4.20 per contact. Nobody has discussed a budget, a latency target, or what happens when the assistant is wrong. You have a thirty-minute meeting with her tomorrow and you would like to leave it with something you can design against.
SCENARIOS.task: Run the elicitation and produce the six-field spec card. Show your arithmetic.
SCENARIOS.model:
Three questions, asked in this order, produce five of the six fields.

Who is harmed by a wrong answer? Her answer — "the customer gets bad advice about their plan and might act on it" — gives blast radius: recoverable but visible, not costly. That sets a defensible quality bar of about 0.92 on a golden set of 300 real contacts, with abstention allowed on 8%. Note that abstention has to be explicit, or you've required the widget to answer every question ever asked, which is the "handle anything" clause and is unaffordable at any rung.

What does the user do in the next ten seconds? They're staring at a widget. Interactive, so p95 in the low seconds — 3,000ms, sourced from the widget's existing abandonment curve rather than invented.

What does the status quo cost? $4.20 per contact, 1,200/day. This is the field that turns your constraint into her business case. If the assistant deflects 60% of contacts, that's 720/day × $4.20 = $3,024/day, about $90,720/month of avoided cost. Against that, a ceiling of $0.30/task is 0.30 × 1,200 × 30 = $10,800/month — you're proposing to spend 12% of the value to capture it. That is an easy conversation, and it's only available because you asked the third question.

Fields five and six: volume 1,200/day with a peak multiplier pulled from traffic history, not guessed; freshness — plan and pricing docs change weekly, so 24 hours is tolerable and she should confirm that with legal, because it's also a statement about deleted records.

Then close the triangle: with 0.92 quality and a 3,000ms budget, tell her plainly which one you're refusing to optimise. Get her name against it.
pts: Uses the three elicitation questions rather than asking the PM to specify a technical requirement
Converts "accurate" into a threshold on a named set, and adds an explicit abstention allowance
Identifies "handle anything" as the unbounded-scope clause and closes it via abstention
Uses status-quo cost ($4.20 × 1,200) to derive a ceiling in comparative form, with the arithmetic shown
Names the impossible-triangle loser explicitly and gets it signed rather than deciding it silently

SCENARIOS.title: The feature that can't afford itself
SCENARIOS.sit: A strong team has proposed an orchestrator-worker architecture for a consumer-facing content assistant: fan out to several specialist workers, merge, return. The design doc is genuinely good — clear seams, sensible failure handling, tested prototype. The surface serves 200,000 sessions/day and is ad-supported at roughly $0.004 of attributable revenue per session. A baseline call on your stack is $0.011. The team has asked for a decision this week and is expecting a yes.
SCENARIOS.task: Decide, and show the team the arithmetic that makes the decision for you.
SCENARIOS.model:
The design is fine. The unit economics are not, and no amount of design quality fixes them.

Orchestrator-worker runs about 14× a baseline call: 14 × $0.011 = $0.154/task. At full scope that's 0.154 × 200,000 × 30 = $924,000/month against attributable revenue of 0.004 × 200,000 × 30 = $24,000/month. The feature is 38× underwater. That is not a number you optimise your way out of.

Walk down the ladder before concluding anything. Single call at 1×: $0.011/task = $66,000/month — still 2.75× underwater. Batch precompute at ~0.5×: $0.0055/task = $33,000/month — still underwater, and that's the cheapest rung that exists. So the honest finding is that no shape on the ladder closes at full scope. The binding constraint isn't the architecture, it's that $0.004/session cannot fund an AI call of any kind at 200,000 sessions/day.

Which means the decision is about scope, not shape. Suppose 5% of sessions are the high-intent ones where the assistant plausibly changes behaviour, and those sessions carry roughly $0.06 of attributable value. Serve only those: 10,000/day on a retrieval read path at 1.9× = $0.0209/task, or 0.0209 × 10,000 × 30 = $6,270/month, against 0.06 × 10,000 × 30 = $18,000/month of value. That closes at about 2.9× coverage, and it's a real feature.

So: no to the orchestrator, not because it's badly designed but because it's 38× underwater and the ladder proves nothing cheaper closes either. Yes to a scoped read path on high-intent sessions, with the trigger rate instrumented from day one — because the whole business case rests on that 5% staying near 5%, and if it drifts to 20% the coverage ratio collapses.
pts: Prices the proposed shape per task and per month, and compares it directly against attributable revenue
Walks down the ladder to establish that no shape closes at full scope, rather than just rejecting the expensive one
Reframes the decision as scope rather than architecture once the ladder is exhausted
Shows the scoped alternative closing with explicit arithmetic and a stated coverage ratio
Identifies the trigger-rate assumption as the thing to instrument, since the case depends on it holding

SCENARIOS.title: The demo that set the SLO
SCENARIOS.sit: DESIGN REVIEW. Six weeks ago a team demoed a prototype that answered 12 curated questions in about 1.2 seconds each. Leadership was delighted and announced a "under 2 seconds, always" commitment externally. You've now been handed the resulting architecture doc to review before build. It specifies six serial stages; the latency section sums the stage p95s to 1.9s and claims 100ms of headroom. Availability is listed as "99.9% per stage." Cost is quoted as "$0.009 per call." There's an escape hatch to a tool loop "for hard cases." Expected volume is 50,000 tasks/day. There is no abstention path and no quality section.
SCENARIOS.task: Find the flaws and rank them by which one invalidates the most other decisions.
SCENARIOS.model:
1. The SLO's provenance. Everything below inherits this. "Under 2 seconds" was derived from twelve curated questions measured at what was effectively a p50 on a happy path. That is not a distribution, and a p95 over real production traffic on 50,000 tasks/day will not resemble it. Every latency decision in the doc is being made against a number nobody sourced. Fix this first or the rest is arithmetic on sand.

2. Cost is understated 6×. "$0.009 per call" across six stages is $0.054 per task. At volume: 0.054 × 50,000 × 30 = $81,000/month, not the $13,500/month the per-call figure implies. This is second because it doesn't invalidate the design, it invalidates the business case — and it's the number that will be quoted back at the team in six months.

3. Composed availability. Six stages at 99.9% is 0.999^6 = 99.4%, not 99.9%. At 50,000/day that's about 300 failed tasks per day against an implied 50. Per-stage nines are not a commitment anyone experiences.

4. The escape hatch has no measured share and no cap. A tool loop runs ~6.5× baseline. The demo set contained zero hard cases, so the trigger rate is not merely unmeasured, it's unmeasurable from the evidence available. At 3% it's a rounding error; at 20% it dominates the blend. This needs a rate cap and an alert before build, not after.

5. No abstention path and no quality section. The system is therefore required to answer every question, which is the most expensive requirement in the document and the only one that isn't written down anywhere. There's also no correctness budget, so quality regressions will page nobody.

6. Summed p95s. Ranked last deliberately: composing properly would give roughly 1.6s rather than 1.9s, so this error is conservative and in the team's favour. It's still wrong and still worth fixing, but it is the only flaw here that isn't costing anyone anything.

The one-line recommendation: don't review the design, re-source the SLO. Five of these six flaws are downstream of a number that came from a demo.
pts: Ranks the demo-sourced SLO first and explains that the other findings are downstream of it
Catches per-call versus per-task cost and computes the 6× gap with monthly figures
Composes availability multiplicatively (0.999^6 = 99.4%) and converts it to failed tasks/day
Flags the uncapped escape hatch and notes the demo set could not have measured its share
Correctly ranks the summed-p95 error last, recognising it errs conservatively, rather than leading with the most technical finding

SCENARIOS.title: The tool nobody audited
SCENARIOS.sit: You are reviewing a sales-research agent two weeks before its launch. It has grown from three tools to nine over the quarter, one at a time, each addition reviewed on its own merits and each perfectly sensible. It reads account records from the CRM, reads prospect replies pulled from a shared inbox, drafts outreach, and — added last month so reps would stop copy-pasting — posts summaries to a team chat channel (Slack) via an incoming webhook. The team is proud of it. Nobody has ever looked at the nine tools on one page at the same time, and the design doc still describes the original three.
SCENARIOS.task: Do the blast-radius pass this system never got: inventory the action surface, run the trifecta check, and say what has to change before launch.
SCENARIOS.model:
Put all nine on one page first, because the problem is composition and no single-tool review could have caught it. Three legs are present. read_account puts private customer data in the turn. read_inbox puts prospect-authored text in the turn — a stranger typed that, which is the entire premise. The Slack webhook moves bytes out of the boundary. Private plus untrusted plus egress inside one turn is an escalation path, and the fact that each tool was individually reasonable is exactly how it got built.

Name the specific path in the doc rather than summarising it: read_account to read_inbox to slack_post. "We have an injection risk" gets deferred; a named path gets fixed.

Then price the fixes rather than asserting one. Removing the webhook costs the reps the copy-pasting it was added to eliminate — call it 40 posts a day at 30 seconds, about 5 hours a month, which is real but small. Narrowing the destination to a single channel id resolved from config, decided before any untrusted text arrived, costs nothing at all and breaks the egress leg outright. That is the move: the channel is not chosen inside the turn, so a compromised turn cannot redirect it, and the content is still constrained to the account already in scope.

Then do the tier arithmetic on the drafting path. At 6,000 drafts a month, a tolerance of two bad sends and an 88% measured accuracy, acting directly needs 99.97% and delivers 720 bad actions a month — 360x over. Approval-gated at a 0.05 escape needs 99.6% and yields 36, still over. Suggest-only yields 2.2 and passes. Ship at suggest, and put the requirement table in the doc.
pts: Inventories all nine tools on one page and identifies that the vulnerability is compositional, not present in any single tool review
Runs the trifecta check explicitly and names the specific path (private read, untrusted read, egress) rather than describing a general injection risk
Proposes breaking a leg structurally — resolving the destination from pre-turn config — rather than adding a rail or prompt instruction
Prices at least two options against lost product value with actual numbers, instead of asserting the safest one
Does the tier arithmetic on the write path and lands on a demotion justified by the required-accuracy figures

SCENARIOS.title: The Monday-morning peak
SCENARIOS.sit: You are two months out from launching a claims-triage assistant for an insurer. The spec card says 40,000 claims a day, 3,200 tokens per claim, and a Monday-morning peak of 8x — the industry's traffic is famously lumpy, since nobody files a claim on a Saturday. The platform team has sized a worker fleet from the latency target and is happy. Procurement has "an account with the provider." Nobody has written a number next to the words tokens per minute, and the launch checklist has a line item called "load testing" scheduled for the final week.
SCENARIOS.task: Produce the capacity plan: the quota to request, the pool to run, and what the system does when the peak arrives larger than predicted.
SCENARIOS.model:
Start with effective tokens, because getting this wrong understates everything downstream. 3,200 splits roughly 2,800 in and 400 out, and output usually counts for more against a throughput meter — at a weight of 4.0 that is 2,800 + 1,600 = 4,400 effective tokens per claim.
