Throughput: 40,000/86,400 = 0.463 claims a second, times 4,400 times 60 = 122,222 TPM steady. At the spec card's 8x peak that is 977,778 TPM and 222 RPM. Add 25% headroom and request roughly 1.22M TPM. Say the important part out loud in the meeting: quota has a procurement lead time measured in weeks, so this is a schedule dependency for January, not a checklist item for the final week.

Pool: Little's Law, L = lambda x W. At peak, 3.70 claims a second and 9.0 seconds each gives 33.3 in flight — a floor, not a target. At 34 workers you are at 98% utilisation and 11.73 seconds of mean wait; at 42 you are at 79% and 0.11 seconds. Six workers, a hundredfold difference in wait, with nothing else changed. Take 42 and stop treating utilisation as an efficiency metric.

Then the part that is actually the deliverable. If procurement returns the 800k tier rather than 1.22M, real capacity is min(280, 182) = 182 claims a minute and the fleet was never the constraint. At a 12x Monday, 333 arrive against 182: an uncapped queue grows 151 a minute and the 09:20 claim waits fifty minutes. So write five rungs — cache-only, smaller model, template deflection, admission-controlled queue with notification, honest reject with a retry-after — each with a trigger, the quality delta, and the name of the claims director who signed it. Then game-day rung 3 in staging before launch, not during it.
pts: Computes effective tokens with an output weighting and shows the steady, peak, and headroom TPM figures as arithmetic
Frames quota as a schedule dependency with procurement lead time, rather than a launch-week checklist item
Applies Little's Law to get the concurrency floor and explicitly rejects sizing at that floor because of the queueing cliff
States capacity as min(fleet, quota) and works through what happens when the quota is the binding constraint
Delivers a five-rung ladder with triggers, quality deltas and a named pre-authorizer, plus a game day before launch

SCENARIOS.title: The undetectable failure
SCENARIOS.sit: A clinical-operations team wants an assistant that answers staff questions about internal care protocols by retrieving from a document library. It is read-only, it takes no actions, it touches no money, and for those reasons it has sailed through two review gates already. In the third review you ask what happens when the library holds both the current protocol and the one it replaced in March, and the room goes quiet. Someone offers to add an LLM-as-judge scorer over a sample of answers. Everyone likes this idea, and the meeting starts to wrap up.
SCENARIOS.task: Score this failure mode properly and say what has to change, including why the proposed scorer is the wrong answer.
SCENARIOS.model:
Score it before anyone proposes anything. Severity 9: a nurse acting on a superseded protocol is patient harm and a reportable event, and read-only systems can absolutely cause it — no action surface is required to be dangerous. Likelihood 6: the library holds every version, superseded documents read almost identically to current ones, and retrieval has no opinion about time. Detectability 9, which is the number that ends the discussion. The answer is fluent, cites a real document, quotes it accurately, and the document genuinely exists in the library. No reviewer scanning outputs flags it. It surfaces when a patient outcome triggers a chart review, months later. RPN 9 x 6 x 9 = 486.

Now the scorer. Follow it one step: to judge staleness, the scorer must know which protocol version is effective for that unit on that date. That means resolving protocol_id plus effective_date against a registry — a deterministic lookup. Which is the whole point: if you can build the detector, build the answer instead. The moment that lookup exists and is reliable, you do not need the model for the question and you certainly do not need it to be graded by a second model on 3% of traffic days later.

So the change is structural. Retrieval is filtered at query time to documents whose effective range covers today, superseded versions are excluded from the index the assistant reads rather than ranked below current ones, and every answer carries the protocol version and effective date on the face of it so a human can see the freshness without asking. Post-change, the mode's likelihood is not reduced, it is zero — the surface is gone. RPN 486 to 0.

Keep the sampler if you like, but for over-abstention, not for this. This row was never a monitoring row.
pts: Scores all three dimensions with justification, and identifies detectability around 9 as the score that removes mitigation from the menu
Rejects the sampler with the specific reason: its oracle, once built, is the correct answer
Proposes a structural fix (effective-date filtering at retrieval, superseded versions excluded) rather than a detection mechanism
Notes that a read-only system with no action surface can still carry severity 9, so tier and severity are independent axes
States the post-change likelihood as zero because the surface is removed, not merely reduced by a control

SCENARIOS.title: The queue that made everything slower
SCENARIOS.sit: You have been handed another team's design doc to review before it goes to the architecture board. It is a document-summarisation service, 15,000 documents a day, tail-heavy Monday traffic. The design reads: "All requests enter a durable queue to absorb bursts. Workers pull from the queue; the pool autoscales on queue depth up to 60 workers, targeting 92% utilisation for cost efficiency. If the primary provider returns errors, traffic fails over automatically to a secondary provider. Under sustained load we will degrade gracefully." The p95 latency target is 8 seconds. Every sentence sounds reasonable. The team has asked for a rubber stamp.
SCENARIOS.task: Review this design: find the flaws, rank them by how much damage they do, and say what you would change.
SCENARIOS.model:
Four flaws, ranked by damage.

One, the uncapped queue is the worst thing here and it is presented as the safety feature. A queue creates no capacity; it converts refusal into waiting. With no depth cap and no admission rule, when arrivals exceed service rate the backlog grows without bound and every request inherits the accumulated delay — so the median user gets slower specifically so that nobody is refused. Against an 8-second p95 target this is fatal: a 60-second backlog means every request misses, not the marginal ones. Fix: a depth cap derived from the p95 target and service time (at 3 seconds a task and 60 workers, a queue deeper than about 160 already guarantees a miss), plus admission control that refuses immediately with a retry-after at the boundary.

Two, targeting 92% utilisation is a latency decision described as a cost decision. The queueing curve is asymptotic near saturation — the difference between 79% and 93% is roughly a twentyfold change in mean wait at fixed load. Targeting 92% means the autoscaler is aiming at the cliff. Fix: target 70-75% and state the p95 cost of the alternative in the doc.

Three, autoscaling on queue depth is a lagging signal that will oscillate. Depth rises only after the wait has already been incurred, so the pool arrives late and then overshoots. Scale on arrival rate with depth as a secondary, and add hysteresis.

Four, automatic failover to an unevaluated secondary. Failover preserves availability and says nothing about quality — a silent 200 at fleet scale. Run the secondary against the golden set, record the delta, and make failover a rung with a known quality cost.

And "degrade gracefully" is not a design. Five rungs, five fields each, with a named pre-authorizer.
pts: Identifies the uncapped queue as the primary flaw and explains that a queue redistributes delay rather than creating capacity
Connects the 92% utilisation target to the asymptotic queueing curve and quantifies the latency cost against the stated p95 target
Flags queue depth as a lagging autoscaling signal that produces oscillation, and proposes a leading signal with hysteresis
Catches the unevaluated failover target as a quality incident hiding inside a capacity save
Ranks the findings by damage rather than listing them, and replaces "degrade gracefully" with five specified rungs including the pre-authorizer

SCENARIOS.title: The 60-day deprecation notice
SCENARIOS.sit: You lead platform for a claims-triage assistant. On 2026-09-01 your provider announces the model you launched on reaches end of life in 45 days. Traffic is 12,000 triage tasks a day, measured task success is 88%, and a 2-point drop would push you below the accuracy commitment in three enterprise contracts. The team's instinct is to swap the model, run the golden set, and ship the following week. The golden set was last refreshed nine months ago and covers the English intake flow; a bulk-upload workflow shipped in April now carries about 30% of daily volume and appears in none of the eval cases.
SCENARIOS.task: Produce the rollout plan: which rungs, what sample, what schedule, and what you have agreed not to detect.
SCENARIOS.model:
Schedule backwards from the kill date. At an 88% baseline, detecting a 2-point drop at 80% power and alpha 0.05 needs about 4,438 scored tasks per arm. Score the whole canary cohort during rollout: a 10% cohort yields 1,200/day, so the 10% stage runs 4 days, and 50% clears in one. Ladder 5 days, ramp 3, shadow 4, offline eval 3, buffer 5, total 20 days against 45 available. Comfortable, which is the trap, because the eval set is the binding constraint, not the calendar.

The golden set covers 70% of traffic. Offline eval on it cannot see the bulk workflow at all, so a rung that is supposed to be your cheapest filter is silently scoped to the minority of your users. Refresh it first: sample 300 bulk-workflow traces, label, write a judge, baseline the current model, about 10 working days. New total 30 days, still inside 45, with 15 days of slack. Start on 2026-09-08 and the plan lands on 2026-10-08, eight days before the kill date.

Rollback trigger, written now: scored task success below 86% over any rolling 1,000 scored tasks, pulled by the assistant on-call without convening anyone. Blind spots to state in the doc: shadow cannot see user behaviour, and 4,800 exposures at the 10% stage leaves you unable to claim you would have seen a failure rarer than about 1 in 1,600.
pts: Schedules backwards from the kill date so the start date is derived, not chosen
Computes sample per arm from baseline and minimum detectable effect, then derives days at each percentage
Identifies the stale golden set as the binding constraint and refreshes it before the ladder, while slack still exists
Writes the rollback trigger as a metric, a threshold, a window and a named puller
States the blind spots explicitly: what shadow cannot see, and the rare-failure rate the exposure count cannot cover

SCENARIOS.title: The customer who exercised deletion
SCENARIOS.sit: An enterprise customer of your document-assistant product submits an erasure request covering one of their departed employees. You have 30 days. The architecture diagram on the wall shows three boxes. The actual system has eight places the person's data reached: the source document store, a change stream, a chunk staging bucket, the vector index, a summary table built nightly, a semantic cache with a 6-hour TTL, per-user agent memory files written by an extraction job, and a trace store with 180-day retention. The spec card sets freshness tolerance at 30 minutes. Legal has asked for written confirmation, and nobody can currently produce it.
SCENARIOS.task: Design the deletion architecture and give legal a number they can sign.
SCENARIOS.model:
Build the register before touching code: eight rows, seven columns each, source, staleness, invalidation, rebuild time, rebuild cost, tenant key, deletion path. Then trace one record. Source store deletes immediately. The change stream emits a tombstone but retains the pre-image for its window. The index accepts delete-by-filter, reclaimed at the next merge, measured lag 90 minutes, which is 3x the 30-minute freshness contract and worth recording. Everything else fails: staging bucket has a lifecycle rule and no path, the summary table has no tenant key so a scoped delete cannot be expressed, the cache serves for up to 360 minutes, 12x over contract, memory files carry no identifier at all, and traces persist 180 days. Three of eight can receive a deletion; two of the survivors never expire.

Fix order is by unboundedness, not by visibility. Memory files: add owner front matter plus a delete-by-owner sweep, 3 engineer-days. Summary table: add the tenant key and a scoped delete, 2 days. Cache: tombstone-driven invalidation replacing the TTL, 1 day, dropping serving-path exposure from 360 minutes to under a minute. Staging lifecycle from 90 days to 7, one hour. Traces: shorten retention to 30 days and add a subject-scoped purge, 1 day. About 7 engineer-days, roughly 1.5 engineer-weeks, plus a quarterly synthetic-record test that proves the sweep still works.

What legal signs is the register plus the test result, not an assurance. The number is: all eight reached, worst residual exposure 7 days, serving path under 60 seconds.
pts: Builds the register first and traces one real record through every store rather than reasoning from the diagram
Counts survivors explicitly and treats that fraction as the finding
Distinguishes TTL as a damage bound from a real invalidation path, and quantifies the breach against the spec card
Prioritises unbounded stores over visible ones, and names the store with no tenant key as unable to express a scoped delete
Prices the fix in engineer-days and proposes a recurring proof, so legal signs evidence rather than an assurance

SCENARIOS.title: The abstraction that leaked both vendors
SCENARIOS.sit: Two years ago your team wrapped its retrieval vendor behind an internal interface so a swap would be easy. The interface now has 19 methods, six of which exist only because vendor B supports something vendor A does not. A grep finds the vendor's SDK imported in six files outside the adapter. Maintaining the wrapper, tracking vendor features, and keeping its conformance tests green costs roughly 5 engineer-weeks a year. Nine eval suites exist and re-baselining them is manual, about 20 hours each. A staff engineer has proposed a rewrite of the wrapper. Renewal is in four months and the contract runs three years.
SCENARIOS.task: Decide what to do with the wrapper, with the arithmetic that supports it.
SCENARIOS.model:
Compute exit both ways before arguing design. With the wrapper: coupling is small on paper but six files import the SDK directly, so real coupling is about 2.2 engineer-weeks, re-derivation 0.6, revalidation 9 suites x 20h = 180h = 4.8 weeks. Exit 7.6 weeks. Delete the wrapper and go raw: coupling rises to about 3.0, everything else identical. Exit 8.4 weeks.

So the wrapper saves 0.8 engineer-weeks at exit and costs 5 a year. Break-even is 0.8/5 x 12 = 1.9 months, against a 36-month commitment. It is not a close call, and rewriting it makes the arithmetic worse by adding cost to an asset that already loses. It is a union abstraction: 19 methods spanning both vendors' feature sets, forbidding nothing, and leaking through six import sites. If you cannot name what an abstraction forbids, it is a second SDK.

Now read where the number actually lives. Revalidation is 4.8 of 7.6 weeks, 63%, and it is invariant to seam placement because the suites are yours either way. Build a re-baseline harness instead: roughly 3 engineer-weeks once, cutting 20 hours per suite to about 7, which drops revalidation to 1.7 weeks and total exit to 5.3 weeks, for every vendor, permanently.

Recommendation: delete the wrapper, ban the SDK outside a four-method boundary, spend the rewrite budget on the re-baseline harness, and stop paying 5 weeks a year for 0.8 weeks of optionality.
pts: Computes exit cost with and without the wrapper before discussing design, and quotes the difference in engineer-weeks
Derives break-even from saving over annual carry and compares it against the contract term
Names the union-abstraction failure using the test of what the interface forbids, not its size
Identifies revalidation as the dominant, seam-invariant term and redirects investment there
Rejects the rewrite explicitly and proposes a smaller boundary plus an enforcement rule instead

SCENARIOS.title: The re-index nobody budgeted
SCENARIOS.sit: You are reviewing another team's architecture document for a knowledge assistant before it goes to a design review. It promises quarterly chunking experiments and monthly embedding evaluation. The corpus is 3.4M documents averaging 1,100 tokens. The doc states that index rebuilds run in place during a 2-hour maintenance window, that the cache's 12-hour TTL is the invalidation strategy, and that deletion is handled by delete-by-filter on the index. The nightly summary table has no tenant key. The golden set is described as refreshed as needed. Spec card freshness tolerance is 20 minutes. Measured full rebuild time is 14 hours and last year's re-derivation budget was spent on one run.
SCENARIOS.task: Find the flaws, rank them, and say which single change you would require before this document is approved.
SCENARIOS.model:
Five flaws, ranked by what you cannot recover from.

1. Deletion fan-out is one store deep. Delete-by-filter reaches the index; the summary table has no tenant key, so a scoped erasure cannot even be expressed, and the cache and any memory or trace stores are unaddressed. This is the only flaw with a statutory deadline attached, and it is unbounded, so it ranks first regardless of engineering elegance.

2. The rebuild is physically impossible as described. 14 hours measured against a 2-hour window. In-place rebuild is not an option, so the document needs dual-index cutover with a bounded two-truths window and a resumable, content-hash-keyed backfill. Without it, no experiment in the document can actually be executed.

3. The experiment cadence is fiction. 3.4M x 1,100 tokens is 3.74 billion tokens, but embedding is rounding error. Verification and eval re-baselining dominate a run, and last year's budget covered one. Subtract the mandatory model upgrade and the discretionary allowance is zero, against four quarterly experiments promised. Say the number in the review before the roadmap does.

4. TTL recorded as invalidation. 720 minutes against a 20-minute tolerance is 36x over contract, and a deleted record stays servable for the rest of the window.

5. Golden set refreshed as needed means every migration rung is unmeasurable, and it will surface when a deprecation clock is shortest.

The single required change before approval: a derived-state register with a measured staleness and a deletion path per store. Everything above is a row in it.
pts: Ranks by unbounded and statutory exposure first, not by engineering interest or by order in the document
Catches that measured rebuild time exceeds the stated window, making the in-place plan unexecutable
Computes the re-derivation budget and contrasts the affordable cadence with the promised one
Identifies TTL-as-invalidation and quantifies the breach against the spec card's freshness tolerance
Names one required artifact, the derived-state register, rather than a list of fixes

SCENARIOS.title: The gate with no authority
SCENARIOS.sit: Priya is staff engineer on a contract-review assistant: 220,000 tasks a month, p95 budget 2,500ms against a measured base of 2,150ms, cost ceiling $0.018 per task against a base of $0.0134, quality bar under 1% wrong clause summaries. Her team's quality plan for the quarter is one line: "add faithfulness evals." Pressed for detail, they mean a model-based grounding check on every response, measured at 620ms p95, $0.0031 per task, with a 1.8% false-block rate on their audit sample. The team also has an eval suite that runs on every release and posts a score to the pull request. It has never failed a build. Nothing is on fire; she has to commit to a quality design this week.
SCENARIOS.task: Design the control-point placement that fits her envelope, assign each one an authority - and say what happens to the CI suite.
SCENARIOS.model:
Headroom first: 2,500 - 2,150 = 350ms. The proposed gate measures 620ms, so the inline version is dead in one line. Note that cost was never the binding constraint: $0.0134 + $0.0031 = $0.0165 against an $0.018 ceiling, so it would have fit on money. Latency is what rules it out, and saying which constraint binds is half the value of the analysis.

Then price the false blocks, because nobody has. 1.8% of 220,000 is 3,960 good answers refused per month. Against the current ~1% escape rate the gate would cut wrong summaries from about 2,200 to about 570, preventing roughly 1,630 bad answers while creating 3,960 refusals. It generates more incidents than it prevents, before you count the p95 breach.

The placement that fits: (1) a deterministic output rail - required envelope plus every cited clause id present in the retrieved set - in tens of milliseconds, authority block_response, owner product. (2) Async sampling, with the rate chosen by detection lag rather than by roundness: 7,333 tasks a day, a regression on 0.5% of traffic is 37 a day, and at 5% sampling with 0.75 recognition you see 1.37 a day, so an 8-event alarm fires in about 5.8 days. At 1% it takes 29 days. Take 5%: 11,000 scored tasks a month at $0.0031 is $34, and zero milliseconds on the request path. Authority open_ticket, pages the quality rotation.

(3) The CI suite: give it authority block_release with a stated threshold, or delete it. Today it is record-only while the team believes it is a gate, which is the most expensive state a check can be in.
pts: Computes headroom (350ms) against the gate's measured 620ms and names latency, not cost, as the binding constraint
Prices the false blocks as a count (3,960/month) and compares it to the ~1,630 wrong answers prevented, rather than quoting 1.8%
Places a deterministic rail inline and moves semantic checking off the request path, preserving headroom for future needs
Derives the sampling rate from a detection-lag division (5% gives ~5.8 days, 1% gives ~29) instead of picking a round number
Names the CI suite's real authority as record-only and forces the choice: give it block_release with a threshold, or delete it

SCENARIOS.title: The eleven-day review queue
SCENARIOS.sit: Marcus is principal engineer on a three-person AI platform team serving eight product teams. Every prompt change routes through platform review: 9 changes per team per month, about 45 minutes of reviewer attention each. Each reviewer can give roughly 270 minutes a week to review before their own roadmap slips, across a 13-week quarter. Median time from review request to merge is now eleven days, and two product leads have escalated. The org is adding roughly one product team per quarter. Marcus's director has offered to fund two more platform engineers to clear the queue, and wants an answer by Friday.
SCENARIOS.task: Decide what to change, and show with numbers why hiring reviewers is the wrong lever.
SCENARIOS.model:
Capacity: 3 x 270 x 13 = 10,530 reviewer-minutes per quarter. Demand: 8 teams x 9 changes x 3 months x 45 minutes = 9,720. Utilisation 0.92, and at a one-day service time the M/M/1 approximation gives 0.92 / 0.08 = about 12 days of waiting, which matches the observed eleven. Break-even is 10,530 / 1,215 = 8.7 teams, so they crossed into the painful zone a quarter ago and nobody noticed because headcount hadn't changed.

Two reviewers raise capacity to 17,550, moving break-even to 14.4 teams. At one team per quarter that buys about six quarters and costs two engineers permanently, and the queue returns on a known date. Reviewers buy linear headroom; they don't change the slope.

The lever that changes the slope: classify the 9 monthly changes by reversibility. A prompt change behind the traffic choke point, with eval coverage above threshold and no new tool grant, is reversible in one revert and should never have required a human. A change that grants a new irreversible action, or moves a route's budget, is the kind that genuinely deserves an approver. In their data that split is roughly 7 to 2. Convert the seven into an interface contract a CI job checks: required trace fields present, budget declared for the route, eval coverage above the threshold, no new irreversible action in the tool manifest. Remaining human demand: 8 x 2 x 3 x 45 = 2,160 minutes, utilisation 0.21, wait about a quarter of a day, break-even near 39 teams.

Same three people, four times the runway, and the human review that remains is the approver role on irreversible changes rather than a style review of prompts.
pts: Computes utilisation (9,720 / 10,530 = 0.92) and connects it to the observed eleven-day wait through queueing, not through effort
Shows hiring moves break-even from 8.7 to 14.4 teams - roughly six quarters at the current growth rate - and names it as linear headroom
Splits the review population by reversibility, and argues that a change revertible in one commit behind the choke point never needed a human
Specifies the interface contract as machine-checkable items (trace fields, declared budget, eval coverage, no new irreversible action)
Recomputes after automation (utilisation 0.21, break-even near 39 teams) and states that contracts change the slope while reviewers move the date

SCENARIOS.title: The 2am quality page
SCENARIOS.sit: Dana is architect at a healthcare scheduling company, six weeks from launching an AI intake assistant at roughly 9,000 tasks a day. Today a single rotation - four infrastructure engineers - receives every page for the service. The quality design is already agreed: an input rail (block_request), an output schema rail (block_response), async sampling at 4% (open_ticket), and a canary quality comparison on every deploy. The degradation ladder has five rungs; rungs 3 through 5 visibly change what patients see. The alert definition currently reads "faithfulness_rate below 0.94 for 30 minutes", and the runbook attached to it reads, in full, "investigate". Nothing is broken yet.
SCENARIOS.task: Design the paging split: which alert goes to which rotation, on what window, with what runbook.
SCENARIOS.model:
Start with whether the alert can even fire honestly. 4% of 9,000 is 360 scored tasks a day, or about 7.5 in a 30-minute window. The standard deviation of a proportion at p=0.94 with n=7.5 is sqrt(0.94 x 0.06 / 7.5) = 0.087, so a single 30-minute window cannot distinguish 0.94 from 0.85. That alert will fire on noise, get acknowledged twice, and be tuned into silence within a month. Widen the window to 6 hours (n = 90, sd = 0.025) or raise sampling on the intake route specifically. Choose the window from the arithmetic, then write it down.

Then split the rotations, because "the API is slow" and "the answers got worse" need different skills and different runbooks. Availability rotation (infra) keeps: gateway error rate, latency SLO burn, rail service unavailable, provider 429 rate. Quality rotation (two product engineers plus one platform engineer) takes: faithfulness_rate below bar on the 6-hour window, canary quality delta versus control, judge agreement below its threshold, and - this is the one people misfile - a false-block-rate spike, which looks like an availability symptom and is a quality failure.

Runbooks, written now: roll back to the previous prompt version; compare canary against control on the same route; check judge agreement against the last human-labelled batch; pull degradation rungs 1 and 2, which the on-call is pre-authorised for. Rungs 3 through 5 change what patients see, so they require the named pre-authorizer from the ladder - the clinical director - which means the 2am action is a phone call to a specific person whose number is in the runbook. That decision is made now, in daylight, by Dana, and not at 2am by whoever happens to be holding the pager.
pts: Checks whether the alert can fire honestly first: 7.5 samples per 30-minute window, sd 0.087, so the threshold is inside the noise
Fixes it by widening the window (n=90, sd 0.025) or raising sampling on the specific route, and derives the window from the arithmetic
Splits availability and quality into separate rotations on the grounds of different diagnostics and different runbooks, not different people
Routes the false-block-rate spike to the quality rotation despite it presenting as an availability symptom
Pre-authorises rungs 1-2 to on-call and binds rungs 3-5 to the named pre-authorizer, so the 2am decision is a phone call rather than a judgement call

SCENARIOS.title: The doc that outlived its reason
SCENARIOS.sit: You've been handed another group's architecture document to review before their 14-month-old support assistant is extended to a second product line. It is thorough and well written. Spec card: p95 3,000ms, freshness tolerance 15 minutes, $0.012 per task, 400,000 tasks a month, peak multiplier 3x, blast radius "user-visible guidance, no automatic payout". Latency stages: retrieval 300, generation 2,100, faithfulness gate 700, serialise and egress 190. A derived claim-summary cache, rebuilt nightly, rebuild time 41 minutes. One FMEA row reads: stale policy document, severity 8, occurrence 4, detectability 9, control "alert on index age", class mitigation. The action inventory lists "issue goodwill credit", reversible: no, tier: auto, approver: none. Every rejected shape names a numeric binding constraint, and every degradation rung has a pre-authorizer.
SCENARIOS.task: Find the contradictions, rank them, and say which one you would fix before the extension ships.
SCENARIOS.model:
Four findings, and the ranking rule is irreversibility times whether it is happening right now - not the RPN score.

First: the action inventory contradicts the spec card. "Issue goodwill credit" is irreversible, runs at tier auto, and has no approver, while the blast-radius line four pages earlier says no automatic payout. This is the only finding where the system is currently doing something the requirements forbid, and because it is irreversible the damage does not wait for a threshold to be crossed. Fix today: tier moves to approve, with a named approver.

Second: the derived store cannot meet the freshness tolerance at any cadence. Nightly rebuild is a 24-hour staleness bound against a 15-minute tolerance, 96x over, and since the rebuild itself takes 41 minutes, no rebuild frequency fixes it. The fix is architectural - an event-driven invalidation on claim update - so it needs planning, and it is silently producing answers grounded in stale policy right now.

Third: the FMEA row is the same defect wearing a different hat. Severity 8 x occurrence 4 x detectability 9 gives an RPN of 288, and the control is "alert on index age", which is a mitigation on a proxy rather than an observation of the failure. Detectability 9 requires a structural fix, and the structural fix is finding two's invalidation path. Merging them makes the roadmap shorter, which is worth saying out loud.

Fourth: the budgets don't sum. 300 + 2,100 + 700 + 190 = 3,290ms against a 3,000ms p95, over by 290 before any queueing at the declared 3x peak. It ranks last only because it is bounded, user-visible and self-announcing: the SLO will tell them.

And say what's good, or the review gets discounted: every rejection names a numeric constraint, and every degradation rung has a pre-authorizer. Both are rarer than they should be.
pts: Finds all four contradictions, each as a disagreement between two artifacts rather than as a flaw in one
Ranks by irreversibility and whether it is currently happening, and states that ranking rule explicitly rather than sorting by RPN
Puts the auto-tier irreversible action first because the system is doing what the spec card forbids, and it cannot be undone
Recognises that the FMEA row and the derived-store finding share one structural fix, shortening the roadmap
Names what the document does well (numeric binding constraints on rejections, pre-authorised degradation rungs) so the review lands as a review rather than as a verdict
